en: *The Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra: Discourse on the Profound and Determination of its Meaning*, Fascicle Two.
Narrated by the Monk Xianyan, a recipient of the purple robe and Grand Master of Perfect Penetration and Realization of Principle at Kai Long Monastery in the Capital.

Regarding the phrase "exhaustively [explaining] the profound essence of the vast and expansive": the character *jin* (exhaustive) refers to the teaching (*jiao*), while all the remaining characters refer to the meaning (*yi*). "Vast" (*hong*) means great;
it is synonymous with breadth and encompasses all five teachings, just as the great ocean universally receives the hundred rivers. "Expansive" (*kuo*) means empty.

This is the profound meaning. It distinguishes itself from the nine schools, being like a celestial pond that uniquely possesses ten virtues. "Vast" (or "Mak") refers to the phenomenal dharma-realm (*shifenjiai*);

"Expansive" (or "Guo") refers to the noumenal dharma-realm (*lifajie*). When these two characters are combined, they signify the unimpeded dharma-realm of phenomena and noumenon (*shili wuai fajie*). When the deeper principle is considered, they signify the unimpeded dharma-realm of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).
Alternatively, when the four characters are taken together, they collectively expound the single true, unobstructed dharma-realm (*yiqizhen wuzhang'ai fajie*).
This is the teaching and its meaning as they can be applied.

Regarding the provisional and the real, the true and the responsive: when wisdom merges with the single principle, it is called "True" (zhen); when compassion accords with the myriad capacities [of sentient beings], it is called "Responsive" (ying).

When the fundamental essence is sublime while the manifested traces are lowly, or when the fundamental essence is lowly while the manifested traces are sublime, these are termed "Provisional" (quan). When the fundamental essence and the manifested traces correspond to one another, this is termed "Real" (shi).
Regarding the "forty-two assemblies": this refers to one assembly of those born together (*sahaja*), namely the Bodhisattvas;
and thirty-nine assemblies of those born separately (*visabhāga*), ranging from the Vajradhara deities to Maheśvara, the King of Devas.
This is because they comprise the assemblies emerging from within the seat and the assemblies emerging from between the eyebrows. Thus, forty-two is assigned to the forty-two stages.

As for the phrase "those summoned by the light from the mouth," this refers to the manifestation of the assembly of teeth and the light from the face-gate (mukha-dvāra) that summons the multitudes of the ten directions;
therefore, that sūtra states: "There were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms within ten billion buddha-fields."

Each [of these] was surrounded before and behind by assemblies of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds, who came together and gathered until they were seated cross-legged upon their thrones. Regarding the phrase "the light from the pores reappears," this also refers to this chapter;
it means that those bodhisattvas who had previously been summoned from the oceans of worlds in the ten directions...
Within every pore of Sākyamuni’s body there is radiance; within each ray of light appear immeasurable bodhisattvas.
All these bodhisattvas, amidst the atoms of dust, draw near to the Buddhas of the three periods of time and, through various Dharma gates, [teach them].
This refers to the transformation and edification of sentient beings. Furthermore, that sutra says:

"Having sat thus, from every single pore of the bodies of those bodhisattvas, there appeared all manner of jewel-colored radiances, as numerous as the atoms within the oceans of worlds of the ten directions.
Within each radiance, there were manifested as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten oceans of worlds."

Regarding the statement that "the *Chao* (Commentary) refers to the Perfect Sound (*yuan-yin*)," this distinguishes it from the teachings residing in the sense organs; it is called the "Root" (*ben*) because it is the source.
The subsequent passage in the *Chao* states: "The single sound universally responds; this is merely the root of the teaching, not the teaching itself. This is precisely its meaning.
As for the statement that "the Sūtra lists twenty [forms]," the first is named "Supreme Light Shining Everywhere" (*Zuishengguang Bianzhao*); its shape is like that of a *maṇi* jewel. It is...
The twentieth is named *Ratnārci* (Wondrous Jewel Flame). Regarding the phrase "forming the existence" (*yǒu*) and so forth, the Sūtra says:
"In each of these individual worlds, there are as many vast worlds as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields.
Alternatively, in the *Ekakusumasaṃcaya-parivarta*, the Sūtra says: "O Sons of the Buddha, the extent of each of those worlds is either the shape of Mount Sumeru, or like a river..."
The shape of rivers, and so forth, up to the shapes of various ornaments—there are as many such world-oceans as there are atoms.
This is from the text of the "Chapter on the Formation of Worlds," which consists of ten sections. As the sutra says:
"At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying: 'O Children of the Buddha, the world-oceans possess various distinct shapes and characteristics.'"
That is to say, they are either circular or square, and so forth, up to being shaped like the form of a Buddha.

There are as many such [worlds] as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds. As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha utters a single wondrous sound (because it is one *brahma-svara*), which is heard throughout the lands of the ten directions (because it is heard everywhere, pervading all in accordance with the nature of phenomena);
all various sounds are fully contained within it (because this one is many, for principle and phenomenon are fused); the rain of Dharma is entirely..."
Pervading everywhere (4), from each and every sound, they rain down the manifold rain of Dharma; (5) within the ocean of all speech, those Dharmas are each distinct;
(6) in all voices according to species, each is identical to the sounds of all sentient beings; (7) throughout all Buddha-fields, these sounds individually pervade every place;
(8) the pure wheel of Dharma is turned, and what is taught each reveals the meaning of worldly purity. In all lands, the spiritual power of the Buddha is seen.
Transformation. Hearing the Buddha’s voice as he preaches the Dharma (9. universally causing all to see and hear it), and having heard it, proceeding toward Bodhi (10.

each and every one attaining ultimate benefit)—possessing these ten meanings, it is only then called the "Perfect Sound" (*pariṣphuṭa-svara*). Within the "Chapter on Manifestation," there are further ten similes, which will be fully cited below.

Regarding the phrase, "The principal and its attendants, in their manifold layers, sing in unison throughout the ten directions": the first clause presents the thesis, while the second clause provides the explanation. The meaning is as follows:
what activity do these principal and attendant elements perform in their manifold layers? Therefore, the second clause states that they "sing in unison throughout the ten directions.

Those who possess power and sovereignty in preaching the Dharma are called "principals" (*mukhya*); those who lack such power and are not sovereign in preaching the Dharma are called "attendants" (*parivāra*). However...
Within this teaching of the Dharma, there is a distinction between the principal and the associates (*sahāya*). It is not that those who listen to the Dharma are called associates;

rather, as for the principal and the associates, they must together bring the task to completion. Since the principal preaches the Dharma, the associates must likewise preach it. How is this known? The subsequent commentary clarifies:

"Singing in unison throughout the ten directions. "Singing" refers to manifestation. Thus, Vairocana is the principal of the fruit, while the others are the associates of the cause. This is what is meant by "the locus of Vairocana."
The Hall of Universal Radiance. Beyond worlds as numerous as the dust motes of ten Buddha-fields to the east, there is a world called Golden Color.
Mañjuśrī comes from there as an attendant. One should ask him: "In the second assembly, did Mañjuśrī act as an attendant while the Sūtra was preached, or did he listen to the Sūtra?
If one says he listened to the Sūtra, it would contradict the subsequent sūtra; for that subsequent sūtra clearly states that Mañjuśrī preached the second [assembly].

Because they assemble. If it is said that [the Buddha] "preaches the sutra," why is it said that "listening to the Dharma" is called being a companion? From this, one knows that although the principal and the companions differ, they are equally preaching the sutra.
Regarding "layer upon layer" (chóngchóng): it means being adjacent and pressing against one another, signifying a great number.

"Ultimate" (jí) means to the limit. "The ten directions" (shífāng) refers to the furthest reaches of the dharma-realm. "Simultaneously" (qí) means at the same time. "Chanting" (chàng) means proclaiming aloud.

The meaning of this is as follows: the teacher and the retinue speak to one another in successive layers throughout the entirety of the ten directions, simultaneously proclaiming the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This distinguishes it from teachings given according to specific circumstances (*yathārhata*), which may be taught in some lands and not taught in others.

The Commentary cites one as the principal and the ten directions as its companions, even stating: "Therefore it is called 'layer upon layer' (*zhòngzhòng*). This is a brief, general explanation. The meaning is this:
among all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, any single one may serve as the principal within the *dharmadhātu*; [all] Buddhas and Bodhisattvas [are thus interpenetrating].
All serve as companions to one another; the principal ones are singular, yet they mutually serve as principals, reaching beyond measure.

The companions are likewise boundless, mutually serving as companions—how could one possibly know their number? Since both the principals and companions are infinite, they are layered and multiplied throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
When the principal speaks the sutra, the companions necessarily follow in speaking it. How could there be a single place where the *Avataṃsaka* is not being taught?

▲ Regarding the phrase "The characteristics of speech are still difficult to clarify," the following provides a detailed and specific explanation. ▲ Regarding the statement "This 'one' is also called an auxiliary (輔翼)":

when superiority and inferiority are equal, one may simply be termed a "companion" (伴). However, when viewed from the perspective of the inferior toward the superior, it is further termed an "auxiliary.
This refers to the eighteen perfections (*aṣṭādaśa-sampad*) within the Pure Land; the present assembly of Bodhisattvas constitutes the perfection of the auxiliaries. This is not—

This refers specifically to this realm. In the "Chapter on Names and Titles," the Bodhisattvas from other directions are categorized by the Commentary into six types of assistants (*parivāra*). Regarding the statement, "They are not called 'cause' as the principal and 'effect' as the attendant": Question: Within the Ten Mysterious Gates (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*), the Gate of Principal and Attendant states that whichever single dharma is raised as the principal, all other dharmas become its attendants.

Why is it not so here? Answer: This is because it is based on the specific meaning [of the context]. It is not that there are no attendants; rather, it is simply that they are not explicitly designated as such. Furthermore, the term "principal" is used here to signify the primary focus of the teaching, while the term "attendant" is used to signify those who support it. Therefore, although the relationship of principal and attendant exists, it is not explicitly named as such. This is because the intent is to clarify the central theme of the current section, and thus the terminology is employed accordingly. Furthermore, if one were to designate a single dharma as the principal, then all others would indeed be its attendants; however, in this case, the intent is to show that within the assembly of the Buddha’s retinue, each member—whether a Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Bodhisattva—possesses their own distinct qualities and functions, and thus they are not collectively designated as "attendants" to a single "principal. This is why the Commentary speaks of them as "six types of assistants" rather than using the specific terms "principal and attendant. This concludes the explanation of the "Names and Titles" chapter.

As for the phrase "not named as cause and effect," it means that while the relationship of cause and effect is present, it is not explicitly labeled as such because the primary purpose is to demonstrate the mutual interpenetration of the various assemblies within the Dharma-realm. Thus, the terminology is adapted to the specific pedagogical intent of the passage.

The same [applies here]. That [previous passage] refers to the meaning of reality as it accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), whereas this refers to the meaning of the formal characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*).

It is like a minister acting as a sovereign; it is not possible for a sovereign to serve as a subordinate assistant. If that is so, according to the commentary below, it says: "There are three types of principal and retinue (*maṇḍala*):

first, the principal and retinue of dedication (*pariṇāmana*), because when one cultivates roots of goodness, they are mutually dedicated [so that upon attaining Buddhahood, they become principal and retinue]; second, the principal and retinue of shared practice (*samāna-pratipatti*), because they cultivate practices such as meditation and precepts together; third..."
"Like the primary and its associates" (the two are both called "in accordance with nature," naturally encompassing one another). The commentary states:

According to what was said there, Vairocana and those bodhisattvas serve as primary and associate to one another in turn. Is this not a case of cause and effect mutually serving as primary and associate? The answer is:
This refers to their former time when they cultivated roots of goodness together and mutually dedicated them; now that one has attained Buddhahood, the others act as bodhisattvas [in his retinue].

Because they act as companions to one another, it is said that they alternate as "principal" (*pradhāna*) and "companion" (*parivāra*). This does not mean that cause and effect mutually serve as principal and companion.

Furthermore, this interpretation concerns the *vyavahāra* (manifestation) of the teaching; it is not that the cause is the principal and the fruit the companion. That [other] perspective is based on the nature (*dharmatā*), and thus cause and fruit alternate as principal and companion.
Regarding the statement that they are called "layered" (*chong-chong*) because they are adjacent and interpenetrate: this refers to the neighboring relationship between this realm and other realms.

"Adjacent. Whether as principal or as associate, they mutually pervade one another and are termed "interlocking. Regarding the statement, "As it is with the Buddhas, so it is with the Buddha-principals and Bodhisattva-associates":
Question: The various Buddhas and Vairocana are mutually principal and associate; why then say "as it is [with the Buddhas]"?
Since there is no such mutual relationship between the Bodhisattvas and Vairocana, why say "so it is"? Answer: This is stated in terms of...
In humans, there is none; it exists only according to the realm (*dhātu*). Why? It should be said that in this realm, the Buddha is the principal while the Buddhas of other realms are the associates;
in other realms, the Buddha is the principal while the Buddha of this realm is the associate. This is the mutual relationship between the principal and the associate regarding the fruit.

In this realm, the Buddha is the principal while the Bodhisattvas of other realms are the associates; in other realms, the Buddha is the principal while [the Bodhisattvas of this realm are the associates].
If a Bodhisattva of the realm acts as a companion, is he not indeed the principal of the fruit? This is the principle of the mutual relationship between cause and companion.

Regarding the statement, "The second refers to the one Buddha acting as the principal within the *śakrābhilagna* [jewel]," whereas previously many Buddhas were viewed as mutually acting as principals and companions to manifest the meaning of the "layered" (*chongchong*) nature, here a single Buddha is taken as the principal for the time being to clarify the meaning of the layered nature. This is as explained in the two middle sections of the preceding commentary.
Regarding the meaning: first, all seven are taken collectively as the pervasive subjects; second, each one is taken individually as the pervasive subject.
As for the phrase "like the vast sky," this explains that when the primary element moves, its attendants move as well.
For example, within the Western River (Xichuan), the moon is situated therein, with Mars about ten feet to the west and Jupiter about ten feet to the east.
Facing toward Dongcheon (East Stream), the stars and moon gaze at one another, just as they do above;

this does not mean that the moon is near Jupiter and far from Mars. Question: Since these [passages] speak of successive shifts upward, does it not contradict the statement that they do not reach the Tree King?
Answer: That [text] refers to arising where there was no prior arising; this refers to shifting where there was no prior shifting. Though the texts differ, the meaning is consistent.
The principle returns to a single path. Again, it was asked: "Is it only the realm of humans that is moved? The answer was: "The realm of humans is moved along with everything else.
This is very clear in the text of the *Chao*; let the student observe it for themselves. Regarding the statement:

"Thus, the presiding Buddha arrives at a location outside the number of lands equal to the dust motes of one eastern Buddha-field, precisely where his own original Golden World is situated"—this refers to the tenth [stage] of the dust-mote lands.

Regarding the "Tenth World Ruled by a Principal Buddha," it refers to the first world, the Golden World (*Suvarṇabhāsa*), and not merely to the tenth world within a number of worlds equal to the dust motes of a single buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*). Please reflect on this; please reflect on this. Question:
When the Principal Buddha arrives at that Golden World, is there still a Principal Buddha remaining in the original Sahā world, or is there no longer one?
Is there not? If there were a presiding Buddha, it would result in confusion, for the Bodhisattva Vasumitra and his retinue are also present in this realm.
If there were no presiding Buddha, then the statement that a presiding Buddha is universal would be incorrect, as he is absent from his original realm where the Golden Light resides.
The answer is: This point is also difficult; I hope you will examine it with care. However, I have merely provided this as a gateway for discussion.

It is the same. One should not raise an objection. Why? If one considers it from the perspective of non-transference, this world-realm has a Buddha as its master and lacks Bodhisattvas such as Vasumitra and his companions.
If one considers it from the perspective of transference, this world-realm has Bodhisattvas such as Vasumitra and his companions and lacks a Buddha as its master during that kalpa.
Thus, there is no confusion; transference and non-transference do not obstruct one another, nor is there any lack of pervasiveness. This is so.
Thus, the previous objections are all simultaneously dispelled. Regarding the statement that the presiding Buddha reaches the limit of the eastern direction:
it is asked, "Is there still further world-systems to the east of the presiding Buddha, or is there no further world-systems?
If one says there are more, how can it be said that he 'reaches the limit' (*kṣaya*)? 'Limit' means exhaustion. If one says there are none more, then the world-systems would have a boundary."
"Mañjuśrī should not come from the east. He replied: "There are further worlds. [The opponent asks: "If that is so, the subsequent objection is well-disposed;
how, then, is the previous objection to be answered? He replied: "In every location where there is a world to the east of here, a presiding Buddha must necessarily be present throughout."
Therefore, it is said "to the limit," which does not mean that the world has a boundary. For this reason, Mañjuśrī also came from the east.

Just as the gates of the vows of all sentient beings are inexhaustible, so too, as long as there are sentient beings—and since all who possess the Buddha-nature are without exception those to be converted—there will never be a time when the conversion of sentient beings is exhausted.
Thus, at the conclusion of his speech, he did not see Mañjuśrī coming from the west.

Regarding the phrase "coming from the east to approach the Principal Buddha," this is intended to dispel the conventional understanding of fixed spatial relations. One might fear that doubt could arise, thinking:
"The Principal Buddha is here in this Sahā world, while the Golden [World] is to the east. Mañjuśrī of that world comes from the east toward the west to approach the Principal Buddha;
yet now, by moving the Principal Buddha to the extreme eastern limit, he would have to pass beyond the Golden World. Therefore, Mañjuśrī of that world..."
From west to east, he approaches the central Buddha. Therefore, it is said that one ultimately does not see Mañjuśrī coming from west to east to approach the central Buddha.
Why? Because if the central [Buddha] moves, his attendants move as well.
Furthermore, it is said that one does not see Mañjuśrī passing before the Buddha to go westward toward him; this is because of the fear of outsiders...

A doubt arises: although Mañjuśrī is not seen coming from the west toward the east to approach the Principal Buddha, it must be that Mañjuśrī passed before the Buddha, turned eastward, and then returned westward to approach the Principal Buddha;

therefore, the *Chao* (Commentary) refutes this by stating, "Nor is he seen," and so forth, to indicate that when the Principal moves, the Associates also move. Fearing that this may not yet be understood, the text again provides an analogy for clarification, as follows:
A certain Dharma Master was performing a ritual in the marketplace. A monk from the eastern gate came to assist with the rite;
because he proceeded from east to west, the Dharma Master moved outside the eastern gate. Thus, the monk from the eastern gate must have come from west to east to assist the rite.
If it were otherwise, that monk from the eastern gate would have had to follow behind the Master.
Moving from the east and then toward the west to assist in that dharma, [the text] refutes these two common interpretations; thus the *Chao* (Commentary) says so.
Regarding the phrase "as if a person were to spread ten coins on the ground," etc.: Question: Previously, ten people were cited as a metaphor; why is it raised again now? Answer:
That was based on the successive arrival of the principal and the associates (*puruṣa*), whereas this is based on the primary and secondary relationship in a single instance. If...
Since the analogy of the stars and the moon has already illustrated one aspect [of the matter], the response states:

within the analogy of the stars and the moon, it has not yet been clarified that the primary Buddha is all-pervasive and that the attendant lands are secondary. Therefore, this is explained again. For example, when a person spreads ten coins upon the ground (this is the "marking"), it does not mean they have already finished spreading them across the ground.
To say that the central coin is the "primary" and the surrounding coins are the "attendants" is the application of these terms to the corresponding Dharma.
▲ Regarding the first coin: the coin placed against the east and west is called "middle" (*chū*).
Likewise, when the master and attendants who do not move from their original boundary face the master and attendants who each move toward the east and west, this is called "middle.
▲ Then, as for placing the second coin upon the first coin near the eastern edge: the meaning of this is that one uses [the second coin] again...
Regarding the second coin: how is it placed upon the first coin? Therefore, the commentary explains and establishes this by saying:
"Gradually approaching the east, one corner is unfolded. This is a metaphor for the second layer of principal and attendant [deities] each shifting closer to the east by one boundary.
As for the phrase "the Kaiyuan Tongbao and others all shift closer to the east by one edge," this demonstrates a single shift.
All are shifting. Regarding the fact that these coins, layer upon layer, press against one another and gradually approach the east:

the correspondence to the Dharma is as follows. Thus, the principal and its attendants press against one another, layer upon layer, all gradually approaching the east. From this, we know the eastern direction.
Every realm has its presiding Buddha, and every realm has its retinue; there is nothing that is not universally pervaded.

If, upon reaching the Golden World, there were only ten presiding Buddhas, the presiding Buddhas would incur the fault of not pervading all worlds. Why? Because each realm contains as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in a dust mote.
If they were to offer this defense, saying that one presiding Buddha [pervades] as many worlds as there are atoms in a Buddha-field...

Regarding the absence of the fault of non-pervasiveness: the primary presiding Buddha should move eastward to beyond as many world-systems as there are atoms in one Buddha-field, and [the other Buddhas] should be within as many world-systems as there are atoms in a second Buddha-field. Why? The *Chao* states:

"To the east, one world-system" would further contradict the principle of immediate adjacency. Furthermore, the case of ten coins placed near the west is likewise; they should be combined with the preceding primary [Buddha].
This shifts [the location] closer to the West. Other explanations, and so forth, likely do not accord with the correct principle.

Regarding the statement that "the first assembly, as it is, pervades the Dharma-realm in successive layers": Question: Are the Dharma-gates of the first assembly also taught in places such as the Universal Radiance Hall and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?
If they are taught there, why does the sutra state only that the first assembly was preached at the Bodhimaṇḍa, and not elsewhere?

[Question: Regarding the remainder: if he does not speak [of it], how can it be all-pervasive? [Answer: There are several interpretations. First, with respect to the Buddha’s virtuous power, it is said to be "all-pervading throughout the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*).

With respect to what the faculties perceive and hear, it is called the "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "It is merely according to what is seen and heard that one speaks of the distinctions between the initial attainment and the nine assemblies.
Second, based on the meaning of the perfect interfusion of the nature (*dharmatā*), it is said to be "all-pervading throughout the dharma-realm. Based on... [text fragment ends]
The meaning of the distribution of the marks of destruction is called the *bodhimaṇḍa*. Thirdly, regarding the meaning of universal integration:

within the *bodhimaṇḍa*, all locations of the *dharmadhātu*—such as the Universal Radiance (*Samantāvabhāsa*) and the Trāyastriṃśa heavens—are entirely subsumed. For this reason, being solely within the *bodhimaṇḍa* is itself pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.
The Sūtra, in order to express this integration, speaks of the "bodhimaṇḍa. As the Sūtra says: "The Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃbhava-lokadhātu*)."
Within every single atom, one perceives the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). If this is true even for a single atom, how much more so for a single location?

Fourth, regarding the sense of pervasiveness: it refers to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), which pervades all locations within the dharma-realm, such as the Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka*) Heaven and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Since the site of enlightenment exists throughout all such locations within the dharma-realm, including the Universal Radiance and Trāyastriṃśa heavens, it therefore resides solely in the site of enlightenment.
Dìchǎng says: "The First Assembly was also not universal. If that is so, do the presiding masters of the First Assembly and those of the other assemblies see one another?
If you grant that they see one another, it would result in confusion. If they do not see one another, how can it be known that [the assembly] is universal? Answer:

"If their characteristics are identical, they mutually negate one another and do not see each other. If their characteristics interpenetrate and both exist simultaneously, we grant that they see one another. Although this is granted...

They meet one another; there is a distinction between having power and lacking power, yet there is no confusion. If this is so, since it is said they lack power, they should not be called "leaders" (*nāyaka*). Answer:

This refers only to the lack of power in the sense of the "entrance through characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-praveśa-mukha*), and does not concern the lack of power in the sense of the "leader and attendant" (*nāyaka-parivāra-mukha*).
If considered in terms of leader and attendant, all become possessed of power, for each is paired with their respective assembly of attendant Bodhisattvas. Now, regarding this...
They enter into one another; their mutual formation lacks independent power because the principal Buddhas, when viewed from their own perspective, further enter into one another.
Furthermore, it is explained that perhaps that which lacks power becomes its companion, as they are identical in nature (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Since these two types of profound gates share the same essence, one should know by inference that if the teachers of the nine assemblies were mutually pervasive, they would lack individual power and instead become principal and companion. Therefore...
There is no confusion regarding other assemblies or other Buddhas; the others should be explained accordingly.
As for the statement, "Therefore, there are three or two bodies," this refers to manifesting the Buddha-body by way of time, place, and faculties, yet it is not fully evident.

Although this commentary is utterly empty and devoid of traces, the constellations and images within the sky of its meaning shine brilliantly. Master Zhaoming said: "The Great Image is hidden within formlessness;
therefore, it is seen by not seeing it. The Great Sound is concealed within rarefied silence;
therefore, it is heard by not hearing it. This is precisely what is meant here.

The commentary states: "Profoundly deep and beyond words. The first phrase directly points to the principle of wordlessness, which is the fundamental source; the second phrase points to the phenomena of speech, which are the derivative extremities.

"The ocean of teaching" refers to the teaching as the essential nature of the Buddha's voice; "the waves and ripples" refer to the teaching as the reflected images perceived by the faculty of hearing.

Alternatively, there may be differences due to the division of teaching and meaning. Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows: the previous mention of "tranquility" (*zhan*) is the negation of speech;

the subsequent mention of "tranquility" is the negation of the absence of speech. Fearing that neither might be simultaneously abandoned, one thus brings about the cessation of words (*wangyan*) to eliminate the traces of both the subject that negates and the object that is negated.

The intent is that the very phrase itself is utterly transcendent. As for the "ocean of teachings," this refers to the aforementioned principle-ground of the cessation of words. Its waves and ripples...
To speak of it in terms of the present moment is merely the secondary aspect of phenomena. If this is so, why is it called the "Ocean of Teachings"? The answer is:

because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of sounds and words is itself the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), and because, as the tenth [aspect], the essence of the teaching manifests clearly within the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
In the commentary, the phrase "The Great Image has no form" borrows terminology from Laozi, yet its intent refers to the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*).

It may be spoken by way of analogy, using the inferior to illustrate the superior. If even the essence of the Way (*tāo-ti*), which is shallow and near, is said to have no form, how much more so the True Dharma, which is profound and mysterious—how could it possess names or characteristics?
The character *xi* (rarely) concludes the preceding point of "no sound," and the character *wei* (subtle) concludes the preceding point of "no form. It is absolute.
I have doubly bound the two above; because the mind is free from agitation (the departure from signs), and because speech is free from conceptual proliferation (the departure from words).
Thus, in the *Nāgaśrī-parivarta* of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it says: "I wish to enter the city for the sake of sentient beings."
He went on his alms-round. Mañjuśrī said, "Go as you wish;

however, while walking, do not lift your foot, do not set it down, do not bend it, do not stretch it, do not give rise to thought, do not engage in conceptual proliferation, and do not conceive notions of paths, cities, towns, villages, or of men and women, great or small. Why is this? Because of Bodhi..."
It is that which is far removed from all conceptualizations; it is without high or low, without contraction or expansion;

the mind is utterly free from agitation, speech has ceased its frivolous proliferation, and it is beyond measure and number. This is it. Having personally entered the truth and realized the holy, what further need is there for extensive exposition?

The characteristics of words (teaching) and meanings (principles) are intended to disturb people. (To not accord with the fundamental Dharma is called "reversal"; to induce perverted understanding is called "disturbance.

This difficulty follows closely upon the preceding discourse on the ritual protocol, which is comprehensive and universally applicable throughout all four sections, as each contains these characteristics.

To say there is "no teaching" (no words) and "no demonstration" (no marks)—meaning either that there is no speech capable of teaching, or no meaning to be demonstrated—or that there is no teaching for those of initial capacity, or no teaching for those who have long practiced.
Regarding "indication by root" (*mūla-nirdeśa*) or "expression without sound": there is no indication by name or phrase.

As for the statement, "In non-existence, there is no duality," the meaning is that within the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), there is no duality whatsoever, such as internal and external, or self and phenomena.
As for the statement, "Non-duality itself is also non-existent," this is because one employs the trace of "non-duality" as a provisional means to eliminate the characteristic of duality.
Within the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), how could there be non-duality? Therefore it is said: "Non-duality is also absent.
To say that all phenomena are neither dual nor non-dual means that non-duality is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and non-non-duality is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
When it says, "If there were any kind of existence to be found," the meaning is this: within the principle of *tathatā*, if there were even a single type of existence...

If it were established that the characteristic of existence is truly existent, then one would have to admit that, in relation to it, there is a single characteristic of non-existence that is truly non-existent. Why is this so?
Because existence and non-existence are mutually dependent. The above was an explanation by way of contraposition. Hereafter follows the explanation in the direct order.
Now, since that characteristic of existence is not established as truly existent, it is verified that this characteristic of non-existence is likewise non-existent.

This is because they can truly be non-existent. Regarding the statement, "If there is nothing to be attained, the very phrase is severed," this refers to the two characters *kōng* (empty) and *kōng* (empty).
When these are divided into subject and object of negation, their traces are ultimately not exhausted. Now, to speak of "severing the traces" means that the nature is originally empty by itself;

it does not require further negation to accord with the ultimate principle. If this were so, one might argue that the aforementioned term "empty-empty" would have no beneficial function, as it still implies subject and object.
It is sent away, like a bird’s footprint in the sand. If it were admitted that [the teaching] is useless, why would there be any need to speak of it? Now, it is explained generally:

when sentient beings awaken to the Dharma, they cannot immediately penetrate the profound mystery; they must first proceed by way of gradual stages. Therefore, one relies on "sending away" and "brushing aside," just as in the contemplation of true emptiness and the severance of marks.

Only after distinguishing deluded emotions and revealing correct understanding through the three phrases and nine gates can one say that all is extinguished and non-reliant, thereby enabling realization.
The true emptiness of phenomena is for the most part like this; let the student understand it accordingly. Regarding the statement "based on the clear sky," etc.:

this is a metaphor for how star-images vividly appear based on the empty sky of the mind; in the Dharma, it refers to how the gates of the Dharma (dharmamukhas) clearly manifest based on the heaven of meaning. This commentary relies on the analogy of shadows to reveal the principle.
It is said that the stellar images of the Dharma-heaven are brilliantly radiant.

Regarding the statement, "If it is obstructed by words," this is because there are two kinds of non-words: first, obstruction; second, non-obstruction. These may be understood in their respective order.
Regarding the statement, "If it is obstructed by words, Śāriputra was rebuked," this refers to the middle fascicle of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Śāriputra said: "The Deva has stopped here."
The deity said, "Venerable One, I have known this for a long time. Śāriputra replied, "I too have been liberated for a long time.
The deity asked, "Venerable One, how long has it been since you were liberated? Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
The deity said, "Why do you, a venerable one of great wisdom, remain silent? The answer to liberation is that there is nothing [to be attained]."
Because of verbal expression, I am at a loss as to what to say. The deva said: "Verbal expressions and written characters are both the mark of liberation.
Why is this? Liberation is neither internal nor external, nor does it exist in between;
written characters likewise are neither internal nor external, nor do they exist in between. Therefore, Śāriputra, do not speak of liberation apart from written characters."
It is liberation. Why is this so? It means that all dharmas possess the characteristic of liberation; this is its significance.

As for the statement, "Speech does not obstruct speech," which was praised by Mañjuśrī, this also reflects the intent of the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality" in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
It refers to how the thirty-two bodhisattvas previously each spoke of entering the dharma-gate of non-duality, thereby manifesting it through words.
The principle still lingers within words. Next, Mañjuśrī says: "As I understand it, regarding all dharmas, there is no speaking and no discourse, no indication and no cognition;
it is free from all questioning and answering—this is the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
The preceding thirty-two [bodhisattvas] all relied on words, whereas Vimalakīrti subsequently remained silent and without speech to manifest the principle of non-duality. This, then, is...
There are no words. Therefore, Mañjuśrī praised Vimalakīrti, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

To be without even the slightest word or language—this is the true entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality. Thus it is said that when one is not obstructed by words, one is worthy of Mañjuśrī's praise;
this is precisely what is meant. It is asked: Vimalakīrti remained silent in order to manifest the sudden principle that transcends speech.
Question: Why do you say that [the teaching] does not obstruct words? Answer: It merely cuts off words of birth, death, and false conceptualization;

it does not obstruct words of meaning that accord with the True Gate. Question: Do words that accord with meaning refer to principle (*li*) or phenomena (*shi*)? If you say they are phenomena, then...

This would contradict the gate of its own reality, for the phenomena of the phenomenal aspect are fundamentally exhausted. If one were to speak of "principle" (li), it would again contradict this provisional [teaching], for principle fundamentally does not obstruct the phenomena of the derivative level.
Now, I say that while the text indeed employs that [passage from the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*], the meaning is somewhat different.
Thus, by using the text of the *Vimalakīrti*, the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka* is established; this is the height of subtlety. As for the statement regarding words and letters:

"Nature is detached, and thus words perish": the first phrase indicates; the second phrase explains. "Thus words" explains the preceding term "nature is detached," while "words perish" explains the preceding term "detached.
Alternatively, this meaning may be stated as follows: moreover, both the written characters and the true nature are equally detached from those two traces of "thus words" and "words perish.
Regarding the phrase "the flow of the eight tones," it may function as the subject (*tǐ*), the object (*yè*), or the instrument (*jù*), serving as a modifier for what follows.

It relies on the eightfold vocal modulations (*aṣṭāṅga-svara*). Or rather, it is the eightfold voice that is most excellent, easy to understand, harmonious, soft, unerring, not feminine, and whose majesty and wisdom are profound and far-reaching.
As for the statement: "The ultimate destination (the principle of non-utterance and non-characteristic is the fundamental source;
it is not distant [as phenomena arise unimpeded by words and signs]; when mental activity attains it, it is exceedingly profound [its limits being impossible to fathom]."—[End of] Upper Section.

The first phrase is concessive; the second phrase is subversive. [To say that] words and images (having words and having forms is the derivative end of phenomena) are not near (not obstructing the fundamental principle of wordlessness and formlessness) is for the sake of one whose numinous mind embodies this (realizing it through untainted, true wisdom) and beholds it directly (vividly manifest and worthy of contemplation).
The first phrase is concessive; the second phrase is subversive. Master Sengzhao said: "Is the Way distant? It is true in every encounter. Is the Sage distant? He embodies it."

This is precisely the meaning of "spiritual" (*shen*). As for the mention of "words and images" (*yanxiang*) above, it originates from the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*). The *Changes* states: "Words are that by which images are clarified;

having attained the image, one forgets the words. Images are that by which the intent is preserved; having attained the intent, one forgets the images. Therefore, those who cling to words do not attain the images;
those who cling to images do not attain the intent. Thus, to preserve the words is not to attain the images; to preserve the images is not to attain the intent.
Images arise from the mind; yet if one clings to the images, that which is retained is no longer the image itself.
Words arise from images; yet if one clings to the words, that which is retained is no longer the words themselves.
Thus, to lose the image is to grasp the meaning; to lose the words is to grasp the image. Now, these words are employed for this purpose.

Furthermore: The principle of the cessation of speech (the state of no-speech) does not mean cessation (it does not obstruct speech); the scripture of manifold arising (speech) does not mean arising (it does not obstruct no-speech).
Regarding the statement, "When the ordinary mind is fused, there is nothing to be discarded," this indicates that delusion is identical to the truth.
The sub-commentary below states: "To perceive the Buddha-mind within the ordinary mind is to fuse the ordinary mind. The scripture below says:
This means that all śrāvakas within the triple world are, in fact, the voice of the Tathāgata; this is the statement of Rongchang.
Had he not said these words, one might fear it would be thought that only the mind and speech of the Buddha are unimpeded with respect to principle.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “If it be such that a thousand gates flow secretly,” etc.: the two characters “if it be such” (*ruò nǎi*) are introductory terms.

As for the statement, “A thousand gates flow secretly, serving as the great source for all scriptures,” this refers to the unobstructed *dharmadhātu* expounded by this sutra, which possesses boundless diverse meanings;
however, because the preceding four faculties were not yet capable of receiving them in their entirety, our World-Honored One [taught] according to the suitability of those faculties.
Within the unobstructed dharma-realm (*anāvaraṇa-dharmadhātu*), the meanings of the Four Noble Truths and so forth are differentiated to form the teachings of the Hīnayāna and other vehicles.

According to the biased attachments of their respective limited faculties, these biased meanings do not exist; however, in terms of what is severed regarding the substance of those dharmas, the universal meaning does exist.
Since this still belongs to the unobstructed dharma-realm of this very sutra, it is stated thus. Question: What is the meaning of "fundamental" and "branch"? [The text here appears to be truncated.]

There are three [interpretations]. First, it is said that the *Hīnayāna* is the "branch" (*mā*) and the *Mahāyāna* is the "root" (*mūla*). As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Except for those who have previously practiced and studied the *Hīnayāna*" (and further):

"These ninefold teachings of mine (the *Hīnayāna* teachings) were spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; they take entry into the *Mahāyāna* as their root. This is [the first interpretation].

Second, it is said that the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) are the "branch" and the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is the "root. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: [as cited above]. This is [the second interpretation].
This refers to the fact that within the Buddha’s One Vehicle, three vehicles are taught through differentiation. Third, it is said:

the first four are the partial teachings (pianjiao) and are termed "branches," while the fifth, the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), is the "root. Therefore, the *Chao* states: "The *Avataṃsaka* is the source of all teachings. Furthermore, the subsequent *Chao* states:

This refers to the passage stating that "the first four causes exist [at their respective stages], while at the time of the fruit, they are all absent," and so forth. Of the two preceding versions, the others may be found in other teachings;
however, this latter version is unique to our own *Avataṃsaka*.
"Like the sea and its hidden depths," etc., refers to borrowing the metaphors from the "Appearance Chapter" (*Prakaraṇa*) to use their meaning as proof for the teaching.

Regarding the phrase "the nine schools," the *Zhengli lun* (Treatise on Correct Principle) states: The *Han Yiwenzhi* (Han Dynasty Bibliography of Arts and Literature) says: First, the School of Confucianism (*Rúliú*), which recounts the legacy of the ages of Tang and Yu and expounds the Way of Zhongni (Confucius);

Second, the School of Daoism (*Dàoliú*), which sets forth the virtue of Yao and Shun’s yielding of the throne and clarifies the protection afforded by governing from the south-facing seat; Third, the School of Yin and Yang (*Yīnyángliú*), which follows the heavenly calendar and celestial phenomena to reverently assign the seasons to the people; Fourth... [text continues].

1. The Legal Stream (*Fǎliú*). (This clarifies the imperial decrees regarding legal assistance and regulations. 2. The Roster Stream (*Wǔmíngliú*). (The correct listing of ranks and positions; it speaks of following procedures to accomplish tasks. 3. The Calligraphy Stream (*Mòliú*). (Pure ancestral temples and solemn sacrifices; nourishing the aged and bestowing benevolence.

4. The Diplomatic Stream (*Zònghéngliú*). (Receiving mandates and dispatching envoys; handling specialized responses and strategic affairs. 5. The Miscellaneous Stream (*Záliú*). (Harmonizing with the principles of great states; there are no matters that it does not penetrate. 6. The Agricultural Stream (*Nóngliú*).

(Exhorting [the people] to agriculture and sericulture, providing a detailed account of food and wealth. This is from the *Shishi liutie* (Six Categories of Buddhist Works). Regarding the mention of the *Fifth Sūtra* and so forth, these were translated during the Sui dynasty;
in the Qin translations, they correspond to the sixth. Regarding the phrase "first seeing my body," this refers specifically to the Bodhisattvas of Perfect Faculties (*yuan-gen pusa*).
At the beginning, beneath the Bodhi tree, I beheld my ten bodies—the unimpeded body of Vairocana Buddha.
As for the statement "those who hear what I have spoken," this refers to the Bodhisattvas of Perfect Faculties mentioned previously;

they heard the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as spoken by me, Vairocana, and all of them believed and accepted it—not a single one of those with perfect faculties failed to believe and accept it. If that is so, why [the deer]?
This refers to the revolving wheel of the Four Noble Truths. Thus, a sutra states: "Except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna.
The meaning of this is that it merely excludes those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna, as they are incapable of hearing this fundamental Wheel of Dharma.
All sentient beings with external, limited faculties have fully believed and accepted this;
thus we know that by comparing faculties to the teachings, since there are those with limited faculties, there must necessarily be limited teachings. Therefore, the *Chao* says what it does.

Now, at this assembly on Vulture Peak, I likewise cause those of the Small Vehicle who have come before to hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, so that they may awaken to and enter the fundamental *Avataṃsaka*.

This refers to the Buddha’s wisdom. That which is called "initially entering the Buddha’s wisdom" is already the *Avataṃsaka*; since one has already entered the Buddha’s wisdom therein, what doubt could there be regarding the principle?
This is because the teaching of initial enlightenment does not belong to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
His wisdom is all-encompassing and yet eternally still. Thus Master Zhao said: "The Sage possesses a vacant mind that reflects in profound stillness; there is no principle it does not encompass.

He holds the six directions within his breast, and his spiritual discernment is more than sufficient. He mirrors the myriad existents within his square inch [of the heart], and his spirit remains eternally empty.
This is precisely the meaning of this.

Regarding the phrase "The ancients said... and so forth, this refers to the refutation of alternative interpretations. The ancients took the single principle revealed by the four non-principles as the Greatness of Essence (體大);
they took the two mysteries of the subtle and the fine Indra’s net as the Greatness of Characteristic (相大);

and they took the wondrous gates of the sovereign freedom of spiritual powers, the identity of the extensive and the narrow, and the ten ages of concealment and manifestation as the Greatness of Function (用大). Question: Why is this?

Question: Do the two types of profound gates (xuánmén) constitute the greatness of the characteristic (*xiàng*), while the remaining profound gates constitute the greatness of the function (*yòng*)? Answer:

It is said that the two types of profound gates pertain to the meaning of original endowment (*běnjù*), whereas the remaining profound gates pertain to the meaning of newly manifested phenomena (*xīnxiàn*).

Therefore, it is stated thus. In reality, however, they mutually interpenetrate. Question: Since this master already allows for the non-obstruction of phenomenon and phenomenon (*shìshì wú'ài*), why does he not allow for the non-obstruction of phenomenon and principle (*shìlǐ*)?

[Objection: It is non-obstructive (*anāvaraṇa*). [Response: You grant that phenomena and principle are non-obstructive; why then do you cite this as a point of contradiction (*pratiṣedhya*) in your alternative interpretation? Now, I shall explain:
it is not that he does not grant this, but rather it was not mentioned in the text because it was intended to be the very point of contradiction.

Regarding the phrase "The *Chao* clarifies the characteristics of virtue" (*de-xiang*), one asks: Does this mention of "characteristics of virtue" refer to the characteristic of greatness (*xiang-da*) among the ten causes, or to the characteristics of virtue within the ten causes?
Question: Regarding the gates, what is the relationship between their similarities and differences? Answer: There are two interpretations. The first states that this is identical to that;

for instance, when the ten mysteries (*daśa-avyāhata*) are considered in terms of their inherent completeness, they belong to the gate of "attributes" (*de-xiang*), which is the "greatness of characteristics" (*xiang-da*). When considered in terms of responding to the faculties of sentient beings, they belong to the gate of "function" (*ye-yong*), which is the "greatness of function" (*yong-da*).
Therefore, the previous commentary states: "The second [interpretation] concerns the characteristics of the ten mysteries as the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai*)."
"Originally complete in itself" is precisely the meaning of the Separate Teaching (biejiao). That statement "originally complete in itself" refers to the gate of the marks of virtue (dexiangmen).
Furthermore, it says: "This [statement] regarding the marks of virtue is not the gate of the marks of virtue. Do not assume that because the names are identical, their meanings are not distinguished.

For example, when the Buddha’s realization is ultimate, it constitutes the gate of the marks of virtue; yet, how could the Buddha’s ultimate realization consist solely of the magnitude of the marks (xiangda)? This is because...
This understanding is incorrect. Furthermore, another analogy is presented to clarify the profound meaning:

it is like a sword in the world that, while originally within its scabbard, inherently possesses the three aspects of essence (*tǐ*), characteristic (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*) (corresponding to the "Three Greats" inherent in the text on the characteristics of virtue). When confronted with an enemy, it is put to use (as in the section on the "functioning of the root and karma").

Even so, the triad of essence, characteristic, and function remains entirely complete (the Three Greats are without deficiency). One should reflect upon this with careful scrutiny. The word "immediately" (*jí*) signifies that which is capable of realizing and capable of manifesting.

Regarding "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*): "stopping" (*śamatha*) is that which realizes, while "contemplation" is that which observes. Alternatively, the stopping and contemplation of the stages (*bhūmi*) are that which realize, while the stopping and contemplation prior to the stages are that which observe.
Or, the stopping and contemplation within the fruit are that which realize, while those within the cause—whether contemplation or otherwise—pervade both phenomena and principle.
Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "Although concentration and wisdom are manifold, they do not transcend two kinds. First..."

There are two aspects: phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*). To constrain them in a single place, there is no task that cannot be accomplished; this is the gate of concentration on phenomena. To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind, acceding with principle without wavering;

this is the gate of concentration on principle. Clearly penetrating the characteristics of phenomena is the contemplation of phenomena; skillfully understanding non-arising is [the contemplation of principle].

This refers to contemplation based on principle (*li*). Within the various sūtras and śāstras, some speak only of meditative concentration on phenomena (*shidìng*), while others clarify only meditative concentration on principle (*lidìng*);

the two types of contemplation (*guān*) are likewise so. Sometimes, phenomena and principle are treated as opposing entities, with calm abiding (*zhī*) and insight (*guān*) set in contrast; or, the contemplation of phenomena is paired with the concentration on principle.
As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Cessation is the non-apprehension of the mind, having brought all marks to rest;

contemplation is the observation of the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions. Alternatively, it may be that contemplation based on principle corresponds to meditative concentration regarding phenomena.
As the subsequent sutra says: "With a single mind unmoving, one enters the various dhyānas; realizing that objects are without arising is called Prajñā. Or, both may apply simultaneously, as follows:

It is said: "In meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the mind is held constantly on a single object; through wisdom (*prajñā*), one thoroughly understands objects as being identical to samādhi.

This is it. Alternatively, both may be extinguished, being neither concentrated nor distracted. Or, when concentration is present within contemplation itself, it is simply called "concentration," such as when contemplating the nature of the mind, which is called "supreme concentration" (*adhyātma-samādhi*).
This is it. Or, when contemplation is present within concentration itself, it is simply called "contemplation," such as when employing non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).
"Wisdom that contemplates is called *prajñā*. This is it. Alternatively, it is explained as "the union of the two," which refers to the illumination within stillness (*śamatha*).

Those who study should understand how these terms are applied to explain this passage. Question: Above, when explaining *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, their names were derived from their objects, referring to them as "phenomenal" (*dharma*) or "principle" (*tattva*).

If one discusses the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, how are phenomenal and principle subsumed? One answer is that *śamatha* constitutes the contemplation of principle (*tattva-vipaśyanā*).

[The question is: "Why do [some] take phenomena as the object of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and stillness (*śamatha*) as the object of phenomena, or take stillness as the object of principle (*li*) and contemplation as the object of phenomena? Why do [others] not take both phenomena and principle together as the objects of stillness and contemplation?

Answer: Because the text contradicts the general section on the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle; or because both stillness and contemplation have initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) as their essence.

Therefore, the *Xiàochāo* states: "All give rise to calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). The topical outline [classifies them] according to the three great aspects, stating that phenomena and principle are unimpeded.

Regarding the statement "the provisional and the real are unimpeded," etc., it means that the calm abiding and insight which penetrate phenomena are called "provisional," while the calm abiding and insight which illuminate principle are called "real."
This also refers to the individual phrases to clarify non-obstruction.

As for the statement, "If one correlates them separately with the three greats," this takes the mind of contemplation and cessation from the fourth phrase and correlates it with the objects of the essence and function from the preceding three phrases.
For example, correlating it with the first phrase: "Merging with the true essence" (which is principle, substance, and object), one gives rise to the fourth phrase, "eternal stillness."

(The cessation of the mind. The realm of myriad transformations. (Phenomena; function; the objective field. It gives rise to the fourth phrase, "universal discernment. (Contemplating the mind. It corresponds to the second phrase, "manifesting the marks of virtue.

(Phenomena; function; the objective field. It gives rise to the fourth phrase, "universal discernment. (Contemplating the mind. The gate of the double mystery. (Principle; essence; the objective field.
It gives rise to the fourth phrase, "ever-abiding stillness. (The cessation of the mind. It corresponds to the third phrase, "functioning in profuse arising."

(Phenomena; function; objects) give rise to the fourth phrase, "universal discernment" (which is contemplation of the mind). Because it is eternally thus (principle; essence; objects), they give rise to the fourth phrase, "constant stillness" (which is the cessation of the mind).
Therefore, the *Chao* states: "Each possesses its own essence and function, yet all give rise to both cessation and contemplation.

What is here called "contemplation" is contemplation that takes phenomena as its object; "cessation" is precisely cessation that takes principle as its object. This is entirely identical to [the section on] "arising."

"Faith," and so forth. Regarding the statement, "If one provides an explanation by means of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), etc.": the contemplating mind is divided into the three contemplations, and the contemplated object is opened up as the three truths (*trisatya*).

In opposition to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*) is opened; this belongs to the Greatness of Essence (*tattva-mahattva*). In opposition to the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), the Truth of the Conventional (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is opened;

this belongs to the Greatness of Function (*kāritra-mahattva*). In opposition to the contemplation of the Middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*), the Truth of Meaning (*artha-satya*) is opened; this belongs to the Greatness of Characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*). Question: [What is...]?

Among the three truths, the truth of meaning (*arthatattva*) is that upon which the other two truths depend. Among the three greatnesses (*trimahātmya*), the greatness of essence (*svabhāvamahātmya*) is that upon which the other two greatnesses depend.

Since these principles correspond to one another, why is it that the greatness of essence is the object of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇamahātmya*) is the object of the contemplation of the middle way (*madhyamaka-vipaśyanā*) within the truth of meaning? Now, the general response is as follows: when we speak here of the "three truths,"...
This does not take the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) as its object; rather, it takes the truths of the real (tathatā), the conventional (saṃvṛti), and the middle way (madhyamā-pratipad).

Taking the "greatness of essence" (svabhāva-mahattva)—which is solely the dharma-dhātu of principle—as the ultimate truth, one gives rise to the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā). Taking the "greatness of function" (karma-mahattva)—the dharma-dhātu of manifold phenomena—as the conventional truth, one gives rise to the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).

Taking the "greatness of manifestation" (lakṣaṇa-mahattva)—which pervades the four dharma-dhātus—as the truth of the middle way, one gives rise to the contemplation of the middle way. The three greatnesses together constitute the basis. Only then...

This is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the fundamental dharma of the single mind. Some say that the three greatnesses (tri-mahattva) are its function, while the ultimate truth is its essence (svabhāva).

Thus, two of the greatnesses are discussed separately from the essence and belong to the two truths of the real and the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya), whereas the greatness of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-mahattva) is discussed in conjunction with the greatness of essence.

This belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). I further hope for a definitive determination. Question: Regarding this Middle Way Truth (*madhyamā-pratipad-satya*), is it a conventional phenomenon (*saṃvṛti*) or is it the absolute principle (*tattva*)?
Answer: The Middle Way within illusory existence is the phenomenon; the Middle Way within true emptiness is the principle.
The Middle Way of mutual fusion penetrates both phenomenon and principle simultaneously. Question: What are its aspects (*ākāra*)? Answer: Because there are five stages. Question: Which are they?
Yes. First, the Middle Way of illusory existence; second, the Middle Way of true emptiness; third, the Middle Way of true emptiness manifesting as illusory existence;
fourth, the Middle Way of illusory existence returning to true emptiness; fifth, the Middle Way of mutual fusion. To facilitate easy understanding, these are presented in a diagram for illustration.
Regarding the statement that the three stops (*śamatha*) and three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) are fused into a single mind (*ekacitta*), it is asked:

Within a single mind, the stops and contemplations are distinguished, and the nine dharmas are clearly manifest; what are their modes of activity (*ākāra*)? The answer is: It is like relying on a single mirror to reflect the three images of beauty, ugliness, and the medium state appearing therein.

The images serve as a metaphor for the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*); this principle is self-evident. The clarity with which the image of beauty appears is like the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
The purity of the manifestation of beautiful reflections is like true cessation (*tattva-śamatha*). The clarity of the manifestation of ugly reflections is like provisional contemplation (*prajñā*).

The purity of the manifestation of ugly reflections is like cessation that accords with conditions (*anupratyaya-śamatha*). The clarity of the manifestation of neutral reflections is like middle-way contemplation (*madhyamā-prajñā*).

The purity of the manifestation of neutral reflections is like cessation free from extremes (*antadvaya-vinirmukta-śamatha*). These three reflections, three clarities, and three purities are distinguished according to their specific meanings; yet when one investigates their essence, they are ultimately [one].
This single mirror serves as a metaphor for the Abhidharma; let the student examine this in detail.

Regarding the phrase "the intersection of the true and the false, whereby one perceives the Buddha-mind within the ordinary mind": the first clause indicates a broad scope, while the second clause explains it in a narrower sense.

"True" refers to principle (li). (It is solely nature, not appearance. "Buddha" (is likewise). (It is solely pure, not defiled; it encompasses both nature and appearance. "Nirvana" (is likewise). (It is solely pure, not defiled; it encompasses both nature and appearance.

"False" refers to delusion (huo). (It is solely defiled, not pure; it encompasses both nature and appearance. "Birth" (is likewise). (It is solely defiled, not pure; it encompasses both nature and appearance. "Birth-and-death" (is likewise). (It is solely defiled, not pure;

it encompasses both nature and appearance. Regarding the statement that "the True encompasses the False and its derivatives": this is the gate of "principle-as-phenomena" (truth as events). Regarding the statement that "the False... [encompasses the True and its derivatives], this is the gate of "phenomena-as-principle" (events as truth).
"One who penetrates the true source" refers to the gate wherein phenomena (*dharma*) are identical to principle (*li*).

Regarding the statement that "there are no waves that are not wet," the first phrase signifies the penetration of the false into the true, while the second phrase signifies the penetration of the true into the false.

Regarding the statement that "the Tathāgata does not sever inherent evil" (*prakṛti-pāpa*), there are two meanings in the Hinayana teachings: first, the fifteen realms prior to the Buddha are outflowing (*sāsrava*) and arise [from conditions].

Because he was evil by nature, he gave rise to incomparable greed and incited the wrath of Aṅgulimāla. Another interpretation says this was a manifestation, for he spoke loving words to Rāhu and rebuked Devadatta;
thus, two meanings were initially taught. One interpretation says it refers to *tathatā* (suchness):
in the past, he took evil as his actual nature, and now, having reached the stage of fruition, although the evil phenomena have been severed, the evil nature remains ever-present.
Second, it is said that this manifests the same as the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) mentioned previously. The Final Teaching (Niṣṭhā-yāna) also has two meanings. First, it is said:

"In the past, True Suchness (Tathatā) followed conditions to manifest as the teaching of the Dharma; now, having reached the stage of fruition, ignorance (avidyā) has been severed. Although the characteristics of evil no longer exist,"
Because the true nature (dharmatā) persists in accordance with conditions. It is like still water that forms waves according to the wind;

when the wind ceases, the waves subside, yet the three natures that constitute the waves persist constantly. As stated in the *Nāgārjuna-śāstra*, the individual characteristics that follow [conditions] are not to be abandoned.

The second [interpretation] states: Evil possesses two meanings. First, the meaning of not destroying its characteristics while remaining distinct from the True [Nature] (this corresponds to the meaning of the existence of the characteristics of dependent origination).

Second, the meaning of being identical to the True [Nature] by virtue of conforming to its nature (this corresponds to the meaning of the emptiness of the essence of non-nature). Here, we rely on the latter meaning; therefore, it is said that evil is "not severed. The Sudden Teaching (*Dunjiao*) states:

The characteristics of evil are fundamentally exhausted and do not require further severance. The nature of evil is fundamentally manifest and is not something to be severed. The Perfect Teaching (*Yuanjiao*) states: It conforms to the nature.
Its evil is like fire in a mirror: it appears yet is always empty, for it is not something to be severed.

Although this applies generally to all five teachings, here we specifically take that which accords with the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhāyāna*) regarding the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*). Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "The Tathāgata does not have an evil nature."
Good and evil both take the mind-nature as their nature. If one were to sever the nature of evil, one would be severing the mind-nature; yet the nature cannot be severed.
This is just as the icchantika does not sever the nature of goodness. Furthermore, Nāgārjuna said: "It is like cutting down a sleeping man—how could it be that the man is not wounded?
If this is so, why does the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* state that the Tathāgata has no unwholesome [qualities]?
"Buddha-nature. Answer: That [text] relies on principle to treat phenomena as non-existent; this [text] relies on the inclusion of phenomena to maintain that they are not severed from principle.
Furthermore, that [text] establishes its name based on the present; this [text] establishes its designation based on the past.
Therefore, the texts of these two do not contradict one another. As for the statement, "Furthermore, within the Buddha's mind there are sentient beings," it is like the master’s mirror.
"I am that disciple. ▲ Now, regarding the "unbroken" (abhaṅga) aspect: first, there is the unbroken aspect of the sequential arrangement (saṃbhoga-vyūha).

Within the gate of sequential arrangement, sentient beings can possess Buddhahood (just as ore contains gold or raw jade contains precious stone), but a Buddha cannot possess the state of a sentient being (just as refined gold is no longer ore, and pure jade is no longer raw stone).
Second, there is the unbroken aspect of the sequential arrangement of the teaching. Upon hearing [the truth], one is immediately...

The Buddha is beneficial to ordinary beings (generating the aspiration for seeking). The Buddha is none other than the ordinary being; this causes people to produce false understandings (generating inverted understandings).

For this reason, it is simply said that by means of the ordinary mind, one perceives the Buddha-mind. Regarding the statement "because they do not depart from the single mind" (as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, among the ten reasons, because all things are manifestations of the mind alone).
Regarding the statement "falsehood is grasped from the True, such that there is no separate falsehood" (the gate of phenomena arising based on principle, as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*).

(From the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*): Regarding the statement, "The true manifests according to the deluded because there is no separate true," (this is the gate of phenomena manifesting principle;

it is the gate of the essence of truth being identical to phenomena, and the gate of phenomenal dharmas being identical to principle). This is because if the deluded were to exist apart from the true, then the principle would not be all-pervasive.

(Section on the Principle Pervading Phenomena through Reverse Explanation) Because there is no basis for phenomena if the true were external to the false. (Section on Phenomena Pervading the Principle through Reverse Explanation) However, some say that the false is empty and the true is real (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*);

some say that the false is existent and the true is emptiness (*Tri-satya-śāstra* and the meaning of the Two Truths); both are empty (the conventional explanation of the Two Truths, which accords with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*);

both are existent (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and *Avataṃsaka*); neither is affirmed nor denied (the meaning of negation that "all things encountered are the Middle Way"); both are affirmed (true and false both pervade the Two Truths). Or...

"Whatever is touched [in the text] all refers to the meaning of the internal and external. Regarding the statement that "the pure portion is identical to the True [Nature]" (meaning the untainted *paratantra* is identical to the *pariniṣpanna*), while "the defiled portion is delusory" (referring to the tainted *paratantra*), the phrase "because the delusion regarding the phenomena of the pure portion is not yet exhausted" means that the untainted *paratantra* is a phantom-like existence arising from conditions.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "All marks whatsoever are entirely empty and delusory. Furthermore, the sub-commentary below states: "It is as follows..."
When True Suchness manifests as the dependent nature, even if there is a pure portion, it is still termed "defiled. This is like a mirror manifesting images:

it makes no distinction between the pure and the impure, for neither is the essence of the mirror itself. Thus, it is called "pure" only insofar as it is capable of manifestation, while that which is manifested is entirely defiled.
This is precisely its meaning. Regarding the statement that "the pure portion (*śuddhabhāga*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) both exist":
the pure portion is the *mahāprajñā* (Great Wisdom) of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); the perfected nature is the Dharma-body of liberation (*vimukti-dharmakāya*).

Regarding the statement that "if one speaks of the two truths according to worldly convention, then both the real and the false are empty" (this is a discernment among the three truths, or perhaps the intent of the three truths, or the ultimate meaning of the Perfect [Teaching]): this is because false phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Emptiness. Because the true Dharma is without marks (*animitta*), it is empty. Alternatively, it is only through the mutual dependence of the real and the false that the names "real" and "false" arise, just like the concepts of long and short;
therefore, both are empty. Or, based on the substance of a handkerchief, one illusorily fashions the appearance of a rabbit (the substance is like the real, while the appearance is like the false).

If one follows the discourse of the deluded, both the substance and the appearance of the rabbit are empty (if one follows conventional discourse regarding the two truths, then both the real and the false are empty).

▲ Regarding the statement that if one considers truth and falsehood in relation to both truths (the two satyas), then both truth and falsehood encompass both emptiness and existence: First, it is said:

Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), both truth and falsehood are existent, because they are both illusory existence and real existence; within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), both truth and falsehood are empty, because they are both emptiness of nature and emptiness of characteristics.

Second, it is said: Within the conventional truth, both truth and falsehood are empty. (This refers to the previous point where, following worldly convention, the two truths were explained; thus, regarding truth and falsehood...)

[The state of] "both being empty" exists in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) where both the real and the false coexist. (Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "If both the real and the false are truly real, then the fundamental and the derivative are of one flavor, clearly interpenetrating.
