Regarding the statement that, according to the [Yogācāra] school, the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and so forth cannot achieve such interpenetration: Question: Both the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*) and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speak of mutual interpenetration;

why do you say it is not possible? Answer: One explanation says it is because of "internal [differences]" and so forth. This is not the same as the case of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the Three Treatises.
Treatise: How is this known? Because the character "equal" (等) is placed above and the character "tenet" (宗) is placed below. One interpretation states that it is also equal to that;

although that treatise and those sutras speak of mutual penetration, they are not the primary tenets [of our school]. Now, our *Avataṃsaka* takes the unobstructed Dharma-realm (*anāvaraṇa-dharmadhātu*) as its primary tenet;
thus the *Chao* says so. ▲ Regarding the statement that the existence of phenomena is precisely the non-existence of principle:

[Question: Regarding the meaning of "non-existent in principle" (*li-wú*), to which of the two natures—pervasive (*biàn*) or perfected (*yuán*)—does it belong? If it belongs to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), why is it called "pervasively conceptualized" (*parikalpita*)?
There are two senses: first, existence as phenomenal appearance (*qíng-yǒu*); second, non-existence in principle (*lǐ-wú*).

If it belongs to the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), why is it said that "existence as phenomenal appearance is itself non-existence in principle"? Does the false penetrate to the true? [Answer: The meaning has two approaches. If, with respect to existence as phenomenal appearance...
It is not of a single meaning. That which belongs to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the sense that [the ultimate] is not different from what exists as appearance (*yathābhāsa*).
That which belongs to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is the sense that it is not different from what exists as appearance. Here, we rely on the first meaning; thus the *Chao* says:

"Furthermore, 'true' is explained as belonging to the imagined nature, because within the imagined nature both the true and the false are included, unlike the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), where it is exclusively false. Regarding the meaning of "lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is to be understood accordingly.

This should be explained. Regarding the statement in this sutra that "there is a pure teaching concerning birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and so forth": the first half is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*).

That is to say, it establishes *nirvāṇa* in dependence upon the aforementioned flow of birth-and-death. Defilements (*kleśa*) are called "contention" (*raṇa*) because they disturb the side of virtue and cause harm to oneself and others;
thus they are named "contention. Because these contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are accompanied by and increase such contention, they are termed "with contention" (*saraṇa*).
Because there is that contention, that which is called "birth and death" (saṃsāra) has outflows (āsrava) as its essence. Because those afflictions (kleśa) are absent, it is termed "nirvāṇa.
The second half [of the verse] is a double negation, meaning that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are merely provisionally established names based on afflictions;
what reality could there be? Furthermore, because the two depend upon each other, both are empty; because the two negate each other, both are quiescent. The above two [points].

The two pairs of phrases both possess mutual penetration through existence; the two pairs of phrases both possess mutual penetration through emptiness. Alternatively, from the perspective of the meaning of "that which can subdue," there is mutual penetration through existence;
from the perspective of the meaning of "that which is subdued," there is mutual penetration through emptiness. Regarding the statement, "Therefore, Master Ying said," and so forth:
This is the preface to the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*. According to the commentary in the subsequent *Chao*, this passage contains four pairs of contrasts. Regarding the statement:

"Because of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); because [the latter] does not exist, there is no 'non-existence'": this constitutes the first pair, which establishes the locus of existence and non-existence. I speak of emptiness from the perspective of the ultimate truth;
this is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-śūnyatā*), which is not the same as the emptiness of non-existent things.

Furthermore, when I clarify existence according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), this is existence by way of conditions; it is not the existence of emptiness. Second, because it is ultimately real, it is non-existent;

thus, although non-existent, it exists. Because it is conventional, it is not non-existent; thus, although existent, it is non-existent. This pair clarifies the essence and characteristics of existence and non-existence:
it is the non-destruction of non-existence within existence, and the non-obstruction of existence within non-existence. Therefore, it constitutes the Middle Way.
The Way: though it exists, it is non-existent, and thus is not burdened by existence; though it is non-existent, it exists, and thus is not obstructed by non-existence.
This pair manifests the virtue of both existence and non-existence. If this were existence as a fixed nature, then this existence would be solely existence and could not be non-existence.
If this were non-existence as a fixed nature, then this non-existence would be solely non-existence and could not [be existence].

It is precisely because they exist that the two are now mutually identical; thus, there is no pervasive stagnation. The *Chao* states: "As for 'even unto' (*nàizhì*), it should be fully expressed as follows:
by not stagnating in non-existence (*abhāva*), the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) ceases; by not persisting in existence (*bhāva*), eternal attachment is forever eliminated.
How could [views such as] both or neither possibly arise? Since all extremes are utterly quiescent, it is said that 'all are transcended. This demonstrates..."

There is freedom from the faults of existence and non-existence. To be stuck in emptiness is nihilism; to be burdened by existence is eternalism. Since one neither sticks nor is burdened, there is no nihilism or eternalism.

Furthermore, regarding the first pair, because both existence and non-existence are abandoned, it is said: "there is no existence and no non-existence. This establishes the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the second pair, because existence and non-existence are not destroyed, it is said: "though existing, it is non-existent; though non-existent, it exists. This...

This constitutes the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*). Because the third pair clarifies that the two truths are mutually identical, one does not remain biased or stagnant in either existence or non-existence.
Thus, one is neither moved by the extreme of existence nor stilled by the extreme of non-existence, thereby accomplishing the contemplation of the Middle Way.

Master Zhao also said: "Engaging with existence, one never begins by being deluded regarding the void; therefore, one constantly dwells within existence without being defiled. This means that one is not burdened by existence. Not...
One grows weary of existence and contemplates emptiness; therefore, one constantly contemplates emptiness without realizing it. This is not to be stuck in non-existence.

The fourth [pair], which avoids error, follows the same principle as before. Furthermore, in the explanation of the first pair: the first member signifies the meaning of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while the second member signifies the meaning of wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara*).
The second pair signifies the meaning of both existence and non-existence. The third pair signifies the meaning of neither existence nor non-existence.
The fourth pair constitutes the four propositions for being endowed with excellence through the departure from faults.

Furthermore, the first pair departs from two faults: first, departing from existence; second, departing from non-existence. The second pair departs from neither existence nor non-existence. The third pair departs from both existence and non-existence.
The fourth pair explains the departure from faults in general. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "True Suchness has no marks of existence."

It is not the absence of characteristics (*animitta*); it is not the non-existence of characteristics; it is not the non-absence of characteristics; it is not the simultaneous presence of both existence and non-existence as characteristics.

This is precisely its meaning. Regarding the statement that "both the true and the delusive are true," one asks: while it may be logically consistent for delusive phenomena to return to the True, how can it be said that true phenomena also return to the True?
The answer is: the former mention of "the true and the delusive" refers to their essential nature (*dharmatā*); the latter statement that "both are true" [refers to their ultimate reality].

It is the True Reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, the "True" mentioned above refers to the truth that is contrasted with the false; the "True" mentioned below refers to the truth that transcends the false.
Moreover, the former is based on the gate of distinguishing characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*), wherein the truth subsumes the false.

Regarding the phrase "cultivating both phenomena and principle together, seeking the wisdom of the Buddha based on fundamental wisdom": the first part is the heading; the second part is the explanation.
"Based on the principle-wisdom of fundamental enlightenment" explains the cultivation of principle; "seeking the phenomenon-wisdom of initial enlightenment" explains the cultivation of phenomena.
The Commentary also states that those who are deluded, when practicing dhyāna, rely on the nature of wisdom, and so forth, concluding that these are all instances of biased attachment;

in meaning, they correspond to the "four illnesses. Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* (Dafangguang yuanjue jing) says that sentient beings practicing cultivation should distance themselves from the four illnesses.
The first is the illness of effort (*zuo-bing*): merely performing conditioned activities without yet recognizing the true mind of *tathatā*. Furthermore—

One cannot be born into the family of the Buddhas; how then could one attain dark harmony with Perfect Enlightenment? Therefore, this is said to be a disease (in meaning, it corresponds to those who cling to dharmas).
Second is the disease of indifference: "Since birth and death are already empty, why labor to eliminate them? Since Nirvana is fundamentally quiescent, why rely on joyful cultivation?"
They abandon all restraint of body and mind, no longer mindful of either sin or merit, until they reach a state of total extinction with nowhere to rest;
thus they fall ill. Alas, in recent times, many have fallen into this category: chanting "Chan songs" while desecrating the Dharma assembly;

vainly seeking out names and characteristics while lecturing on the nature of reality away from stupas and monasteries; recklessly claiming to recognize fields of merit and arbitrarily establishing sectarian paths, thereby deluding and confusing sentient beings.
"Consciousness! To sever the seed of the Buddha is truly a matter for deep lamentation. Any true son of the Buddha ought to distance himself from such things.

Yet you do not realize that while the blue walls are just being repaired, the bhikṣu’s lifespan increases; while the temple foundation is about to shift, the eyes of devas and humans move in response.

Furthermore, when engaging with affairs, one should ascend to the principle: by cutting off the perception of form within emptiness and contemplating emptiness, yet not abandoning the manifold conditions—this is true *dhyāna*. As it says in the *Vimalakīrti*:
In the *Māṇavikā-sūtra*, in the chapter on the Bodhisattva Practice, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas of the World of Fragrant Multitudes:
"Regarding the practice of a bodhisattva, one does not hold seclusion to be precious; one does not cling to one's own pleasure while neglecting the welfare of others.

While dwelling in various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), one should regard them as if they were hells. This is what the bodhisattva truly realizes regarding dhyāna. Thus did the Buddha still admonish them.

If one is not attached even to that which has already entered [the mind], how much less could one falsely become attached to what has not yet entered? Furthermore, for a śramaṇa to collect the mind in meditation is truly the universal rule;
who would not do so? To boastfully display oneself through false pretenses, while simultaneously administering medicine in the wrong place, results in harm that is no small matter.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 96, states: Knowing that Subhūti delighted in expounding the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), Maitreya Bodhisattva instructed him, saying:
"One should not speak of this before newly initiated bodhisattvas. Why is this?
If there are those with little merit or roots of goodness who hear the dharma of ultimate emptiness, they will immediately become attached to emptiness and will consequently think: 'If..."
If all phenomena are empty and non-existent, what merit can I possibly create? In that case, one would lose the fruits of prior karma and so forth.
Thus, while the Tathāgata in the sutras and śāstras exhorts us to abandon illness, and Maitreya warns against discussing emptiness with the uninitiated, if one possesses only faith, it is not enough;

one must be vigilant and cautious. Third, as for the cessation of illness: the true mind is free from conceptualization; to stir a thought is immediately to deviate from it. If one ceases [thoughts]...

When deluded thoughts do not arise, the true nature manifests spontaneously. This occurs because one does not realize that deluded thoughts are themselves the truth, and that greed and anger are the fundamental Way;
instead, one seeks the truth apart from delusion. How is this different from removing waves to seek the water? Thus, it becomes a sickness.

Fourth is the cessation of illness. The Path is obscured by delusion; when delusion is exhausted, the Path manifests. Therefore, one seeks to sever delusion and realize the Truth, thereby attaining eternal tranquility of body and mind.
Now, the Bodhisattva’s application of the mind takes benefiting others as its foundation. To now wish to avoid clamor and seek only solitude is truly not the way of a Great Being (Mahāsattva);
how much less so to abandon movement in pursuit of stillness, or to fail to deliver sentient beings out of fear of delusion.

The True Awakened One is a person of true realization. Now, though one desires to leave behind hindrances and seek tranquility, if one is still entangled with the narrow views of the Two Vehicles, how could one attain the profound penetration of Perfect Enlightenment?

Therefore, these are said to be "illnesses" (these three illnesses refer to those who cling to the practice of dhyāna). Regarding these four modes of practice (*caryā*): if they are heard of separately, they become erroneous;
if they are applied simultaneously, there is no fault. If one can constantly practice, constantly cease, constantly sustain, and constantly extinguish [these states], it is easy to be liberated.

They support one another; there is nothing that does not provide benefit. It is just as the four great elements create form: they may alternately cause harm, yet when they exert their power together, they accomplish a success.

Now, this involves the simultaneous cultivation of both principle and phenomena. Relying on fundamental wisdom to seek Buddha-wisdom, one eliminates the former maladies—namely, that if one clings to meditation (*dhyāna*), one mostly falls into the three maladies of stasis, indulgence, and extinction;
whereas if one clings to phenomena (*dharma*), one merely falls into the malady of activity.
Because of this single illness, these two practices together constitute true cultivation. Furthermore, the sub-commentary below states:
"Nowadays, those who study the Dharma mostly abandon the internal while seeking it externally; those who practice meditation prefer to eliminate external conditions while illuminating within.

Both are instances of biased attachment and are equally mired in the two extremes. It further says: "Exert yourself in seeking awakening; do not merely weary your body in vain. (This is a prohibition.)
This refers to those who cling to the observance of precepts; they must strive in practice and not deny the law of cause and effect (this serves to refute those who cling to mere meditation).
The statement, "Within the state of seeking nothing, I therefore seek it," cryptically cites the words of the *Vaipulya* sūtras regarding the mendicant.

The first phrase explains relying on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while the second phrase explains seeking Buddha-wisdom (*buddha-jñāna*). Thus, the *Vaipulya* sūtras state that the Buddha was like a thunderclap.
Having thus spoken of the past causes and conditions, he further said: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Candanapuṣpa.
That Buddha entered parinirvāṇa long ago; at that time, I was no different from you.
There was a bodhisattva named Agrasārathi who acted as a mendicant and entered the city to beg for food. At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Gaṅgā who addressed the mendicant..."
The gentleman asked, "From where have you come? He replied, "I have come from the realm of reality (*bhūtatathatā*). He asked again, "What is meant by 'reality'?

He replied, "Because it is the mark of quiescent extinction (*śāntilakṣaṇa*), it is called reality. He asked again, "Within the mark of quiescent extinction, is there anything to be sought, or is there nothing to be sought?
He replied, "There is nothing to be sought. He asked again, "If there is nothing to be sought, for what purpose would one seek?"
The answer begins with, "In that which is sought for nothing, I therefore seek it," and continues until it says, "Having heard this, Gaṅgā sold her body to make an offering.
The sub-commentary explains: "When both nature and characteristics are simultaneously realized, one seeks all day long yet there is nothing sought."
Regarding the phrase "the principle follows the transformation of phenomena": one interpretation holds that "one" refers to principle (*li*) and "many" refers to phenomena (*shi*).

That which is established by Xianshou is such that its broadness and narrowness are one and the same, entirely free from the aforementioned obstacles.

"How can those of the Three Worthies reach the Ten Stages? If that is so, why does the subsequent passage state: 'The Ten Stages of the Distinct Teaching are completed, yet this merely refers to abiding in the stage of the Perfect Teaching'?

Answer: It is for the purpose of manifesting what is unique (*asādhāraṇa*). Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that there are both common and unique [teachings].

This is because it points to this inconceivable sūtra as being taught uniquely, not shared with the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). Furthermore, the modes of the Great Sage’s transformation (*nirmāṇa*) are not uniform:

some hear [the teaching] but do not believe it, which serves as a distant seed, as cited above; others are caused to attend the assembly through his majestic power (*prabhāva*), as in the case of the Dharma [preaching].
Five thousand people among the assembly cleared their seats; some were made to leave so that they would not hear [the teaching], as in the present sutra.

At the conclusion of the gradual teaching of the *Lotus Sutra*, because the "seeds of the defeated" were about to be gathered, they were specifically ordered to depart. Those remaining in the assembly were earnestly encouraged so that they might believe and accept it.

This present sutra marks the beginning of the sudden teaching; in order to manifest its profound excellence, those [previously excluded] are left behind so they do not hear it, thereby causing future students to practice.
The phrase "seeing and hearing" (jiàn-wén) refers to the "Grand Assembly" (jiā-huì). This is precisely the *Wényán* (Explanatory Text) of the *Qián* hexagram in the *Zhou Yī*.
Therein, it explains the four virtues of *qián*: "Yuan is the primacy of goodness; Heng is the assembly of the auspicious;

"Sufficiency to accord with ritual" means it is sufficient to harmonize with the principles of benefit. "Sufficiency to benefit things" means it is sufficient to reconcile with righteousness. "Firmness and steadfastness" means it is sufficient to serve as the backbone for accomplishing affairs.

The noble person practices these four virtues; therefore, it is said: "Qian: Great Primordiality, Success, and Firm Adherence. At present, we merely borrow the expression regarding this auspicious assembly.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Sū) that "those who see or hear [the teachings] plant the seeds for transcending the stages of the ten bhūmis despite being in the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*)," the intended meaning is as follows:

it merely states that those in the eight difficult conditions who see or hear the *Avataṃsaka* perfume the seed of the *Vajra*. It does not mean that they attain realization as a saint while still manifesting in those eight difficult conditions.

Therefore, it is because one transforms their retribution in hell and is reborn in heaven that they can then ascend to the tenth bhūmi. Thus, the *Chao* (Commentary) says: "All are permitted to take seeing or hearing as the planting of the seed; this principle has not yet been seen [in other texts]."

The *Míngwén* states that those with bodies in the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) can enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). If it were granted that they could enter the Path of Seeing, how could they be called "difficult conditions"?

Furthermore, this would contradict the treatises, which state: "Extreme joy does not exist above the two [realms]; extreme suffering does not exist in the three miserable destinies (*apāya*); only among humans and devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is there the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) when a Buddha appears in the world.

If you claim that these merely constitute obstacles and that the Path of Seeing in the provisional teachings is what is termed "difficult," then if even an inferior path is obstructed, how much more so [the supreme one]?

Regarding the "Victorious Path" (*jina-mārga*), once the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) have been fully realized, one merely abides in the stage of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).

As long as the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*) have not yet arrived, how could it be permitted that those at the level of the Three Worthies (*tri-kalyāṇaka-pudgala*) of the Separate Teaching attain realization in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching? Furthermore, according to Tiantai’s *Mohe Zhiguan*, this refers to one who is "urgent in their vehicle but lax in their precepts."
It is permissible to allow those with bodies in the three miserable realms to attain the holy path; this should be further considered with careful scrutiny.
As for those who harbor doubts and do not believe, they shall never again hear such teachings. Question:

Regarding the celestial beings in hell, because they heard the sutras in the past, they formed firm seeds [of understanding]; yet due to their lack of faith and their slandering [the Dharma], they fell into the Avīci Hell. As for them—
Although one may not believe, they can still hear the sutra, which perfumes the mind to form firm seeds. Why, then, does the present text state:

"Those who harbor doubts and do not believe shall never hear such meanings"? Answer: One interpretation states that those who lack faith and engage in slander fall into the Avīci Hell, where they will not hear [the Dharma] for long kalpas;
thus, when the sutra says "never," it does not mean they will never hear it at all. A second interpretation states:
It merely negates their hearing; it does not say they will never hear at all. Third, it says that even if they do hear, because they lack faith, it is as if they have not heard. It asks:
when these sons of gods in hell were hearing the sutras in the past, they did not believe and instead slandered them.

How could the seeds for the firm realization of Buddhahood be infused within such unwholesome minds? If the seeds for Buddhahood are firm, they are the cause for attaining enlightenment; how then could they fall back into the Avīci hell?
Regarding the Nāraka hell: furthermore, if an unwholesome mind perfumes a firm seed, it would follow that a wholesome mind must instead perfume an unwholesome seed.

If this were granted, then the noble ones of the Three Vehicles would fall back into the evil destinies; this would result in a confusion of cause and effect, which deeply contradicts both scripture and reason. Some say:
"That unwholesome mind merely perfumes the [seeds of] the evil destinies, thereby summoning the retribution of the hells. As for its flower...

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that this perfumes the seeds until they become firm, serving as the cause for attaining Buddhahood. This is because the fundamental awakening (*mūla-avabodha*) within the bonds of existence constitutes one's original nature;

when it abides in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the sound of the sūtra enters the ear and perfumes that fundamental awakening, thereby increasing its functional efficacy. Thus, it is called the "lineage accomplished through practice.
When the original and the new combine, they together form a firm seed. Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The Buddha-seed arises from conditions."

Therefore, it is said that there is but one vehicle (*ekayāna*). If this is so, when one hears the sounds of others as a condition but lacks the wholesome mind within oneself as a cause, how can seeds be perfumed (*vāsana*) in the absence of causal power?
Answer: Because *mūla-jñāna* (fundamental awakening) serves as the cause.

If this is so, when one hears the sounds of others killing, stealing, and so forth, and compassion arises within oneself, would this not perfume seeds of evil? Furthermore, while there are evil sounds acting as conditions, *mūla-jñāna* remains [the cause].

For this reason, it is not possible for original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*) alone to serve as the cause solely for wholesome seeds. Is it not possible that unwholesome seeds could be established through principle without being grasped?
Now, it is said that the mind which hears the sutras possesses two kinds of meanings: first, the meaning of spiritual intelligence (*vijñapti*); second, the meaning of dullness and obscurity.
By virtue of the meaning of spiritual intelligence, one understands the words and meanings of the *Avataṃsaka*; the internal mind serves as the cause, and the sutra...

With sound as the condition, through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the seeds of solidity are perfumed. Due to the sense of dullness and obtuseness, one slanders the meaning of the words of the *Avataṃsaka*.
With the internal mind as the cause and the sound of the sutra as the condition, through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the seeds of the hells are perfumed.
Within a single thought-moment, both types [of seeds] are simultaneously perfumed; this is truly inconceivable. As it says regarding the slander of the *Noble One of No-Little-Regard* (Maitreya):

"What use have we for such false prophecies? Because they understood those words, the prophecy that they would themselves become Buddhas was established, thereby perfuming the diamond-seed (vajra-bīja).
Because of their lack of faith, they perfumed the seed of hell. Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "If one merely understands the Dharma Master, one will attain awakening."
One receives the precepts. At the time of receiving those precepts, one also perfumes the firm seeds.

If one does not understand how it is that one can perfume firm seeds—given that there is not a single sentient being who lacks firm seeds—then according to the principles revealed by all dharmas, since in essence there is not a single dharma that is not the Avataṃsaka, how could there be any sentient being who has not seen or heard it?

If all possess these seeds, for what reason [is this so]? (The *Chao*)... *Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "何故鈔" (For what reason, the *Chao*). The translation reflects the available portion.*
[The Master] said: "Because there was no cause in the past. The outsider asked: "In the text, it simply says that seeing and hearing serve as the seeds;
why must one necessarily understand [them]? Now, [the Master] further explains in general: "If one does not understand them, they do not truly qualify as 'seeing and hearing.

For example, when Śāriputra and others were in the Jeta Grove, the World-Honored One whom they saw was none other than the Buddha of the Inexhaustible Cloud of Bodies; the Jeta Grove which they saw was none other than the Flower [Grove]."
The realm of the treasury and the verbal teachings one hears are precisely the *Avataṃsaka*. However, as long as one does not understand them, they cannot be called "seeing" or "hearing.
Furthermore, it is said that upon seeing the body of Vairocana Buddha, one's eyes attain purity.
Since all present perceived objects are none other than the ten bodies of Vairocana, for what reason have the eyes of all sentient beings not yet attained purity? For this reason...
One may know it, yet one has not yet realized it; both are the Buddha-body, but this is not called "manifestation.
It is like a person who sees gold but understands it to be iron. An outsider asks him, "Do you see gold? That person replies, "I do not see gold."

If one merely perceives the iron [without further cognition], it should be understood that this does not constitute "seeing" or "hearing," as it lacks comprehension. It should be understood that seeing and hearing necessarily involve comprehension;

because of this cognitive mind, one accords with the nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-vijñāna*). By acceding to original enlightenment, one perfumes and establishes firm seeds, which is profoundly subtle in principle.

The *Subcommentary* (Part 8, Second Half, 69) states: "Regarding the second [section], 'Citing Causes for Comparative Manifestation,' this is for the purpose of manifesting excellence.

This has several layers: first, because the virtues of the semblance-mark (*anuvyañjana*) are so profound and vast that words cannot fully encompass them, it is better to set them aside and speak of the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

"The 'fully knowing' below refers to the capacity for extinction; that is, one realizes the fundamental nature of delusion."
Being empty and tranquil, it does not arise. Thus, the Jin translation says: "All these afflictions are entirely extinguished. Because they are extinguished, there is purity;

delusion vanishes and wisdom manifests, which is the light of mastery and the fulfillment of roots of goodness. As for the phrase "clouds of fragrant banners," this refers to the roots of goodness of the ninth stage.
Regarding the statement, "If there are sentient beings who see its canopy," it reaches [the first]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*
Regarding the phrase "roots of goodness as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," the commentary explains:

According to the Jin translation, it says, "planting roots of goodness equal to those planted by one *cakravartin* king as numerous as the sands of the Ganges"—referring to kings such as the Pure White Jewel Net (*śukla-ratna-jāla*) *cakravartin*.
This refers to many *cakravartin* kings, not the many roots of goodness of a single *cakravartin*. The Sanskrit original is likewise; however, it describes them as "pure."
Regarding the "golden net," according to the first volume of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (or *Yingluo jing*), the golden wheel is found at the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

From the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, all possess wheels of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*), distinguished by an increase in the number of jewels. Thus, we know that the "jewel net" mentioned in older translations refers to a superior version of the golden net.
Therefore, that sūtra states: "On the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), there are necklaces (*hāra*) of a hundred jewels and wheels with seven-jeweled rims."
The Four Heavenly Kings have ten thousand sons as their retinue. Within a hundred dharma-bodies and a hundred Buddha-lands, they transform the world throughout the ten directions;

thereafter, there is no further delineation of their transformative scope. Regarding the precious numbers, each increases one by one up to the seventh stage, which has thirteen precious *cakra* (wheels).
At the eighth stage, it simply says "great responsive precious *cakra*. At the ninth stage, it says "white..."

Furthermore, its scope of gathering and transforming beings is identical to the fruition of retribution gathered in the aforementioned tenth bhūmi; thus, it is clear that this realizes the tenth bhūmi.
Therefore, when this king emits light below, those who encounter it also ascend to the tenth bhūmi. As for the phrase "one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*," it refers to [the number] from nine...

According to the interpretation of Qingliang, only the ten stages are taken as "birth through realization and entry," while the rest is the same as Xianshou.

Regarding the statement that these refer to the two preceding lines: taking seeing and hearing as the seeds, one simultaneously brings understanding and practice to bear upon oneself. Regarding the statement that these refer to the two following lines:
one transcends the stages of the ten bhūmis and attains the fruit of the perfect [enlightenment] after kalpas of vast cultivation.

The commentary states: Compassion constitutes the body [of the samādhi], because the body upon which the concentration relies is permeated by compassion (and thus compassion itself is the body, as it is the essential substance upon which the concentration relies).

Great compassion constitutes the gateway, because the act of benefiting others occurs solely through compassion, causing sentient beings to enter [the path]; for the function of entering concentration takes compassion as the means of entry. Great compassion constitutes the head, because in all acts of benefiting others, compassion serves as the precursor; within wisdom and concentration, compassion is the most predominant factor.

One employs the dharma of great compassion as the skillful means (upāya), meaning that when entering concentration to benefit others, compassion is the means—such that both wisdom and concentration are inseparable from compassion, free from attachment or biased views. Furthermore, these four...
This is the gradual progression from the Buddha toward the sentient beings. It pervades all of space (1) because it is vast and universal, and (2) because it is without conditions.
Regarding the statement "entering the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*," the older translation uses the term "furyun" (奮迅), which carries the same meaning as "frequent stretching" (*vijṛmbhita*).

Both refer to the state of the four limbs being fully extended and the body being thoroughly relaxed. To explain this according to its general characteristics: it is the essence of function, yet quiescent.
When reaching the ultimate, the myriad distinctions are all none other than the Dharma-realm; it is the function of the very essence, omnipresent without being contrived.
Thus, small and large interpenetrate, and dependent origination is inexhaustible; this is termed the meaning of "the sovereign power of frequent stretching.
Furthermore, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, a true lion king knows the strength of its own body and the sharpness of its fangs and claws, even as early morning arrives.
Emerging from its lair, it stretches its limbs, yawns, and looks toward the four directions; it lets out a roar that causes the earth to tremble—these constitute eleven matters.
What are these eleven? First, because he wishes to destroy [the false claim] that one who is not actually a lion falsely pretends to be a lion.
Second, because he wishes to test his own strength. Third, because he wishes to purify his dwelling place. Fourth, for the sake of his offspring...
1. Because he knows the location; 2. Because he has no fear toward the herds; 3. Because he awakens those who are asleep; 4.
Because he causes all heedless wild beasts to become heedful; 5. Because he causes the various beasts to approach him;
6. Because he tames the great fragrant elephant; 7. Because he instructs his offspring; 8. [Eleventh...]
In order to adorn his own retinue, all birds and beasts hear the lion’s roar;
those belonging to the water and land sink into deep abysses, those that move on land hide in burrows, and those that fly fall down.
Even the great fragrant elephant king, out of fear, loses its excrement. Using the coolness of the Dharma and its meaning, he unites them with that lion, meaning they are of the same essence.
Great compassion constitutes the body; supreme great compassion is its head; the great compassion that is itself wisdom is its eyes; pure wisdom constitutes its fangs and claws;
and the skillful means of great compassion constitute its waving tail. Since compassion is the fundamental basis for skillful means, it is the "tail" in the sense of being the primary mover.
Taking the four types of compassion collectively as the feet, it is established upon them. Thus, by means of...
The Samādhi Cave of the Dharma-realm is so called because it is that which is entered and realized. Great Compassion without object serves as its cave-door, for entry and exit occur by means of this.
The non-obstruction between essence and function constitutes its stretching and yawning, for there is sovereign expansion therein.
The expounding of the Dharma-gates of the Dharma-realm constitutes its roar, definitively proclaiming that all sentient beings are fundamentally identical to the Tathāgata.
Because it is the *dharmadhātu*. Just as with this lion, each and every hair is said to be the *dharmadhātu*.
Next, regarding the statement that he stretches his limbs for eleven reasons: first, to crush the deceptive lion-like armies of Māra;

second, to demonstrate his supernormal powers, as the ten powers and other powers constitute his physical strength; third, to purify the *dharmadhātu* realm, which is the Buddha’s dwelling place; fourth...
1. To provide a place of refuge for ordinary people with wrong views; 2. To comfort the multitude who fear birth and death;
3. To awaken sentient beings sleeping in ignorance; 4. To cause those wild beasts of unwholesome dharmas to abandon their negligence; 5.
To cause all bodhisattvas and the wild beasts of wrong views to come and take refuge; 6. For the sake of all non-Buddhists and the two... [text continues].

10. By mounting the fragrant elephant, one causes those who are like the blind and deaf to abandon heedlessness. 11. One instructs the sons of the Bodhisattvas so that they may realize [the truth] instantaneously;

one adorns right view and the fourfold retinue, whereby their majesty and power increase together, such that they do not fear any faction of the heterodox, for all factions of the heterodox are terrified [of them]. Furthermore, the jackal follows after the lion.
For a hundred years they have been unable to utter the lion’s roar; because those of the Two Vehicles abide within the Dharma assembly as if blind or deaf.
Regarding the statement that the extensive explanation consists of the "ten ways of entry" and so forth, the Sūtra says:
"Those Bodhisattvas, by means of various understandings, various paths, various gates, various entries, various principles, and various conformities..."
They cultivate various kinds of wisdom, various aids to the path, various skillful means, and various samādhis.
They enter the ocean of the Tathāgatas’ skillful means, which is as numerous as the atoms within ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Regarding the phrase "The Elephant King turns in six thousand ways, accomplished in the moment of speech": it is because Mañjuśrī surveys those who are vessels for the Dharma.

Just as the Elephant King turns, with both body and head rotating together without a light or hurried motion, this assembly of six thousand bhikṣus represents the purification of the six sense faculties, making them capable of entering the Dharma-realm.
Question: To what stage does this "attainment of the Way" through these words correspond? Answer: It resides solely in...
The Ten Faiths. How is this known? Therefore, in the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshù*), within the section on accomplishing that work of transformation, there are generally three assemblies:

first, the Assembly of the Bhikṣu, which reveals the turning away from the Small Vehicle and entry into the Great Vehicle; second, the Assembly of All Those Who Come, which universally gathers all those of provisional capacities into the single reality;
and third, the Assembly of Sudhana, which reveals the pure One Vehicle, wherein roots are perfected in a single lifetime. Furthermore, regarding the first two assemblies:

This refers to the fact that for those whose outward expression of faith has not yet endured long and remains unstable, it is necessary to reach the culmination of Sudhana’s faith before they can enter into realization.

Furthermore, the *Piṇḍārtha* states: "At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra... and so forth; from this point downward, the fulfillment of that transformative work consists of three assemblies in total.
The first assembly consists of six thousand bhikṣus; it is presented to demonstrate the turning away from the Hīnayāna and the entry into the Mahāyāna.
The second begins from the start of the sixty-second sūtra up until the passage stating that there are again innumerable sentient beings who each attain discipline within the three vehicles;

this is the assembly of those belonging to the various vehicles, presented to signify the comprehensive inclusion [of all]. The third begins from the passage: "At that time, the people of Puṇḍravardhana heard of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta..."

The section below is the "Assembly of Sudhana" (*Sudhanakumāra-parivarta*). The three preceding sections all pertain to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*); because faith has not yet entered the formal stages (*bhūmi*), there are these three categories.

Below this, Sudhana possesses the faculties of the pure One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); after entering the stages, he is solely a single individual. Therefore, until the end of the sutra, it speaks only of Sudhana;
the text is very clear on this point, so do not harbor further doubts.
Regarding the commentary on the ten virtues of Mañjuśrī, the sub-commentary states: first, the excellence of the physical body; second, the excellence of the constant radiance;
third, the excellence of the emitted light; fourth, the excellence of the assembly; fifth, the excellence of the path (indicating that he constantly relies upon the Eightfold Noble Path);

sixth, the excellence of the dwelling place (for every step taken is a site of enlightenment [bodhimaṇḍa], as it turns according to the mind); seventh, the excellence of adornment (constantly contemplating the two extremes of emptiness and existence, yet beneath the ground of the mind, he possesses the Tathāgatagarbha with its ocean-like inherent virtues, which are non-dual).

Because the mind is free from subject-object duality, it manifests as spontaneous, quiescent awareness. (8) The excellence of the grove of trees: because the myriad practices are established to adorn the essence of the Dharma. (9) The excellence of sovereignty:

because one attains the non-dual understanding of self and non-self, becoming the most supreme among sovereign lords. (10) The excellence of supreme inclusion: this has two meanings: first, regarding the actual practice, the mind constantly and supremely includes all Buddha-dharmas;

second, regarding the symbolic meaning, all manifestations of the Buddhas rely upon Prajñāpāramitā to ultimately reach omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). [The text] says: "To cause the arousal of ten kinds of tireless minds."
That is to say: (1) accumulating all roots of goodness with a mind free from weariness;
(2) beholding all Buddhas, serving and making offerings to them; (3) seeking all Buddha-dharmas; (4) practicing all pāramitās;
(5) accomplishing all bodhisattva samādhis; (6) entering all three periods of time in succession; and universally adorning and purifying [them].
(7) To teach and transform all sentient beings in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions;
(8) to accomplish the practices of a bodhisattva throughout all kalpas in all lands;

(9) to practice all pāramitās as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields for the sake of maturing all sentient beings, thereby accomplishing a single power of the Tathāgata. Thus, in succession...
Furthermore, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment, one must accomplish the Tathāgata’s powers (the phrase "a mind free from weariness" appears after each of the ten powers).
Since the Dharma-gates are inexhaustible and sentient beings are boundless, if one practices while grasping at signs, weariness will arise in abundance.

If one becomes weary, one will fall back into the two vehicles. However, if one practices without craving or views, there will be no weariness. Even though there is no weariness, [if one still grasps...]
"The fruit of Buddhahood is not far off; how much less so for my own person.

Regarding the statement, "By speaking thus, one attains samādhi named 'Unobstructed Eye' (*anāvaraṇa-cakṣus*) and so forth," the sub-commentary (*śūtra*) explains that there are briefly three meanings: first, the ability to see because of being free from obstructions; second, that which is seen is without hindrance;
third, it possesses manifold functions. Although it possesses these capacities, because it lacks the characteristic of seeing [as a subject], it is called "Three."
"Attaining this samādhi... and thereby serving as an adornment" correctly clarifies the function of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
"And furthermore, hearing that... and understanding them all" refers to the function of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*). "Furthermore, being able to observe...

the faculties, minds, and desires" refers to the function of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*). "Furthermore, being able to recollect... the ten kinds of eloquence" [refers to the function of recollecting past lives].

"Genius" (cai) refers to the function of the supernormal knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, it is the accomplishment that reaches all Buddha-dharmas," this universally reveals many gateways.
Since the function of the aforementioned concentration is thus, so too are the inexhaustible examples of these many gateways.

This reveals that in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), one who has established the Great Resolve and attained the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) subsequently acquires the functions of the ten supernormal powers (*daśa-abhijñā*). This is the beginning.
Because it summarizes the conclusion, as explained in the "Chapter on the Merit of First Resolving the Mind" (*Prathamacittotpāda-puṇya-parivarta*) and elsewhere.
Regarding the phrase "The Commentary Reveals the Eastern Temple," this refers to the "Revealing Bodhi-Wisdom" (*Bodhijñānaprakāśa*).

As for the stage to which this bodhicitta belongs, and whether the youth Sudhana is a saint (*ārya*) or an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there have been many ancient interpretations. One school says he is a bodhisattva on the stages (*bhūmi*). Another...
Some say he is a worthy person prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). Others say he is included within both the stages prior to the *bhūmis* and the stages of the *bhūmis*.

These various interpretations above are all not the correct meaning. Therefore, Xianshou said: "He should be one among those of the 'faithful practice' (*śraddhācaryā*) within the happy realms (*sugati*).

According to the school of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there are three positions: first, the position of seeing and hearing, which refers to Sudhana; next, his body in his previous life; and [finally] seeing and hearing as..."

This is because it is the Dharma of Samantabhadra. One accomplishes the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), as explained previously in the section on praising his virtues.
Second is the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), wherein one suddenly cultivates the practices of these five stages, just as Sudhana attained in this very life.

Upon reaching the stage of Samantabhadra, this is the third, the birth of realization (*praveśajanman*); that is, the causal stage reaches its ultimate conclusion, and one merges into the ocean of the fruit (*phalasamudra*). Sudhana came...
This refers to "arising. If that is so, what stage is this definitely? It means that when one is in faith, it is the stage of faith; when one abides, it is the stage of abiding.
A single body traverses five stages, and whichever stage one currently occupies, one is subsumed under that very stage. Because it applies to all [stages], it is like the stage of Samantabhadra.

This first interpretation is highly consistent with the core tenets of the sutra. The Master of the Commentary himself states: "It means that while one practices by traversing the stages (*bhūmi*), one attains the vision of Samantabhadra all at once.
Even the celestial son in hell [attains] the threefold sudden perfection; why then should Sudhana be restricted to fixed temporal periods?
This implies that while the practice (*caryā*) is gradual, the realization of the stages (*bhūmi*) is sudden; this is the present meaning.

Regarding the phrase "reaching the eastern part of the City of Blessings" (*Fóchéng*): the inhabitants of this city possess great merit and virtue; thus it is called the "City of Virtue. A city serves as a bulwark against wrongdoing.
The east is the foremost of all directions and the beginning of illumination; it symbolizes following one's portion of blessings and entering the path of goodness at its inception.
Furthermore, it symbolizes the fundamental basis for entering the stage of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna*). [The Buddha] dwelt at the Śāla tree of the Banner of Adornment.

"Forest" (Lin) here means "lofty and remote," so called because the trees and woods rise up in dense profusion; it symbolizes that one shall proceed toward the adornment of the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*).
The "Great Stūpa Temple" is the site where Guizong resided. Tripitaka Master Rizi said: "This city is located in South India.
The Great Stūpa Temple to the east of the city is the stūpa of an ancient Buddha. It already existed during the time when the Buddha was in the world."
Regarding this stūpa, the Tripitaka Master personally visited its location. It is extremely tall and large;
while musical performances and offerings are heard on its eastern side, none are heard from the western side. Even now, the inhabitants of this place frequently sing the verses of Sudhana.
The people within this city all possess the roots of goodness conducive to liberation and are fit vessels for the Path. This represents the Dharma upon which he relied.
The fundamental awakening of the realms (*dhātu*) is the true nature upon which all Buddhas equally rely; hence it is said, "the place where all Buddhas of the past once dwelt," and so forth.
The mention of the five hundred *upāsakas* signifies the realization and entry into the five stages.

The mention of Sudhana’s individual contemplation means that a mind that accords with principle is called "good" (*śubha*), while the inexhaustible accumulation of merit is called "wealth" (*dhana*). To know this...

The Assembly. Specifically, regarding the phrase "the Sage’s favor was turned toward him": it means that he was further commanded to recollect his past roots of goodness, so as to cause him to remember his former merits and not disparage himself.
Regarding the phrase "he spoke in verse following Mañjuśrī," and so forth: [this refers to the subsequent verses].
Partaking together of the wondrous essence, he alone excelled among the multitude of streams. Out of reverence for the Dharma, he followed his teacher;

reciting a verse, he sought ordination. Thus that verse says: "The three realms of existence are the city walls; pride is the rampart; the various destinies are the gates; the waters of craving are the moat.
May the wheel of vows have great compassion as its hub, faith as its axle, and firm axles as its linchpins. Adorned with the jewels of merit, may it [deliver] me..."

"Mounting this vehicle. As for the statement "one hundred and ten *yojanas*," it serves to symbolize that each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as well as the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is fully endowed with the merits of all the stages.
Alternatively, if one does not distinguish the stage of Equal Enlightenment, one instead opens up the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*).
Whether taken inclusively or exclusively, both cases represent one hundred and ten. Since initial faith encompasses the ultimate fruit, it is said to be "extended afar. This follows...

Because it is accomplished through following [the path], it is called the "right hand. Regarding the phrase "if one is separated from the faculty of faith" up to "that which is recollected," there are nine lines of sūtra text.
In the first seven, the causes are missing: (1) because the root of practice is lacking;

(2) because one seeks the inferior, the mind is weak and one suffers with regret while dwelling in saṃsāra; (3) lack of horizontal completeness; (4) lack of vertical progress; (5) stagnation in a single good; (6) ... [text truncated].
One does not seek extensively. Seventh, one does not give rise to non-abiding vows. The latter two lack conditions; the latter cannot be resolved below. There are fifteen phrases:
the first five concern the principles and phenomena of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), while the latter ten concern the limits of the subject that knows.
One should reflect upon them by analogy with the preceding texts.
Regarding the phrase "entrusting the stages to those who seek in the south": "entrusting the stages" (jìwèi) refers to entrusting them to the characteristics of practice.

"Entrusting" (jì) means to rely upon; it carries the sense of dependence. "Stages" (wèi) means sequence; it carries the sense of gradation. This, then, is the simultaneous manifestation of the gradual through the sequential and the perfect through the circular;

it is the manifestation of the Dharma through persons, and the manifestation of the nature through characteristics. As the sub-commentary below states: "For now, following the ancient masters, they are assigned into five."

The "Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refer to the forty-one persons who are designated as "entrusted stages. This means that the characteristics of cultivation are entrusted to these forty-one stages; by relying on these persons, one seeks understanding, thereby manifesting the practice of cultivation.
Second, from Māyādevī downward through the nine assemblies and eleven persons, it clarifies the "uniting of conditions to enter the true characteristic" (*dharmatā*).

This refers to uniting the preceding stages (*vihāra*) and so forth to accomplish the two types of practice—the universal and the particular—and thereby realizing and attesting to the *dharmadhātu*. Thus, one first attains illusory wisdom (*māyājñāna*).
The subsequently attained state, "abiding like an illusion," encompasses the intermediate stage; for illusory conditions enter into the single reality.
Third, the single section on Maitreya is titled "The Cause-Phase of Gathering Virtuous Qualities," because it unifies the virtues of the preceding two gates as the causes for realization and entry.

Therefore, this Dharma-gate is named "The Unforgetting Mindfulness of the Three Times. It thus encompasses the boundless Dharma. Fourth, the subsequent Mañjuśrī is named "Wisdom Illuminating the Non-dual Aspect.
This means that when practice is perfected and ultimate, clear awakening resides within one's breast;

one illuminates the preceding practices and so forth as nothing other than a single, perfect wisdom, for there is no longer any distinction between before and after, clarity and obscurity, or the like. Fifth, the single personage Samantabhadra is named "Manifesting the Vastness of Causes."

Regarding the marks (*lakṣaṇa*): initial awakening is identical to the fundamental [awakening]. Perfect awakening manifests before one, pervading the entire Dharma-realm because there is nothing it does not encompass.
Consequently, the latter four marks may also be termed "provisional stages" (*yu-wei*), for the meanings of the first three are equal to that of Equal Awakening (*samyaksambodhi*).

Māyā and Maitreya both enter the gate of the "twofold mystery. Mañjuśrī represents the exhaustion of the Bodhisattva stages, wherein the mind is free from the mark of beginning. The meaning of Samantabhadra is likewise.
The Subtle Enlightenment (Miaojue): because upon merely seeing Samantabhadra, one becomes equal to a Buddha. Now, following a specific interpretation, it is provisionally presented as five aspects.
These five are also the five types of conduct of a Bodhisattva: first, High Conduct (ascending through the stages); second, Great Conduct (entering together into the single reality);

third, Supreme Conduct (possessing the aforementioned vast accomplishments to become a cause for the stage of the Future Buddha); fourth, Profound Conduct (Prajñā transcending all marks); and fifth, Vast Conduct (each and every nature being fully realized). Furthermore, regarding the character "Nan" (南), there was [a tradition] in antiquity...

There are many meanings. The first is based on the physical object (*vastu*), meaning that one instance serves as an example for all others; since virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in a single direction are already immeasurable, how much more so in other directions?
The remaining four are based on symbolic representation (*saṃketika*). Second is the meaning of illumination (*prakāśa*): it symbolizes abandoning darkness and turning toward wisdom.
That the south is luminous so that all things may be seen, and that sages face south, is derived from this. Third is the meaning of departing from deviance (*viparīta*); the east...

Regarding the two sides of the west: it signifies the true Way that accords with the center. Regarding the meaning of the four births: the south presides over yang, generating all things, symbolizing the growth of the practices of Sudhana.
The north presides over yin, manifesting the meaning of cessation; thus, when the World-Honored One entered nirvana, his golden coffin was placed with the head toward the north.
Fifth, regarding the meaning of conformity: turning the back to the left and facing toward the right is the meaning of conformity, as is the custom of the Western Regions.

Because the customs, cities, gardens, and dwellings all face east, one proceeds from the east toward the south, following the movement of the sun and moon. This demonstrates that Sudhana accords with the principles of the teaching.
Among these five meanings, the first is general; the next one pertains to the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), while the latter two signify the realization of the Middle Way.
The [meaning] subsequent to the grounds also applies generally to the stages prior to the grounds, as it represents the direct realization of the stage free from signs (*lakṣaṇa-vigata-bhūmi*).

In the center, it is not represented by the south. The earth subsequently manifests its functional activity, which differs from being within the earth. Later, Mañjuśrī has no fixed direction and manifests *prajñā*;
because there is cultivation in the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and non-duality in the realization of the truth, he is so depicted.

Samantabhadra has neither direction nor manifestation, representing the universal pervasiveness of the *dharmadhātu*. Some take only the single meaning of "conformity," which is not among the aforementioned explanations, namely:

Regarding the meaning of "correctly clarifying" (*zhèngmíng*): since it originates from this region [China], how could one know that in the Western Regions (India), "non-illuminating" (*fēnmíng*) and so forth do not exist?
Moreover, as a discourse that encompasses all quarters, its purport contains many layers of meaning; thus, it accords with five meanings.

Regarding the passage in the *Commentary* stating that "when Sudhana arrived at the stage of teaching and transforming sentient beings," this refers to the manifestation of Samantabhadra through his own body.

The statement "not perishing in this land and appearing in that land" is because the characteristics of perishing and appearing are identical to the Dharma-nature (dharmatā), and because the characteristics of "this" and "that" are mutually identical.
The statement "equal to Samantabhadra" means equal in the perfection of causes. "Equal to all Buddhas" [refers to]...
This refers to the fulfillment of the equal fruit. Regarding the passage from "the single body is filled" to "all are entirely equal," this specifically reveals the characteristics of equality.
If one relies on the general characteristic, the meaning corresponds to Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), for it is beyond words and cannot be expressed.

Regarding the phrase "the gateway that exhausts the vows for all sentient beings": one asks whether there will ever come a time when sentient beings are completely exhausted such that they attain Buddhahood.

If this were so, what would be the fault? There are defects in both positions. If one says there is an exhaustion [of sentient beings], then the realm of sentient beings would cease to exist and the realm of Buddhas would increase;

furthermore, this would contradict the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, which states: "If the realm of sentient beings were to be exhausted, my vow would then be exhausted. Yet, sentient beings can never be exhausted.
Therefore, these roots of goodness from my great vow would have no end;

yet, if the Tathāgata’s merit for benefiting others were also subject to exhaustion, one would know that the very last sentient being would certainly not attain Buddhahood, and from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, there would be none at all who are transformed.
Sentient beings who have entered the holy path lack the practice of benefiting others; since their causal practices are not perfected, how could they attain Buddhahood?

If you say that [the number of sentient beings] is not exhausted, then exhausting the great vow for all sentient beings would be in vain. Furthermore, this contradicts the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states: "All who possess a mind will certainly become Buddhas.
Within the entirety of the Dharma-realm, is there even one being who lacks Buddha-nature? Since they do possess it, [their attainment may be delayed].

How could there be even one being who does not attain Buddhahood in this lifetime? Do not say that because sentient beings arise in continuous succession from moment to moment, sentient beings therefore have a beginning.
The *Renwang jing* states: "Outside the three realms, there are distinct sentient beings who first arise."
This is stated extensively in the scriptures of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Do not say that after attaining Buddhahood, one becomes a sentient being again.
This is because gold has no double ore; likewise, a Buddha is not reborn. Since ignorance is exhausted, there is no principle for a second birth.

Therefore, Nāgārjuna called it the "ground of abiding which is beginningless but has an end. From this, it is known that [the opposing view] is unreasonable whether one advances or retreats. Now, it is said in response: as in the world...
Suppose there is one person who has attained the art of longevity and flies freely, leaping through the void (as if that person had already attained the Way of the Buddha).
One should ask: "Is the void greater to the west of that person? Or is the void greater to the east of that person? The answer would be: "It is impossible to discuss its quantity.

Why? Because the void is boundless. (One should likewise ask: "Of those who have attained Buddhahood before this Buddha, are they many? Of those who have not yet attained Buddhahood after this Buddha, are they many?")

[Question: Which is more numerous? [Answer: It is impossible to discuss their number. Why? Because Buddhas and sentient beings are infinite. This person, by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), travels eastward;

in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, they traverse hundreds of thousands of myriads of *li* of empty space. Just as this Buddha employs the power of compassion (*karuṇā*) to transform hundreds of thousands of myriads of classes of sentient beings in a single thought-moment, causing them all to attain the Buddha-way, so too does this person—neither aging nor dying, and not even pausing for a moment—travel in this manner until the end of the future.
"Is there perhaps a single realm of space in the eastern direction that this person cannot transcend? (If so, then this Buddha would neither migrate nor perish, nor would he even dwell for a moment;

yet he transforms beings in this manner until the end of the future. Is there perhaps a single sentient being whom this Buddha does not transform and lead to Buddhahood? One should know that the realms of space in the eastern direction can all be transcended by that person, as they exist in the western direction.
(One should know that every single sentient being can be transformed and led to the path of Buddhahood. Although it continues thus until the end of the future..."
And yet they travel. Do they exhaust the empty space of the eastern direction? (Though they manifest such transformations throughout the future, do they exhaust all sentient beings? Why is this?
Because space is boundless. (For what reason? Because sentient beings are boundless. Do not say that space is newly produced in the eastern direction;

do not say that space already transcended in the western direction returns to the eastern direction. (Do not say that sentient beings are newly produced; do not say that those who have already attained the Buddha-way return to being sentient beings.
Even if one were to travel for immeasurable kalpas, one could never say that the space to the west of that person is more than the space to the east of that person.

(“Even if one were to transform [beings] for immeasurable kalpas, one could never say that those who have already attained Buddhahood are many and those who have not yet attained it are few. For this reason, all difficulties are suddenly and completely exhausted.
