This also refutes the opponent's position; thus it is said. One interpretation holds that one must not fail to slay the venomous snake;
another holds that one must not fail to cut off one's own hand. If one does not cut it off, the venom will pervade the entire body, and life will be difficult to preserve.
To manifest that the matter is inexhaustible, one must not be frivolous.

Regarding the statement that it is "good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end," this is an implicit citation of a scriptural passage. The Sūtra says: "It is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end;
its meaning is profound and far-reaching, and its phrasing is exquisite."

Regarding the phrase "The Commentary states that it is not by a single cause, etc.": A question is raised that the *Lotus Sūtra* says, "It is solely for the sake of one great causal matter (ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya) that the Tathāgata appears in the world," whereas the present text speaks of "not one.
If one were to attempt to harmonize these two, the present commentary explains:

this [text] says "not one" because it refers to more than a single minor cause and condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), whereas that sūtra speaks of "one" because it refers to a single great causal matter. Alternatively, this expression "not one" indicates...
Regarding the "many conditions" of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), that [text] states it is "only one," because it distinguishes it from the "many conditions" of the other three vehicles.

As for the phrase "the commentary shifts its application," it means to apply it again in a different segment. That [text] correlates Mount Sumeru with the Buddha’s body, wisdom with the treatise (*śāstra*), and movement with the teaching (*pravacana*);
the sutra also encompasses both the common and the uncommon. In the present text, Mount Sumeru is correlated with the body, and wisdom with...

"Combined ocean" refers to the combined explanation of movement and agitation; however, this discussion concerns only what is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), not what is common (*sādhāraṇa*), and is thus called "shifting the momentum.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, in the sūtras... and so forth: the previous explanation held that wisdom (*jñāna*) alone penetrates both subject and object, whereas the subsequent explanation holds that the body (*kāya*) likewise penetrates both.

Regarding the phrase "the commentary [proceeds] by means of the ten meanings, etc.," there are generally three interpretations. First, all take the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka* as being identical in essence (*tattva*) as the cause.
Second, all take the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka* as being distinct in essence (*anyatva*) as the cause. Third, they are applied indeterminately according to the context.
As for the first interpretation, taking the meaning of identity in essence as the cause, one should first ask: what is the reason that the Buddha preached the *Avataṃsaka* as a single dharma?
It is because it ought to be so, just as heat belongs to fire by its very nature (*dharmatā*) and not through any other cause;
the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* constantly and universally teaches this, for it is taught by its very nature and not through any other cause. Second, it is because it recompenses past causes;

one takes only the meaning of the sūtra that is capable of recompensing, rather than taking that which is recompensed as the cause. Third, it is because it accords with the faculties of those who perceive it; one takes only what is in the sūtra...
1. Regarding the meaning of being able to accord with the faculties and induce [results]: it does not take that which is accorded with as the cause;

rather, because the four [truths] are the basis of the teachings, it takes only the meaning of being able to serve as the foundation for all teachings as found in the sūtras, not taking the various teachings themselves as the cause. 5. Because it manifests the merit of the fruit.

1. It takes up that which can manifest the meaning, because it elucidates the stages of realization (*bhūmi*). 2. It takes up that which can reveal the meaning, because it explains the sublime practices (*viśeṣa-caryā*).

3. It takes up that which can express the meaning, because it demonstrates the true Dharma. 4. It takes up that which can indicate the meaning, because it opens up the nature of the cause (*hetu-bhāva*). 5. It takes up that which can disclose the meaning.

Regarding the ten benefits for the sake of the future, the meaning of "beneficial" is adopted. All these are the functions of the *Avataṃsaka* as its very essence (*tattva*), which serve as the reason for preaching this sutra.
Second, the meaning of "distinct essence" serves as the cause, because the single Dharma is naturally so. According to the commentary on the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World," it says:
"The second [point], that the Dharma is thus—Sanskrit: *dharmatā*; here translated as 'Dharma-nature' (*fǎ'ěr*), or simply 'Dharma' (*fǎ*)."

Regarding "nature" (*dharmatā*): if it refers to the *dharmatā* of phenomena, then it takes the fundamental consciousness, the *tathāgatagarbha*, as its support, constantly and simultaneously transforming to give rise to the external vessel-worlds (this can be used to prove the latter sense).
If it is said to be "the nature of things" (*dharmatā*), this refers to a question such as:

"Why do Buddhas and sentient beings arise within lands? The answer is: "The nature of phenomena is thus; it cannot be further questioned" (this can be used to prove the former sense). If one synthesizes these...
2. "The Dharma should arise as such from the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna*. The commentary states: This explains both meanings simultaneously.

Just as the cause of the world in that treatise is thus, so too is the cause for the arising of this Sūtra. It simply says "it is the nature of things" (*dharmatā*). Based on this, one should understand that both [the world and the Sūtra] respond to past causes;

taking the vows and practices previously undertaken as the response, they are explained as the cause for the teaching of the Sūtra. 3. "Conforming to the faculties of beings" also takes what was previously...
1. "In accordance with" (anuloma). 2. "As the basis of the teaching" (śāsanamūla) also takes the various teachings as its cause.

Just as one who wishes to graft a pear tree first cuts it to a stake—thus knowing that the pear tree is the cause of the stake—so too, wishing to bestow the derivative teachings (anta-śāsana), one first reveals the fundamental dharma (mūla-dharma); thus we know that the derivative teachings, in turn, serve as the cause for the fundamental dharma.
3. "Manifesting the merit of the fruit" (phalaguṇa-prakāśana) refers to what is manifested. [The remaining sections] up to the ten benefits (daśānuśaṃsa) are all [to be understood] hereafter.

Because they grasp what is beneficial, the third [category]—the indeterminate according to circumstances—is the basis of the teaching. "Grasping" (*upādāna*) has the meaning of "essence" (*svabhāva*) as its cause;

"benefit" (*artha*) refers to the subsequent [state]. For the most part, "grasping" takes the meaning of "essence" as its cause, while the remainder all take "distinct essence" (*anyasvabhāva*) as their cause, or perhaps both apply universally.
Let the student examine this further.

Regarding the phrase "the commentary does not depend on other causes": Question: Since the Dharma-gate of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) does not rely on external causes, does it not fall into the position of the naturalist heretics (*svabhāvavāda*)?

Answer: It is not that there are no causes at all; rather, it simply employs the single cause of "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*). Question: If that is so, why do the nine causes mentioned below not likewise not depend [on anything]?
Answer: That [previous point] was stated hypothetically; there are no other causes besides the single cause of dharma-nature, which is sufficient for what is being explained here.

Because it is stated in the Sūtra, it is said that "it does not depend [on other causes]. Alternatively, regarding the "natural cause" (*dharmatā-hetu*), since it possesses both substance and efficacy, it subsumes the remaining nine causes; therefore, it is said that "it does not depend [on others].

In the Commentary, the passage beginning with "Why is it that such a natural transformation occurs? It is because the past causes are profound," etc., asks in response to the question regarding past causes.
[Question on] Meaning: If our World-Honored One, upon first attaining the Buddha-way, immediately preached the *Avataṃsaka*, then one must acknowledge that there is a beginning.

How, then, can this be explained as the Dharma turning according to its own nature (*dharmatā*)? [Answer]: This is permissible only if one considers a single Buddha of the present; such a being may indeed have a beginning.

However, when tracing back through the succession of many past Buddhas, it becomes beginningless. Alternatively, our World-Honored One merely transmitted ancient events rather than speaking them anew himself, just as in the world...
When a sovereign first ascends the precious throne, he merely follows the established path rather than innovating new regulations; thus, it is established as the natural order (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, according to the present Buddha, he is none other than the Buddhas of the past; therefore, it is said to be "beginningless. Moreover, according to the present single moment, it is identical to the many moments of the past;
therefore, it is said to be "beginningless. Thus, the Commentary states: "Time, though measured by the *kṣaṇa*, endures through the vast ocean of *kalpas*."
Regarding the phrase "The Commentary first treads upon the profound tracks," etc., this explains the greatness of cause and effect.

One interpretation holds that from "first treading upon the profound tracks" up to "suddenly illuminating the myriad dharmas" explains the profundity of the cause, while the following two phrases explain the greatness of the fruit.

Another interpretation holds that from "first treading upon" up to "completely encompassing" explains the profundity of the cause; thus, from "therefore" up to "the wondrous gate" explains the greatness of the fruit. "First treading upon the profound tracks" explains the beginning.
To give rise to the bodhicitta of phenomenal characteristics is to traverse the traces of the profound gateway of the One Vehicle.

To cause the spirit to dwell in wondrous stillness is to be free from all marks and to accord with the principle of quiescence; it is to settle the divine mind within the subtle and wondrous principle of cessation.

The first phrase refers to the bodhicitta that retains characteristics; the second phrase refers to the bodhicitta that dispels characteristics. When phenomena and principle are unimpeded, one is neither bound by retention nor by cessation; this is the true arousal of the mind.

Alternatively, the first phrase represents contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and the second represents quiescence (*śamatha*); when quiescence and contemplation are unimpeded, this constitutes true cultivation.
Regarding the statement "compassion and wisdom operate in tandem," it means benefiting both oneself and others. Regarding the statement "practice and vows are equally perfected," [it means...]
Each and every one accords with the nature (*dharmatā*); it is profound and without limit. Each and every one is equal to space; it is vast and without limit.
The phrase "therefore" (*yi*) serves to connect the preceding to what follows: because the cause is profound, the fruit attained is great.

Regarding the statement that "delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) are not severed, yet they are thoroughly penetrated as empty by nature": this is to sever them without severing them, awakening from the dense darkness of the great night [of ignorance] to the reality of suchness (*tathatā*).

This is wisdom (*jñāna*). Regarding the statement that the "spiritual mirror is not polished yet suddenly illuminates the myriad dharmas": this is cultivation without cultivation, which illuminates the profound depths of the myriad dharmas;

it is the conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) of *yathāvadbhāvikatā*. It employs the power of the unobstructed wisdom of liberation (*anāvaraṇa-vimokṣa-jñāna-bala*) to proclaim and expound this subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the *Avataṃsaka*.
The two aforementioned causes are both aspects of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*), as they pertain to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

[The first cause] is "Power" (*bala*). This refers to the Buddha’s virtuous capacity, as it is taught as being constant and all-pervasive. The subsequent eight causes are all "functional activities" (*karmaprayoga*), because they verify the faculties and demonstrate guidance.
Alternatively, only the very first is a cause for the marks of virtue (*guṇalakṣaṇa*), while the intermediate eight causes are causes for functional activity.

Thus, the Commentary states: "By means of unobstructed liberation (*anāvaraṇavimukti*), he elucidates this wondrous gateway; for supernatural powers and liberation are exclusively functional activities."
The final cause encompasses both qualities (*guṇa*) and functional activities (*karmaprayoga*). How is this known? Because the preceding nine are specific while the tenth is general;

that which is general necessarily subsumes the specific. Alternatively, the first one also encompasses functional activities, as the *Yìshìfēn* (Inconceivable Chapter) cited in the *Chāo* explains the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Regarding the phrase in the *Śāstra* (鈔), "The dependent and the supported manifest within one another," etc.: Question:

Within the section on the "Mutual Entry of Characteristics" (相入門), since there is already "the supported manifesting within the supported-and-supported" (正中現依) and "the supported manifesting within the supported-and-supported" (依中現依正), there should also be "the supported-and-supported manifesting within the supported-and-supported" (依正中現正) and "the supported manifesting within the supported-and-supported" (依中現正).
Since mutual entry necessarily involves reciprocity, if this were granted, there would be eight propositions; why are there only six? Now...
The general response states: "In principle, this is indeed so. However, for the sake of manifesting the superior, one manifests two within one; it is not that two are taken to manifest one.
This is like the example of raising a portion of dust or a hair to manifest its roundness, rather than taking the roundness of the body or the *kṣetra* to manifest a portion.

Question: Why are there six propositions regarding mutual identity (*xiāngjí*) that differ from those for mutual inclusion (*xiāngrù*), such that two are added here? Now, add two [propositions]: 1. One is identical with two. 2. Two are identical with one.
The verse states: "This Buddha’s support and manifestation is precisely that Buddha’s support; this Buddha’s support is precisely that [Buddha’s] manifestation.
Now, it is said that the first phrase of the four-line verse is not different from the upper line, because the first of the four lines contains only the *kṣetra* (land/support).

The lower line is not different from the second of the four lines, because the second of the four lines contains only the *sambhoga* (manifestation). If one further attempts to defend this by saying that those four...

Within the phrases, that which is capable of identity can immediately form a single [identity]; these latter two phrases can immediately form a pair. Why then do you say they are not different? Later, it is further explained:
"The capacity for identity may be either single or paired, yet its substance is entirely relinquished; there remains only that which is identical.

Because it is either the land or the body, they are not different. Therefore, the *Chao* states: "Because they mutually negate one another through mutual identity, the six [realms] do not exist. Even if..."

An objection is raised: "The basis (*āśraya*) of this Buddha is precisely the basis-and-supported (*āśraya-ālambana*) of that Buddha; the supported (*ālambana*) of this Buddha is precisely the supported-and-basis of that Buddha.

Since these two phrases preserve both the basis and the supported simultaneously, are they not different? If one allows them to be different, it would result in six propositions. Now, the response further clarifies:
"They are also not different from the third proposition among the four propositions. If that were so, [the fourth...]"
Regarding the third phrase of mutual existence and the fourth phrase of mutual negation: are they mutually identical, or are they not mutually identical?
If you say they are mutually identical, how can the two phrases of "body" and "land" possess substantiality when both are actually without substantiality?

If they are not mutually identical, how then can the gate of identity fulfill the required number of phrases? Moreover, within the gate of dependent origination, that which possesses substantiality and that which lacks substantiality do not coexist. What then of that which lacks substantiality?

Because that which lacks substance cannot coexist [with that which possesses it]. Now, the general explanation states: upon each body and each land, there are two meanings—possessing substance and lacking substance.
The meaning of possessing substance is the "object of identification" (*so-ji*), while the meaning of lacking substance is the "agent of identification" (*no-ji*).

Although these are explained sequentially, their coexistence is simultaneous. Regarding the first two lines, each takes one instance of possessing substance and one instance of lacking substance as they mutually function as...
The identity of the object and the subject: the third phrase takes both objects as identical; the fourth phrase takes both subjects as identical.
Each object-identity corresponds to its respective subject-identity, and each subject-identity corresponds back to its respective object-identity.

This does not mean that the two exist as substantial entities together, nor that the two are simultaneously non-existent. Alternatively, the fact that the two possess substantial existence is the meaning of "non-identity. It is precisely by virtue of this non-identity that...
"Because they are mutually identical. This is known from the *Chao* (Excerpts) itself.

Regarding the statement, "The substance of the *Chao* has no function outside [itself] because it is only mutually identical," this meaning refers to the mutual identity of substance (*ti*) and the mutual entry of function (*yong*).

It signifies that substance and function encompass one another, and identity and entry mutually include one another. Question: Since the substance is already mutually identical, why is the function not [so]?
If functions are already mutually inclusive, why would their essence (*tattva*) not be so? One master says: "The principle is such that the meanings differ;
one should not demand uniformity. Do not challenge one aspect (*mukha*) by means of another. Another master says: "It is indeed so.

When essences and characteristics are mutually identical at that very moment, functions are also mutually identical. When functions are mutually inclusive, essences are also mutually inclusive. Therefore, the Commentary states: "Whichever gate one takes up..."

This encompasses everything. Now it is said: to speak generally, having substance or lacking substance, having function or lacking function—this is the gate of the mutual dependence of conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Mutual identity and mutual inclusion, however, are the profound gates (*gūḍha-mukha*). For example, the Buddha’s entire body is clearly manifested within a single atom;
how is this not profound and mysterious? Since the profound gate of mutual inclusion has already been established, both [substance and function] exist.
If their substance were not established as dependent origination, how could the Buddha’s body exist within those particles?
This is because a single particle possesses the power to act as the grasper, while the Buddha’s body lacks the power to be the grasped. That which lacks power must rely on that which possesses power;

that which possesses power must depend on that which lacks power. Thus, the principle of dependent origination is established, serving as the reason for the mutual penetration of appearances. This meaning is based solely on existence.
The reason why effort can encompass that which is entered is because there is no effort to encompass that which enters.
Their essence and their characteristics enter one another; it is not meant that only the characteristics enter while the essence does not. It is like a bracelet being gold:
when the bracelet is discarded, its substance is simply the substance of gold. This is the profound gate of mutual identity (*xiangji*). Why is it that the bracelet is simply gold?
This is because the bracelet has no separate substance apart from the gold that constitutes it; whereas the gold possesses its own intrinsic substance and is able to form the bracelet.

Therefore, the bracelet is in turn nothing other than the gold. This is the principle of dependent origination through mutual reliance, the reason why the characteristic of the effect is identical to the characteristic of the cause.
This mind possesses substantiality and is able to establish that which lacks substantiality; it is merely a matter of mutual dependence within dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

This functioning of characteristics is precisely the reason for the "Mysterious Gate" (*xuanmen*). That is to say, it is not only that substance and characteristic do not mutually subsume one another, but rather that they do not fail to mutually subsume one another.
Now, based on the gate of dependent origination, because substance and function mutually encompass one another, the gates of entry likewise fully include one another.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that “a single path leads to the fruit,” there are two interpretations. First, it refers to a single cause and a single fruit.
Second, it signifies that the myriad sages and thousands of worthies all cultivate the myriad practices together, following no divergent paths; this is the meaning of “the one path.”
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra*, "If this stage did not exist, practice would not be accomplished," the subsequent commentary explains that there are briefly ten meanings.

First, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts, there are five stages. 1. The Stage of Provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*): This refers to the three levels of the *Śaikṣas*. From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), one accumulates merit and wisdom as provisions for the Path.
For the sake of sentient beings, one cultivates the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*). 2. The Stage of Application (*prayoga-avasthā*)...
Once the *mokṣabhāgīya* (aids to liberation) have been perfected, one further cultivates the *prayoga* (preparatory application) in order to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

This consists of the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), which are also called the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (aids to penetration). Third is the stage of realization (*prativedha-avasthā*), which is the path of seeing; this refers to the two types of paths of seeing that first enter the stages (*bhūmi*).
Fourth is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), beginning from the second stage up to the diamond-like immediate mind (*vajropama-anantarya-citta*).

The stage is called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Fifth is the Stage of Ultimate Perfection (*niṣṭhāgata-bhūmi*): following the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it encompasses all states until the end of the future.
Second, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She-lun), Chapter Six, there are said to be four stages: first, the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

Beginning from the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and ending with the stages prior to the *bhūmis* (the stage of preparation), the remaining three [stages]—namely, the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) and the two ultimate stages—are identical to the latter three among the five [stages].

These three are based on what is taught in the forty-seventh fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Regarding the thirteen abodes (*trayodaśa-vihāra*), the first is the abode of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*).

This refers to that bodhisattva whose nature is inherently benevolent and virtuous, who naturally accomplishes the merits of a bodhisattva, and who maintains the seeds of all Buddha-dharmas; his nature is free from...
Coarse defilements cannot manifest as higher afflictive entanglements.

Second is the stage of dwelling in conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*), which refers to all bodhisattva practices from the initial generation of the mind of awakening until one has not yet attained pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*). Third is the stage of extreme joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).

4. Higher training in ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*). 5. Higher training in mind (*adhicitta*). 6, 7, and 8 are called the three divisions of higher training in wisdom (*adhiprajñā*); these refer to: 6.
The dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); 7. The dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths (*satya*); 8.
The dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the forward and reverse progression of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). 9. The dwelling with effort in the signless (*animitta*). 10.

The dwelling in signlessness and effortlessness; the eleventh, the dwelling of the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); the twelfth, the supreme bodhisattva dwelling; and the thirteenth, the supreme Tathāgata dwelling.
The second [dwelling] corresponds to the three stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). From the third onwards, they correspond respectively to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The fourth [section] also relies on the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the seventh chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, which establish ten stages (*bhūmi*) within the thirteen abodes (*vihāra*).

These are: first, the stage of the nature of the lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*); second, the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); third, the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), which comprises the first three abodes;
fourth, the stage of correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti-bhūmi*), referring to the fourth through the ninth abodes; and fifth, the stage of certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*), which is the tenth abode.

Sixth is the Stage of Definitive Practice (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*), which is the eleventh dwelling (*vihāra*). Seventh, the final two dwellings constitute the Stage of Ultimate Attainment (*nisthā-gamana-bhūmi*).

Regarding the first six stages, they pertain exclusively to Bodhisattvas; the seventh stage is established as a ground shared by both Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas. This is based on the explanation in the lower fascicle of the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra).
Thirteen Dharma Masters each abide in a single position: first, the lineage of practice (*śikṣā-gotra*); second, the innate lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*); third... [and so forth].

1. The lineage of the path-essence (*mārgākāra-gotra*). 2. The Mahāyāna of excellent awakening. 3. Virtuous wisdom (*guṇa-prajñā*). 4. Luminous wisdom (*vidyā-prajñā*). 5. Suchness-flame (*tathatā-jvālā*). 6. Supreme penetration (*abhyudgata-prativedha*). 7.

Constant manifestation of reality (*satya-sadā-pratyakṣa*). 8. Mysterious penetration (*gambhīra-prativedha*). 9. Equal awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which corresponds to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). 10.

Wisdom-light supernormal transformation (*prajñāloka-ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*), which corresponds to the ninth stage. 11. Contemplation of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which in meaning corresponds to the tenth stage and equal awakening. And...
The Buddha is not included within the number thirteen. The six [categories] rely on the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra), upper fascicle. The five patiences (*kṣānti*) are:

the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*), the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*), the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*), the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*), and the patience of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*). Each of these has superior, middling, and inferior grades, which correspond respectively to the stages of the three levels of worthiness (*trīṇi śaikṣāṇi*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
The seven [categories] also rely on the *Renwang jing*, regarding the fifty-two stages. The eight [categories] rely on the *Ratnakaranda-śrī-sūtra* (Yingluo jing), regarding the forty [stages].

Second, the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*). This is because the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are not established as a separate category, as they are subsumed within the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).

According to the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Ābharaṇa-sūtra*), there are six types of lineage (*gotra*): first, the lineage of practice; second, the lineage of nature; third, the lineage of the path; and fourth, the lineage of the noble ones.

Fifth, the nature of equal enlightenment; sixth, the nature of wondrous enlightenment. Furthermore, according to the lower fascicle of the *Yao* (p. 18, recto, line 2), these are also called the six firmnesses (*ṣaḍ-dṛḍha*):

namely, firmness of faith, firmness of the Dharma, firmness of cultivation, firmness of virtue, firmness of the summit, and firmness of awakening. They are also called the six patiences (*ṣaḍ-kṣānti*):

namely, patience of faith, patience of the Dharma, patience of cultivation, right patience, stainless patience, and patience of all-knowledge. They are also called the six wisdoms: the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection... [the wisdom of cultivation].
Wisdom, cultivated wisdom, signless wisdom, wisdom that illuminates stillness, and wisdom that is still while illuminating—these are called the six contemplations.

They are known as the contemplation of abiding, the contemplation of practice, the contemplation of orientation, the contemplation of the stages, the signless contemplation, and the contemplation of all-aspect omniscience. There is also a traditional transmission that speaks of the six concentrations.

The *Yingluo* (Garland) lacks this text. Regarding what are called the "six concentrations" (*ṣaḍ-samādhi*): first, the concentration of practicing characteristics; second, the concentration of nature; third, the concentration of the wisdom of the path;

fourth, the concentration of the wisdom of the aspects of the path; fifth, the concentration of great wisdom; and sixth, the concentration of correct contemplation. These five types of six [categories] all take the fifth as [their basis].

One should [realize] Equal Enlightenment. (From this point onward, it is again the previous commentary. According to the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other sutras, there are no further stages (*bhūmi*). However, based on this sutra, forty-two stages are taught.

There are no separate names such as "provisional equipment" (*sambhāra*) or "preparatory application" (*prayoga*). Nevertheless, the stages thus described are established according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
they are both sequential and holistic, with neither aspect being obstructed. The commentary states: It is not only this sutra that uniquely elucidates the stages.
These are indeed the remaining teachings, each manifesting its own gradations of stages, intended to guide all sentient beings so that they may together ascend to the realm of the sages.
As for the commentary on the second assembly regarding "clarifying faith" and so forth: "faith" refers to the ten levels of faith.

First is the mind of faith (believing in the Buddha’s eternal abiding, the Mahāyāna teachings, and taking refuge in the non-dual ultimate truth with certainty and unimpededness). collectively, they are termed "perfect fusion."
Regarding the statement in the *Commentary* that the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" speaks of "cutting off one [delusion] and thereby cutting off all," a question is raised:

Once the stage of the fulfillment of faith has completely severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), are further afflictions severed upon reaching the stages of the "dwelling" (*vihāra*) and so forth? If there were [further afflictions to be severed], the previous stage would not constitute a complete severance;

if there were none, then the subsequent stages would be established in vain. A certain master answers: "It is simply that the afflictions already severed previously are [now seen as] the essence illuminated by wisdom."

Because emptiness is fundamentally pure, it is called "perfectly severed. From the perspective of the meaning of the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*, its provisional marks persist eternally;
thus, it is further said that there is a sense of mutual, perfect non-interruption. Just as fire in a mirror has no actual burning or heat, so too are essence and function:

they resemble afflictions that are fundamentally empty yet have persisting provisional marks, and they resemble afflictions that are provisionally existent. This is the meaning: when wisdom illuminates them, their essence is one with emptiness.

All things are entirely empty; this is termed "perfect severance. Yet, conventional characteristics persist, and thus afflictions remain in subsequent stages. This has already answered the previous objection. Now, one should question them:
does the meaning of the emptiness of the essence of afflictions, and the meaning of its primordial purity, belong to the category of "severance" or to the category of "non-severance"?

If it belonged to the former, it would contradict both scripture and reasoning. From the perspective of the meaning of the emptiness of essence, it is identical to the true essence and is therefore not subject to severance. If...

It is said that they are not severed. Why? Because wisdom illuminates that their essence is empty and fundamentally pure; therefore, it is called "perfect severance" (*pariccheda*). One should further question them:

as for the remaining provisional marks (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*), are these the dharmas to be severed? If they are the dharmas to be severed, they should have been severed in the preceding stage and should not persist into the subsequent one.
If they are not the dharmas to be severed, then in the subsequent stage there would still be no afflictions to be severed. Regarding this difficulty, one must apply diligent effort.

Regarding the power [of the path], I shall now explain it generally. It is like viewing the moon from a solitary boat upon a clear river: two boats in the north view the same single moon for a thousand *li*;
two boats in the south view the same single moon for a thousand *li*. The single moon in the north is not the one in the south; the single moon in the south is not the one in the north.
Likewise, the delusions severed at a preceding stage are not the delusions severed at a subsequent stage; they are not the same as those previously traversed.
It is like this: there are two boats in the north. One boat remains stationary while observing the moon, and that moon remains entirely in the north of it.

The other boat travels southward until it reaches the position where the southern boat is looking at the moon. The moon observed from the northern boat follows the boat to the south and merges indistinguishably with the moon seen from the south, becoming one.
Yet the moon remaining in the north stays entirely in the north and does not become partially situated there, just as in its previous position.

The delusions are entirely present in the preceding stage, yet they do not abide there partially; this is the meaning of sequential progression (*xingbu*). When the moon comes to the south, it comes entirely to the south rather than coming there partially;

this refers to the delusions of the subsequent stage. These delusions are entirely the delusions of the subsequent stage, yet they are not partial; this is the meaning of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).
Regarding the two boats in the south, one boat remains stationary while observing the moon, which is entirely situated in the south; the other boat travels northward directly.
When one arrives at the northern boat and looks at the moon, the moon seen from the south follows the northward movement of the boat and merges indistinguishably with that northern moon.
Yet the moon remaining in the south stays entirely in the south and does not stay partially there;
this is like a later delusion that exists entirely in its own position rather than staying partially. The moon coming to the north stays entirely in the north.
It is not that they come from separate parts; rather, it is the delusions of the preceding stage in their entirety, yet not as separate parts. This is the meaning of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).

Thus, one knows that while there are two months in the north, there is one month of the original resident and one month of the newly arrived; by combining the new with the original, [they become one].

Since they constitute the same single month, it is known that there are two types of delusions in the preceding stage: one delusion from the original stage and one delusion that arrives from the subsequent stage.

Thus, the subsequent stage consists of these two, which together with the original delusion constitute a single [composite] delusion. The case of two delusions in the subsequent stage should be understood by analogy with this.

In the south there are two months: one month for those who have long resided there, and one month for those newly arrived. By combining the new with the original, they are unified into a single month.
In the center of the north, one wishes to stir up that month; within the preceding state, one wishes to sever delusion through wisdom.

When one examines the nature of that month, it is fundamentally empty; its essence is eternally moist and requires no further stirring. How much less, then, does it matter whether it is stirred or not?

Picking them out is no different [from the previous case]. When discussing the essence of those delusions, it is fundamentally empty; its nature is eternally true and does not require further severance. Moreover, whether severed or unsevered, it is always one.

When discussing the appearance of that moon, it exists only as a provisional construct; its form is round and white, and thus requires provisional picking. Once picked, it becomes non-existent; if unpicked, it appears to exist.
When discussing the appearance of those delusions, they exist only as provisional constructs; their form is that of saṃsāra. Therefore, they must be provisionally severed.

If severed, it becomes non-existent; if not severed, it exists. Just as one uses a pole to remove the appearance of the moon, so too does one give rise to wisdom and severance to eliminate false conceptualization.
When the pole is used to remove the moon in the north, it is not only the old moon dwelling in the north that is absent;
even the new moon coming from the south and arriving in the north lacks its prior position. Likewise, when wisdom severs delusion, it is not only the original [delusion] that is gone.
When the afflictions of the preceding stage have perished alone, yet the afflictions of the subsequent stage are subsumed [within that process] until those of the preceding stage also perish;

thus it is known that the principle of "one severed, all severed" is established. When the moon has not yet moved south from the north, it is not only the old moon residing in the south that remains, but the new moon arriving from the north and reaching the south also remains.
This is likewise when the wisdom of the subsequent stage has not yet severed the afflictions. It is not...

Only the afflictions of the subsequent stage remain originally, yet they encompass the afflictions of the preceding stages; when the afflictions of the subsequent stage persist, it is known that when one is not abandoned, all are not abandoned.
Do not raise the objection: "Once the afflictions of the preceding stage have been severed, what afflictions would there be to be encompassed?
For they have been constantly encompassed since beginningless time. Do not raise the objection: "Once the moon has already moved north, how could there be a moon coming from the south?"

Because it has already been discussed previously. The preceding analogies and teachings have been assigned to their respective sections with such clarity that they are as plain as if held in the palm of one's hand;
do not remain stuck in conventional views or fall into frivolous laughter.
If this commentary (*chao*) accomplishes these ten points, then the sutra below says: "That is to say, the mind does not abandon any sentient being."
They are born, and so forth, until they dwell in all worlds with minds free from attachment; these constitute the ten [practices]. (This is the exhortation to practice.
Thus, one immediately accomplishes fifty kinds of practices. Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells securely in these ten dharmas, they are then able to fulfill ten kinds of purity and ten kinds of vast wisdom."

This refers to the seeds that universally enter the ten kinds of supreme and wondrous minds and the ten kinds of skillful wisdom regarding the Buddha-dharma. (The commentary states: These are listed extensively in the sutra;

thus, through such successive stages, all are accomplished by first cultivating these ten dharmas—hence it is said as follows). Regarding the statement, "If a single thought of anger arises, one million gates of obstruction are produced," the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* chapter of the sutra says:
"O Son of the Buddha, I do not see a single dharma that constitutes a greater fault than this."
One loses [merit] as do those bodhisattvas who give rise to a mind of anger toward other bodhisattvas. Why is this?
O Son of the Buddha, if any bodhisattvas give rise to a mind of malice toward another bodhisattva, they immediately bring about one million gateways of obstacles.

(From the second half of the eighth fascicle of the Sub-commentary) The commentary states: Since a single delusion constitutes one million gateways of obstruction, the principle that "one obstruction is all obstructions" applies equally to every delusion.
Now, speaking from the perspective of what is most grave, if one searches exhaustively beyond anger, there is no other evil as heavy as anger.
Therefore, the Jin translation says: "To give rise to a single thought of anger is [the gravest] among all evils."

There is no evil greater than this. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "It would be better to give rise to a hundred thousand thoughts of poverty than to give rise to a single thought of anger;
for nothing violates and harms great compassion more than this. The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* also speaks in the same way.
Regarding the phrase "toward another bodhisattva," if one gives rise to anger toward a bodhisattva, the transgression is even more grave, as it causes [the cessation of] the bodhi-mind.

Because they abandon the Great Practice, for this reason, within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, when the celestial Māras see various Bodhisattvas mutually criticizing one another, they always rejoice greatly.
Although the [obstructions] are enumerated as one million, I shall briefly list them in one hundred categories. Ancient masters categorized them by stages into five groups.

First, from "not seeing the obstacle to Bodhi" downwards are forty obstacles; these correspond to the ten stages of faith and practice (*daśa-śraddhā-caryā*). (According to the Sūtra, there are thirty-three "obstacle" characters; the subsequent opening...)

(8) Because of these eight [factors], there are forty-two obstacles: (1) the obstacle of not delighting in the Buddha-dharma, which comprises nine obstacles; (2) the stage of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*);
(3) the obstacle of not attaining the faculties of a bodhisattva, which comprises eleven obstacles; (4) the stage of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*);

(5) the obstacle of delighting in slandering the words of the Omniscient One, which comprises five obstacles; (6) the stage of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*); (7) the obstacle of not delighting in dwelling together with bodhisattvas, which comprises three [obstacles].
There are fourteen obstacles to the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Therefore, the previous conclusion stated: "The myriad practices of a Bodhisattva do not exceed these five;

yet if even a single thought of anger arises, they are all immediately obstructed. This explanation is not without reason. However, if one seeks the Dharma with a thieving mind, how could it merely obstruct the stages?
It should be understood that this universally obstructs everything; if even faith does not arise, how much more so the subsequent stages?
Furthermore, the dharma-realm that is obstructed is like a celestial net (indrajāla), layer upon layer; the obstructions themselves, being identical to what is obstructed, are likewise inexhaustible.
Thus, one should know that even "one million" is merely a brief explanation.
The commentary states: "If one does not take the principle as the substance, then practice is also not true.

This is like bowing to a high minister while dreaming (cultivating to attain the rank of Mahābrahmā while the mind is deluded), which does not compare to becoming a commandant while awake (attaining entry into the stage of the Ten Faiths upon awakening).

It is like obtaining the seven treasures in a dream (cultivating immeasurable merit while deluded), which does not compare to obtaining a hundred coins while awake (attaining entry into the observance of the five precepts and ten wholesome actions upon awakening). In all cases, because one is false and the other is true, they cannot be equated. (Various Teachings...)

All say that giving away the seven treasures throughout the three thousandfold world-system is not equal to hearing a single verse; this is the intended meaning. The Dharma and its metaphors are clear and manifest, so students may fully understand them.
"That which encompasses the nature-virtues (*xingde*) as its essence" refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*) among the five dharmas, and to this *nirvāṇa* among the two bases.

"That which relies on the ocean of wisdom as its source" refers to Correct Wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) among the five dharmas, and to Bodhi among the two bases. "But when appearances transform and the essence differs" means that when one is deluded regarding True Suchness, names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) are established.

"Sentimentality creates a barrier to wisdom" means that one loses correct wisdom and falls into deluded thought. "Now, I shall cause [you] to... (this explicitly clarifies the meaning of opening up): to know the mind is to realize that names and characteristics are fundamentally empty;

to merge with the essence is to unite with the fundamental substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*); to reach the root is to realize that the root is originally non-abiding; and for sentimentality to perish is for deluded sentiment to vanish and correct wisdom to arise.

Regarding the statement that "the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally non-abiding," this refers to the second chapter of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, which investigates the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Thus, the sutra says: "What is the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome? The answer is: "The body is the root. Again it asks: "What is the root of the body?
The answer is: "Desire and greed are the root. Again it asks: "What is the root of desire and greed? The answer is: "False conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is the root."
[The interlocutor] asked: "Furthermore, what is the root of false discrimination? He replied: "Inverted perception is the root.
[The interlocutor] asked again: "What is the root of inverted perception? He replied: "Non-abiding is the root. [The interlocutor] asked again: "What is the root of non-abiding?"
The answer is: "Non-abiding is itself the absence of a fundamental basis. Mañjuśrī, from this non-abiding basis, all dharmas are established.
Master Rui’s commentary states: "Non-abiding is another name for the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).

Regarding the statement that 'the true basis cannot be accomplished through effort,' Kumārajīva said: 'The establishment of the Way cannot be attained by setting up deliberate effort; noble wisdom cannot [be produced in such a manner]...'"
Because one knows through the existence of mind, the True Truth cannot be realized through the persistence of the self;

because ultimate merit cannot be achieved through the management of affairs, only the cessation of speech can be made to accord with the Way (*dharma*), and only an empty mind can penetrate principle (*li*). One whose mind is darkened in stillness can be unified with the Real, and one who has cast away intellect can be identical with the Sage.
This is fully cited in the *Commentary on the "Inquiry into Clarity" Chapter* (*Wenming-pin Sū-chāo*); those in need should consult it further.

Examination: Regarding the statement that "tranquility and illumination flow as one," this refers to cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), essence and wisdom (*jñāna-prajñā*), substance and function (*tattva-vṛtti*), and bodhi and nirvāṇa.
The commentary uses a single term to reveal [this truth] so that one may know there are two aspects, thereby enabling the practitioner to realize and enter into their manifestation.
This refers precisely to sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation. Fearing that the principle may be difficult to clarify, I shall employ analogies for illustration.

Just as when water (the true mind) is stirred by the wind (ignorance deluding the mind), it forms many waves (boundless afflictions), there arises the calamity of drifting and drowning (transmigration through the six realms).

Or, when the influence of cold and darkness (the nature of wisdom obscured by ignorance and craving) freezes into ice (rigid attachment to the four elements and material obstructions), it blocks irrigation (being unable to rain down the great Dharma rain to provide nourishment).

It serves the function of moistening and nourishing the sprouts of the Way for all living beings, and washing away the defilements of afflictions and transgressions that cannot otherwise be removed. (Yet it cannot give rise to the wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

However, the moist nature of water, whether in motion or stillness, whether frozen or flowing, has never changed; even when greed and anger arise, it knows them, and when compassion and salvation are exercised, it knows them. Amidst the various fluctuations of sorrow, joy, grief, and pleasure, it has never failed to know them.

Therefore it is said that [the nature] does not change. Now, through sudden awakening, one realizes the fundamental permanence and knows that the moisture-nature of the *tathatā* (suchness) is unchanging. Since the mind is no longer deluded, it is no longer ignorance.
Just as when the wind suddenly ceases, after awakening, the grasping at objects naturally subsides gradually, like waves gradually coming to rest.

By means of meditative concentration and wisdom, one nurtures and perfumes the body and mind, gradually attaining mastery and unimpeded spiritual transformations to universally benefit all sentient beings.

This is like the melting of ice by the spring sun, which irrigates and washes away impurities to bring beneficial benefits to all things. Fools often say that greed, anger, kindness, and compassion are all Buddha-nature and ask what difference there is between them.
It is like a person who observes only the quality of moisture and, from beginning to end, feels no fear.
One knows that the merit and fault of saving a drowning person versus overturning a boat are vastly different.

Regarding the statement "revealing, awakening, entering, and realizing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," according to the sub-commentary (*śūcāo*) below, there have been many ancient interpretations.

First, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fahua lun) commentary explains: "Revealing" (*kāi*) has the meaning of "unsurpassed" (this is the title designated in the treatise). This means that apart from the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is nothing further...

Other matters. (The "opening" [kāi] refers to the *sarvajñajñāna*. "All-knowledge" (*sarvajña*) is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). To speak of it again as "wisdom" is the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

Fundamental wisdom is called "knowing" (*jñāna*), while subsequently attained wisdom is called "seeing" (*darśana*). Apart from these two matters, there is nothing else that can surpass them; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed. This immediately opens up *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. (This explains the "all-knowledge wisdom" that was opened.

That is to say, the nature of knowing and seeing is *nirvāṇa*, while the characteristics of knowing and seeing are *bodhi*. (This is the commentary by the *Lun* [Treatise] on the meaning of "opening. Master Qingliang’s commentary states:

Sentient beings possess this from the very beginning (consisting of both the *dharmatā-nirvāṇa* of original existence and the *bodhi* of original enlightenment). Because it is obscured by hindrances and does not manifest, the Buddha removes them;

thus, original wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) becomes manifest. Regarding the term "opening" (*kai*), Ci'en’s commentary explains: "Opening" means the sense of giving birth to, manifesting, and realizing. (This refers to the meaning of the Faxiang school:

that based on the four kinds of wisdom-seeds of original existence, the four kinds of wisdom-bodhi are born, thereby manifesting and realizing the *tathatā*-nirvāṇa. However, in the present Dharmatā school, the principle is not so. One knows and perceives that the characteristics of phenomena are all, from the very beginning, the radiance of great wisdom.)

Because it universally illumines the meaning of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*): stillness itself is the nature of knowing-and-seeing, and illumination is the function of knowing-and-seeing. When these characteristics reside in the cause, they constitute the nature; when they reside in the fruit, they constitute Bodhi and Nirvāṇa. Although sentient beings possess this from the beginning, it does not manifest due to obscurations. The obstacle of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) obscures Bodhi, and the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) obscures Nirvāṇa.
When both obstacles are absent, Bodhi and Nirvāṇa are simultaneously manifested. "To show" has the same meaning as [the previous point], because the Two Vehicles share the same Dharma-body.

"To specifically show the nature of knowing-and-seeing" is for the purpose of establishing Nirvāṇa. "Awakening" means not knowing; because they do not know that there is only this single reality, the present teaching causes them to know it, thereby bringing it to completion.

Because it is the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) bodhi. (The single reality is precisely the knowledge and vision; by separately demonstrating the characteristics of knowledge and vision, one accomplishes bodhi.

"Entering" means causing one to realize the stage of non-retrogression; this is the meaning of "cause. That is to say, having realized the first bhūmi and above, it serves as the cause for bodhi and nirvāṇa.

(Realizing suchness upon attaining the bhūmis is the cause for nirvāṇa; the wisdom that realizes the bhūmis is the cause for bodhi. Second, Dharma Master Xixiang said: "Opening and showing" refers to the capacity to transform others, while "awakening and entering" [refers to the capacity to be transformed].

Regarding those to be transformed (*vineya*), there are two modes of transformation: the "Great Opening" (*mahā-vivaraṇa*) and the "Indirect Demonstration" (*kuṭila-nidarśana*). To speak only of the existence of the nature (*dhātu*) is called the "Great Opening.

To state, "This is the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)," "This is the nature of noble ones (*ārya*"), and to explain the principles of cause and effect and the practice [of the path] is called the "Indirect Demonstration. Regarding those to be transformed, there are two stages: initial awakening and final entry. To suddenly and completely understand is termed "Awakening" (*bodha*);

this refers to the sudden awakening to the nature elucidated above. To practice and realize through accord is termed "Entry" (*praveśa*); this refers to the gradual cultivation and realization of the causal dharma demonstrated previously. Furthermore, Qingliang [Xuanzang] said: "The 'Opening' removes delusion..."

[This] obstructs [delusion], reveals the ultimate truth, causes one to realize the emptiness of essence, and leads to the realization of the nature of mind. The Northern School of the Three Dhyāna Gates says: "The non-movement of the mind is 'opening.
Opening refers to opening the gate of expedient means. Non-movement is 'indicating. Indicating refers to indicating the true aspect.

Awakening means that delusive thoughts do not arise; entering means that all phenomena are eternally quiescent. Furthermore, regarding "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*), it is explained as the function of wisdom.

Thus it is known: when wisdom functions as this seeing, and the mind does not arise, it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*). When knowledge can know that the five faculties are immovable, it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
Wisdom is able to see; this is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The Fourth Southern School says: "Sentient beings’ Buddha-wisdom is falsely obstructed and thus not seen.
If one simply attains non-thought, then the fundamental and the derivative self-nature are opened through stillness. Within this stillness, there is inherently original wisdom. By means of...

This fundamental wisdom is able to see that the original self-nature is inherently quiescent; this is called "pointing out. Once it has been pointed out, one immediately perceives the fundamental nature.

That Buddhas and sentient beings have been fundamentally non-different is "awakening. After awakening, whether all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena exist or whether Buddhas appear or not, one constantly perceives the fundamental nature.
Because one knows for oneself that delusive thoughts lack inherent nature through the self-awakened noble wisdom, this is *bodhi*.

That which was known by the sages of the past and transmitted from one to another is precisely the meaning of "entry. Regarding the term "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*), the sub-commentary (Volume 10, Part 31, Middle) further states that there are two senses:

first, the specific sense, wherein "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is wisdom (*jñāna*)—the provisional wisdom that illuminates phenomena—and "vision" (*darśana*) is insight (*prajñā*)—the ultimate wisdom that illuminates principle.
Second, the general sense, wherein both characters "knowledge" and "vision" refer to the Tathāgata’s capacity to realize and know reality as it truly is.

Because it is the meaning [of direct perception]. It is precisely the unobstructed wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*). If this is so, why employ these redundant terms? They are used to distinguish it from inferential knowledge (*anumānajñāna*);

thus, it is called "seeing" (*darśana*), for inferential knowledge—such as seeing smoke and knowing fire—is unable to illuminate the distinctions between various characteristics. They are also used to distinguish it from the vision of the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*);
thus, it is called "knowing" (*jñāna*), for the fleshly eye of the desire realm cannot know subtle forms, distant objects, or things that contradict its nature; it merely follows what others say.

The *Chao* states that the Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*zheng yin*) serves as the cause (this is the Buddha-nature of principle), while the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause (*yuan yin*) serves as the condition (this is the Buddha-nature of practice).

That which is realized by the revealing cause (*liao yin*) is the cause (the seed abiding in the original nature), and that which is produced by the producing cause (*sheng yin*) is the condition (the seed accomplished through cultivation). Therefore, that sutra says:
"The Buddha-seed (the direct cause) arises from conditions" (the conditional cause). Generally speaking, there are four kinds of Buddha-nature: first, the Buddha-nature as the direct cause.
First, the nature of the cause (dharmatā-buddha-nature) is the sentient being itself, because it serves as the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*) for the production of curd from milk.

Second, the causal condition (pratyaya-buddha-nature) consists of virtuous friends, correct teachings, and the myriad practices; these serve as conditions such as warmth and yeast through skillful means (*upāya*).

The resulting Buddha-fruit is like the curd that is produced. Third, the direct cause (direct buddha-nature) refers to the aforementioned two natures—the direct and the conditional—which are capable of...

The cultivation of birth [in the stages] leading to the fruition of Buddhahood are all the direct causes (*hetu-bīja*), just as a seed gives rise to a sprout. Fourth is the Buddha-nature as the revealing cause (*parijñā-hetu*);
with the exception of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), everything else can manifest the primordially existing fruit of Buddhahood, and is thus further termed the revealing cause.
Because it is like a lamp that reveals a treasure, the Great Commentary states: "That which can produce the fruit of Buddhahood is called the producing cause (*janakahetu*).
There are two kinds of causes for the Buddha-nature of sentient beings: first, the direct cause (*dharmatāhetu*); second, the contributing cause (*pratyayahetu*).

The direct cause refers to all sentient beings; therefore, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are themselves the direct cause. The contributing cause refers to the six *pāramitās*. It is not [the case that...]"

The mutual arising of the aggregates is called "condition" (*pratyaya*). However, this very causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is itself the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*). It is not necessarily the case that a revealing cause is [itself] a condition;

for among conditions and causes, there is a distinction between the proximate and the remote. A virtuous friend is a conditional cause, yet he is necessarily a revealing cause of the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
This refers to the *vijñapti-hetu* (revealing cause); it is not necessarily the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause), as this is based on the nature of wisdom (that is, its fundamental nature;

as the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because it possesses the meaning of the great light of wisdom," and so forth). If one takes ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) to be the Buddha-nature, it is solely the *hetu-hetu* (causal factor) and not the *vijñapti-hetu*.
It is merely that which is revealed by the *vijñapti-hetu*, rather than being produced by the *hetu-hetu*. If one takes wisdom...

That which constitutes the Buddha-nature is the *jñāna-hetu* (the cause as illumination). If one takes the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) to be the Buddha-nature, it is called the *dhātu-hetu* (the causal substance);

it is also termed the *dhātu-hetu*. Furthermore, arising necessarily corresponds to illumination, and the causal substance necessarily corresponds to conditions. Moreover, there are four kinds [of these].
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Buddha-nature has a cause, it has the cause of the cause; it has a fruit, and it has the fruit of the fruit.
The 'cause' refers to the twelve links of dependent origination. The 'cause of the cause' is termed wisdom. The 'fruit' is great bodhi. The 'fruit of the fruit' is called great nirvāṇa.
Now, when we speak of the Buddha-nature, it should be explained by assigning these categories accordingly.

The *Shu* (Commentary) further states: "Suppose there were bodhisattvas... The subsequent commentary explains: "If one does not rely on this teaching, even if one practices for many kalpas, it will still not be truly real;
how much less could one swiftly attain bodhi? Regarding the phrase "suppose there were" (*she you*) used here:

It appears that this is merely a provisional hypothesis. Maitreya praised Sudhana, saying: "Other bodhisattvas require hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas to fulfill the vows and practices of a bodhisattva, yet now Sudhana is able to purify Buddha-fields and so forth in a single lifetime. This is an instance of using the provisional to reveal the ultimate; it is not a mere hypothesis.
