This has already been discussed in terms of coarse impermanence. It is also said: "The impermanence of a single lifetime is a law of rapid decay and cannot be relied upon.
This refers to subtle impermanence. It is also said: "Momentary impermanence. If one awakens to impermanence, [liberation] can be attained.

The four fruits of the śramaṇa. Regarding the *Fahua yaocao* (Excerpts on the Lotus Sutra), which states that there is no longer a combination of the "exclusive" and "inclusive" [teachings], but rather speaks only of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*):
Question: The *Lotus Sutra* says, "The three realms have no peace; they are like a burning house. The world is not solid;

it is like foam, bubbles, or flames. This refers to the Treasury Teaching (*zangjiao*). It further says, "We all equally enter the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). This refers to the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). [Then it mentions] the Golden Color...
Thirty-two. The ten powers and various liberations are all within a single dharma, yet one does not attain this matter;

it is "great" rather than a "small portion," which is precisely the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). Why, then, do you say that only the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is taught? Answer: All of these are descriptions of past meanings and are not what is ultimately accepted.
Question: The three types of grass and two types of trees are different; is this not the Separate Teaching? Answer: At one time...
Because they are produced from the same source and moistened by the same rain, this belongs to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Regarding the statement:

"Not severing lust, anger, and ignorance" (because they are dependently originated and lack intrinsic nature, they cannot be severed); "nor being accompanied by them" (because they are dependently originated and lack intrinsic nature, they can be severed and extinguished); "not destroying the body" (the ten bodies are distinct, forming a structured array);

"yet conforming to the single characteristic" (the ten bodies manifest their characteristics in perfect fusion); and "without extinguishing delusion and craving, giving rise to clarity and liberation" (delusive thoughts...).
Without being heated, the nature of the hall is transparently empty; the numinous mirror is not polished yet suddenly illuminates the myriad dharmas).
Regarding the analogy of the new and old physicians in the *Yichao* (Commentary on the Meaning), it says: "For example, there was a king who was dull-witted and lacked wisdom.
He had a physician who was stubborn and ignorant, yet the king did not discern this and generously bestowed upon him a high salary. This physician treated various illnesses..."
Regarding the medicinal milk, they likewise do not know the root cause from which the illness arises. Although they prescribe the medicinal milk, they lack skillful understanding;
they instruct those with wind-disorders (*vāta*), cold-disorders, heat-disorders, or any other ailment whatsoever to consume the milk.

Then, there is a skilled physician who understands the eight branches of medical science, excels at treating various diseases, and is well-versed in all prescriptions and medicines; he arrives from a distant land and immediately [acts for them].

The king expounded various medical prescriptions. Upon hearing them, the king developed respectful faith; recognizing that his former [attendants] were foolish and deluded, he expelled them from the country.
He commanded the masses to cease taking milk and treated their various ailments with diverse medicines, whereby they all attained peace and happiness, and so forth.
"The ten paths of wholesome action" refers to abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so on. "To be enlightened regarding the eight" refers to...

Regarding the various arts [of medicine]: first, knowing the nature of the disease; second, knowing the cause of the disease; third, knowing the symptoms of the disease; fourth, knowing the location of the disease; fifth, knowing the timing of the disease;
sixth, knowing the medicine for the disease; seventh, knowing the practitioner; eighth, knowing the prohibitions. As for the five ways of obtaining the precepts:

they are through "Come hither" (ehi-bhikṣu), "seeing the truth" (darśana), "three refuges," "eight respects" (gurudharma), and "formal ritual" (karmavācanā). It is said that there is both "unmanifest" (avijñapti) and "manifest" (vijñapti) action.
"Those" refers to the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). Regarding the statement "the Vinaya of the five schools": first, the Mahāsāṃghika; second, the Dharmaguptaka;
third, the Sarvāstivāda; fourth, the Kāśyapīya; and fifth, the Mahīśāsaka. Regarding the statement "the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*)," this refers to the eight deliverances (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*).

Regarding the statement "entering the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*)," etc., these pertain to the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the [four] formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The four [aggregates] and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Regarding the so-called "sixty-two views": one interpretation states that four views arise with respect to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*):
first, the view of self (*ātman*); second, the view of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), which includes [the categories of] servants (1), ornaments (2), and dwellings (3).
Since there are likewise four such views for each of the remaining four aggregates, this totals twenty. When these are further distinguished according to the three time periods, they become sixty.
Together with the two views regarding one’s own person, these constitute the sixty-two views. This is not the correct enumeration. Second, it is said:

In the *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma), there is a chapter on the sixty-two views, consisting of forty views of eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*), seven views of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), and fifteen views of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Those who require this should consult it. Regarding the statement "eleven knowledges" (*jñāna*): first, dharma-knowledge; second, subsequent knowledge; third, knowledge of suffering; fourth, knowledge of the origin; fifth, knowledge of cessation.

Sixth, the six destinies (*ṣaḍ-gati*). Seventh, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). Eighth, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Ninth, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*). Tenth, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Eleventh, knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

Regarding the three untainted faculties (*trīṇy anāsravendriyāṇi*): first, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*); second, the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*); and third, the faculty of "having fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Regarding the citation from the *Dharmapada*: that sutra contains verses for each of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). The verse on giving (*dāna*) states:

"When one speaks of the merit of various acts of giving, therein the three factors are empty; ultimately they cannot be apprehended; the merit of giving is like a mirage. Regarding precepts (*śīla*), it says:
"If one speaks of various observances of the precepts, there is neither goodness nor dignified conduct; the nature of the precepts is like space."
Regarding "Holding": it is to be deluded and inverted. Regarding "Patience" (Kṣānti): if one sees an angry person, one should take patience as a collar;
knowing that anger and the like are like a mirage, there is nothing for patience to endure. Regarding "Diligence" (Vīrya): if the mind of diligence arises, this is delusion and not true diligence;
if the mind can remain non-delusive, diligence will be boundless. Regarding "Concentration" (Samādhi): if one studies various samādhis...
This movement is not sitting in meditation; the mind flows following after objects. How can this be called samādhi? The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra says:
"The myriad phenomena and all forms are sealed by a single Dharma. Why, within this single Dharma, do you give rise to various views?"
Even "one" is not established as one, for the purpose of destroying all numerical designations. Those of shallow wisdom, upon hearing this, perceive it as "one.

The commentary concludes: "If there are those who hear this Dharma and constantly cultivate the practice of quiescence, knowing that cognition itself is also quiescent—this is the path of the Bodhisattva.
To say that *prajñā* is "without cognition" means that it is free from deluded cognition.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states that regarding the distinct cultivation of the six perfections throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, each has its own time of fulfillment.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter eighteen, explains: "During the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one successively makes offerings to seventy thousand Buddhas, then sixty, fifty, and seven thousand Buddhas.
When the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are completed, one encounters, in reverse order, the Buddhas Vipaśyin, Dīpaṃkara, and Ratnaśikhin."
First, regarding Śākyamuni: the commentary states that within these two verses, the first verse clarifies the number of Buddhas [served] through Dharma-offerings.
That is to say, during the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to seventy-five thousand Buddhas; during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to seventy-six thousand Buddhas;
and during the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to seventy-seven thousand Buddhas. This concludes the subsequent verse.
Regarding the Buddhas he encountered: as for the statement "in reverse order," this refers to the period leading up to the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Specifically, at the completion of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he encountered the Buddha Vipaśyin; at the completion of the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
at the completion of the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he encountered the Buddha Ratnaśikhin; and at his initial generation of the mind of awakening, he encountered Śākyamuni.
The Bhikṣuṇī made a vow, saying: "May I become a Buddha, exactly as the World-Honored One is now.

The preceding section clarified that in the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), one must pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before attaining Buddhahood. I have not yet understood how the time periods and kalpas are reckoned in the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).

According to the subsequent commentary (*Chao*), for instance, if we compare the Sahā world with the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), one kalpa in the former is called a single day in the latter; thus, it is peaceful and blissful.
It takes three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) for [the Buddha] to reach the world-system *Kāṣāyadhvaja*. This is not even a matter of months or years;
how much less so for subsequent world-systems where an eon is reckoned as a single day?

Thus, one cannot determine the number of eons required to attain Buddhahood by classifying them according to this single direction. As for the second type, the "class of world-systems," it refers to those within a single realm.
The various realms possess distinct characteristics; they do not see one another, and their time periods and kalpas differ as well. How could one know the length of their duration?

Thus, the morning mushroom (*chao-jun*) does not know the transition between the dark and the bright [the new moon and the full moon], let alone the spring and autumn; how much less could it comprehend the years of the great cypress (*da-chun*)?
The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "Good son, a bodhisattva cannot conceive of the realm of the Tathāgata; it is beyond measure and calculation. It is only for those who are shallow..."

Regarding those who approach sentient beings, it is said that Bodhi is attained through cultivation over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; yet in reality, from the time the aspiration was first awakened, the duration is incalculable.
The *Xiánshǒu* (Bhadramukha) commentary states: "Incalculable" means an incalculable number of *asaṃkhyeyas*. The *Yìfēnzhì* (Siddhānta-vibhāga) states:
If one follows the Hīnayāna, there are naturally three types of persons. Those of inferior faculties refer to the various *śrāvakas*.
It is heard that for those of the sharpest faculties, the exhaustion of outflows and the attainment of the fruit may occur as quickly as within three lifetimes, or as slowly as after sixty *kalpas*.
Those of middling faculties refer to the Pratyekabuddhas; for them, the attainment of the fruit may occur as quickly as within four lifetimes, or as slowly as after one hundred *kalpas*.

Those of the highest faculties refer to the Buddhas, who certainly require three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Within this context, the number of *kalpas* is calculated by taking one *kalpa* of water, fire, and so forth as a single unit.
Ten "ones" constitute the second number. Continuing in this manner through successive multiplication up to the sixtieth stage, one reaches one *asaṃkhyeya*.
It is by means of this calculation that the three *asaṃkhyeyas* are reckoned. According to the Mahāyāna, the cultivation of practice leading to Buddhahood necessarily traverses three *asaṃkhyeyas*;
however, the calculation of these kalpas differs from that of the Hīnayāna. Why? Because here [in the Mahāyāna], one takes water, fire, and so forth as the basis.
When the number of kalpas reaches one hundred thousand, and that [hundred thousand] again reaches one hundred thousand, it constitutes one *kuli*, which is called the first calculation.
When this *kuli* is counted again until it reaches another *kuli*, it becomes the second calculation.
Following this sequence, by taking such numbers and counting them up to one hundred, it is called one *asaṃkhyeya*. This is the first among the ten great numbers.

First is the calculation. Based on this calculation, it takes three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* to reach completion, yet it is further said that one cultivates the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) for one hundred *kalpas*.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refutes this separate cultivation of the marks, not permitting their cultivation apart from the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; this is precisely the intent of the "True Teaching" (*saddharma*).
However, the intent of the True Teaching itself contains two meanings: first, the fixed duration of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; second, [the inclusion of the hundred *kalpas* within that period].
This is because it is a manifestation of the Buddha’s pedagogical methods (*vyavahāra*), and because he is the true Buddha. The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"He may manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment by transcending the stages for the sake of sentient beings who are timid;
or he may say, 'I shall attain the Buddha-way after immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, for the sake of sentient beings who are indolent. He is thus able to manifest such immeasurable skillful means."

It may seem inconceivable; yet in reality, for Bodhisattvas, their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), faculties (*indriya*), and so forth being equal, their generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) is equal, and what they realize is also equal.
There is no method by which one could surpass another, because all Bodhisattvas must pass through three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas.

This refers to the fixed [teaching]. The second is the unfixed, which further comprises two intentions. First, it is for the purpose of encompassing other miscellaneous types of worlds, as stated in the *Sūtra of the Victorious Heavenly King* (Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra);
this refers to the aforementioned tree-shaped world and so forth. Second, it is based on the fact that the Buddha’s virtues are limitless, as in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*.
If one explains according to the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) through the principle of integration and inclusion, it is as in the case of the seer Vimala.
The person took Sudhana by the hand; because they passed through many kalpas and traversed boundless realms, this cannot be conceived in terms of long or short duration.
If manifested as transcendent excellence, it is perfected instantaneously in a single lifetime; if considered from the perspective of profound depth, it remains inexhaustible even after many kalpas.
Therefore, it is said that one must not adhere rigidly to fixed positions; what is valued is entry into the profound mystery (*xuan*). Regarding the statement "thirty-four moments of mind":

within the sixteen moments of mind, the eight *kṣāntis* (patiences) directly sever the discriminative afflictions of the three realms and, concurrently, sever the innate (*sahaja*) afflictions of the lower eight stages.

Among these, the eight *jñānas* (knowledges) realize the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) manifested by those patiences—namely, the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of the dharma of suffering).

First, the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*); second, the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*); third, the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*); fourth, the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
Since there are four [moments] for the truth of suffering, it is the same for each of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path; thus, there are sixteen.

As for the nine grades of innate afflictions in the single stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they are unsurpassed and not to be desired; the mundane path does not subdue them, and the preceding sixteen moments of mind cannot [subdue them].
They are severed because they arise separately. Nine paths of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) sever the delusions, and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) realize the principle;

together with the preceding sixteen, these constitute thirty-four moments of mind. Question: Since the Mahāyāna is taught within the Tripiṭaka, why did Tiantai not designate it as Hīnayāna, considering it to be in accord with the principle?
Why then did Qingliang establish it as the "Hīnayāna Teaching"? Is this not a contradiction?

The answer is: Tiantai relies solely on what is taught, asserting that because there is Mahāyāna therein, it is Mahāyāna; Qingliang, conversely, relies on the speaker, asserting that because the speaker is exclusively of the Hīnayāna, it is Hīnayāna.
For instance, when the Buddha speaks in a sutra and discusses the doctrines of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), would that not be called the Buddha’s teaching?
Since that [teaching] does not follow what is being said but is named the Buddha’s teaching based solely on the speaker, why should this case be any different?
The commentary states that "it does not explain a distinct principle" means it does not explain the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).

"It does not sever distinct afflictions" means it does not sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which are the objects of wisdom. "The term 'one characteristic and no characteristic' refers to the single characteristic of true emptiness, because it is devoid of those deluded thoughts.
"The phrase 'and because it has already been attained' refers to the previous Hīnayāna teachings (the *piṭaka*), which initially corresponded to the precepts of the 'old physician.'"

Because of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Because one newly attains the physician’s [remedies for] precepts, concentration, and wisdom, the designation "Tripiṭaka" may be established.

Since the subsequent teaching is already encompassed within it, no separate title is established; this is like the stage of the "Extremely Good Ground" (*sudarśana-bhūmi*) or the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), which receive their designation from the very beginning.

Alternatively, since the name "Piṭaka" was already attained through the preceding teaching, the subsequent teaching cannot be established with a new title. If it were to be established anew, there would be redundancy.

Because it is excessive. Regarding the statement "the three types of arising and ceasing are distinct": this is because each of the three trainings possesses immeasurable characteristics, yet all three trainings are unified by a single principle.
Regarding the statement "emptiness of the unobtainable": this refers to emptiness that carries within it wondrous existence.

Regarding the statement "although it speaks of sequential distinctions" and so forth: the meaning is that even within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there exists the principle of sequential arrangement (xingbu).

When [the teaching of] "separate progression" (xingbu) is subsumed within and returned to "perfect interfusion" (yuanrong), it belongs exclusively to the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) and not to the Separate Teaching (biejiao).

If this is so, why does the subsequent section of the *Chao* state: "Being deluded regarding its separate progression, one regards it as the Separate Teaching; taking only its perfect interfusion, one regards it as the Perfect Teaching"? Answer:

That master’s original intent was to subsume the Separate Progression that is accompanied by Perfect Interfusion back into the Perfect Teaching; however, the meaning of Separate Progression practiced in isolation is judged to belong to the Separate Teaching.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* alone possesses two modes of exposition: the sequential exposition prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), which incorporates the perfect interpenetration and is thus categorized as belonging to the Perfect Teaching;
and the sequential exposition from the stages onward, which does not incorporate the perfect interpenetration and is thus categorized as belonging to the Separate Teaching.
Question: For what reason do the holy teachings present these [teachings] alternately? Answer: There is a profound reason for this. Thus, Xianshou said: "For example, within the Three Vehicles..."
Furthermore, there are those who speak of Indra, the subtle [atoms], and so forth, yet they lack the complete relationship between the principal and its attendants (*pramukha-parivāra*).

Or again, some speak of the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃbhava-lokadhātu*), yet do not mention the ten [stages] and so on. Within the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), there are also the doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the Three Vehicles;

that is to say, within the ten eyes, the five eyes are fully contained, and within the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the six supernormal powers are likewise present. Such is the underlying principle (*arthanaya*).
All are distinct; this is the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) that descends into the Three Vehicles, while the Three Vehicles participate in the One Vehicle.

This is the meeting point of the two schools, where they are linked and drawn together to form the faculties, desires, and natures of beings, thereby enabling them to enter the Distinct Teaching of the One Vehicle.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Sū) that "the distinction between the names for the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and so forth is not yet clear," this means that because it speaks only of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it is termed "narrow" (*bié*);
furthermore, because it speaks of the emptiness of phenomena, it is termed "broad" (*tōng*).

As for the statement in the *Chāo* (C) that "this is truly a self-humbling [remark]," the *Zhou Yī* (Book of Changes), in the hexagram Qian (*Qiān*), says: "Qian brings success; the noble person attains their end. The *Tuan* (Commentary on the Hexagram) states: [The text continues with the *Tuan* commentary.]
It is said: "Qian brings success. The Way of Heaven descends and bestows light; the Way of Earth is humble and yet ascends. The Way of Heaven diminishes the full and augments the humble;
the Way of Earth transforms the full and flows toward the humble. The spirits and deities harm the full and bless the humble; the way of humanity detests the full and loves the humble.
Humility is honorable and luminous; though it is lowly, it cannot be surpassed. This is the ultimate end of the noble man."
The commentary states: Among all the hexagrams, only that hexagram is without fault; among the various masters who establish their doctrines, only this master is without error.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The Small Vehicle [understands] that True Suchness remains unchanging while following conditions,” this explanation is abbreviated. In full, it should state:
within the two aspects of True Suchness—remaining unchanging while following conditions—it attains only the aspect of remaining unchanging; therefore, it is called “one part.
Furthermore, among the two kinds of emptiness, it speaks only of the principle revealed by the emptiness of persons; therefore, it is called “half.”
Regarding "Confucianism and the like": those who are gentle, expansive, and benevolent, and who necessarily bring salvation to all things, are called Confucians (*ru*).

That which is inexhaustible in its application and necessarily penetrates all things is called the Way (*dao*). As for their nine schools and seven classics, they have already been fully detailed in the preceding text.

Regarding the question, "Since the *śāstra* has already attained one part of non-change, how can it be called 'complete'?"—the answer is: although they differ according to their respective meanings, they are established as distinct names;
thus, how could one raise an objection based on one while following the other? Is this not merely an objection against a different category using another category? The response is:

although they differ in meaning, the way the names are established is not convenient [for your objection]. Why? For what wise person would call a man five feet tall a "short Chinese" or a "tall Chinese"?

When looking at a person six feet tall, one calls them "short"; when facing a person four feet tall, one calls them "long. These are likewise distinguished according to their relative meaning; there is no room for other objections.
Following this principle, what is refuted here is only the third [position]. Why, then, does the topical outline state that "the latter three" are refuted?

This clearly indicates that the refutation of the third implies the inclusion of the other two by extension. That is to say, these names of "partial" and "complete" are not established for the other two [positions], as they are merely partial.

How could the designation "complete" (pūrṇa) possibly be established? Furthermore, since the two designations of "partial" and "complete" for the objects of comparison cannot be established, how can the two titles of "half" and "complete" for the subjects of comparison remain valid?

The refutation of the latter three [categories] is indeed not in vain. Moreover, regarding the distinctions between gradual and sudden, or partial and perfect, the Commentary does not mention them because they are not understood;
students should infer this accordingly.
The phrase "the year-cycle [falls under] Juezi" refers to a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). The *Yǎ* states: "Juezi’s mouth consists of the Eastern Wall of the Encampment (*Yíngshì*) mansion;

because the four directions resemble a mouth, it was given this name. According to the principles of Yin-Yang, there are such things as the Year-Head (*niánzhí*), Month-Head (*yuèzhí*), Day-Head (*rìzhí*), and Hour-Head (*shízhí*);
this likely refers to the Year-Head or the Month-Head.
The first four names in the preceding list refer to Master Yuan’s *Four Tenet Systems* (*Sijiao yi*), which were established at the very beginning [of his work].

The subsequent text states: 1. The School of Causality (*Inyuan zong*). This refers to the Sarvāstivāda (which clarifies true causality by establishing the nature of conditioned fruits). 2. The School of Nominal Designation (*Jiaming zong*).

This refers to the Sautrāntika (which refutes fixed natures, asserting that all things exist only through conditions; since all phenomena arise from conditions, they lack fixed reality. For example, it is clearly known that the hardness of iron melts when exposed to fire, and the moisture of water solidifies when met with cold).

1. The School of Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): This holds that things have no fixed nature and exist only as provisional designations. 2. The School of the Various Prajñās: This second school merely negates intrinsic nature while acknowledging the existence of characteristics; it is like joining fingers to form a fist—though the fist has no fixed nature, its characteristic as a fist is not non-existent.

Now, this [third school] further negates even those characteristics to clarify that both nature and characteristics are empty, thereby establishing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). 3. The School of Non-Reality: This third school merely eliminates false conceptualization to reveal the meaning of emptiness, yet it does not yet manifest the wondrous existence of the true nature that is not empty.

It is only here [in the fourth school] that the true nature of wondrous existence is revealed. 4. The School of Reality: This refers to the teachings on the True Principle of Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). While the third school merely removes false imaginings to reveal the meaning of emptiness, it did not yet manifest the wondrous existence of the true nature that is not empty; now, this [fourth school] finally reveals that wondrous existence.

Regarding their natures: the first school [teaches] that these are phenomena produced by causes and conditions; the third school [teaches] that what I call "existence" is itself emptiness; the second school [teaches] that they are also mere designations; and the fourth is the meaning of the Middle Way. Therefore, these are not discussed here.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Discourse on the Profound and Determination of the Meaning*, Fascicle Four.
Excerpts from the Record, Explaining the True Body:
"It is equal in essence to its union with the Dharma-realm. — Three Rivers. "Identical to the Cloud of the Single Dharma-body."
Approximately ten bodies correspond to the ten Buddhas; based on their arising, they are unimpeded. The Buddha-body is not insentient matter.

In the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, Bodhisattvas manifest great and lofty bodies. Regarding the merits of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), if one does not integrate them with the preceding meanings, one also loses the core intent of the Sūtra.
There are many ancient explanations concerning the two divisions of cause and effect regarding the ten classes of beings.

The twelve divisions of the sūtras have the Confucian Master as their sovereign; the three categories, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the twelvefold teaching are an ocean profound and vast.

With the four types of eloquence, the eight qualities of voice, and the four wheels of non-arising and non-ceasing, one realizes the four truths and the twelve links of dependent origination, attaining perfect awakening at the very moment of first resolving the mind.
Opening [the teaching] widely results in little loss; ten parables appear. In some lands, only the three vehicles are taught, yet there are ten differences.

The four propositions, the four sudden approaches, and the four gradual approaches are all revealed through parables. The three vehicles are unified into one, and the three dots form the character "yi" (伊).
Though one cultivates the six perfections over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and attains the thirty-four moments of mind, [it remains as such].

A Commentary by the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Xianyan:
As soon as the dark whirlwind [of calamity] arose, those who were without attachment were led like sheep. The *Analects* states: "Weizi went into exile; Jizi became a slave;
and Bi Gan died for his remonstrations. (The note says: Wei and Ji were the names of two states; "zi" refers to their noble rank. Weizi was the younger brother of Zhou; Jizi and Bi Gan...)

Regarding King Zhou’s paternal uncles: Wei Zi saw that Zhou was devoid of the Way and departed early; Ji Zi feigned madness and became a slave; Bi Gan was put to death for his remonstrances. King Wu then led a combined force.
Eight hundred feudal lords assembled without prior appointment. In a single array they engaged in combat, and the army of Zhou was utterly defeated.
After King Zhou was defeated, he held a cat in his left hand and led a sheep with his right; this was the posture of one surrendering.

The phrase "the wings of the chariots momentarily soar" implies that Chen-na’s tracks fall into disorder. The expression "disordered tracks" originates from the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals), in the tenth year of Duke Zhuang of Lu.
In the year [X], the army of Qi invaded Lu. As Duke Zhuang of Lu was about to engage in battle, Cao Gui (pronounced Guì; "cai" with the *yòng* tone) requested to follow him.

The Duke allowed him to ride in the same chariot (meaning they were together in the war chariot). They fought at Changshao (a place name, pronounced sháo with the *shàng* tone). The Duke was about to beat the drum to signal the charge.
Zi Lu said, "It is not yet possible. When the men of Qi had drummed three times, Zi Lu said, "Now it is possible. The army of Qi was utterly defeated. The Duke intended to gallop toward them;
Zi Lu said, "It is not yet possible. He looked down at the ruts of the chariot wheels, climbed onto the crossbar to gaze at them, and said, "Now it is possible.
He then pursued the army of Qi. After the victory, the Duke asked him the reason for this. He replied, "War, my lord, depends upon spirit. The first drum-stroke arouses the spirit."

"It declines after the second [attack] and is exhausted by the third. Their strength was spent while ours was full; therefore, we were victorious. Now, a great state is difficult to deal with; one must fear hidden ambushes.
I observed that their tracks were in disarray and saw that their banners were lowered; thus I pursued them, knowing this was no deception. Commentary:
The combination and elimination of these phrases can be understood through the intended meaning.
Regarding the statement that Dharmapāla and Nanda had no recorded accounts of attaining sainthood:

while this may be the case for Nanda, as for the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, according to the *Yuèshì lùn shūyào* (Essentials of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*), on the day of his passing, celestial music welcomed him from the heavens with a mournful sound that shook the realm.
A voice resounded from the sky, announcing to the Brahmins: "This is one of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa."
This is the first [point]: the Buddha.

Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) that "at the initial stage, according to the dependent [nature], it is said to exist": among the Four Truths, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);

and among the seventy-five dharmas, the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas are also the perfected nature. However, this is stated merely from the perspective of the majority. Thus [it is said].
It is said: First, regarding "the absence of nature in terms of characteristics," this is because their substantial characteristics do not exist.
Second, regarding "the absence of a nature of spontaneity," this is because they exist by depending on causes and conditions; thus, a nature of spontaneity does not exist.

Finally, regarding "by means of being far removed from the self and dharmas grasped previously" (referring to the imagined nature in relation to the dependent nature), this is the gate through which the two absences give rise to the perfected nature.
The phrase "among these" in the *Chao* (Commentary) refers to the meaning of the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) for this section.

It is the second of the four gates within the *Chao*, which discusses the realization or non-realization [of truth] based on the emptiness or existence of the mind and its objects. The statement "the parikalpita is only the object;

the paratantra and pariniṣpanna pertain to the mind" refers to the third section mentioned previously, specifically pointing to the *Shu* that explicitly establishes the thesis. This is the fourth... of the *Chao*.

This is the first gate among the gates. It is called "inclusive" (*saṃgrāhaka*) because at the first stage it does not state that [phenomena] exist by way of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and at the second stage it does not state that they are empty by way of the three non-natures (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*);
only at the third stage does it speak of both the three natures and the three non-natures.
Therefore, it is called "inclusive. As for the remaining two gates, these concern the attainment of Buddhahood through either the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) or the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).
One does not attain Buddhahood.

In the *Commentary on the Treatise on the Light of the Two Wisdoms*, the Master Zhiguang states that the Mahāyāna of No-Characteristics (*animitta*) constitutes the true definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Question:

According to this explanation, the teachings of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the teachings of Nature (*prakṛti*) are combined into a single category. For what reason, then, did Guifeng distinguish between the School of Nature and the School of Emptiness?

Thus, ten distinctions are established. Therefore, that master said: "The first and second [emptinesses] involve the relative nature of existence; the third and first involve the relative nature of essence and characteristics.

These are all clearly and easily discernible. Only the second and third—the emptiness of destroying characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of manifestation (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*)—are points where both lecturers and practitioners alike are confused.
They all claim these belong to the same school and the same teaching, asserting that both are merely the 'emptiness of destroying characteristics.'"

This is precisely what constitutes true nature (*tathatā*). Therefore, it is necessary to extensively distinguish between the ten differences between the school of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the school of Nature (*svabhāva*): 1.

**The difference between phenomena (*dharma*) and meaning (*artha*) regarding the conventional and ultimate:** In the school of Emptiness, the nature of spiritual awareness is not yet revealed; rather, all differentiated characteristics are taken as "phenomena" (*dharma*). These phenomena belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

To illuminate these various phenomena as being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), signless (*animitta*), neither increasing nor decreasing, and so forth, is taken as "meaning" (*artha*). This meaning belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhìdù lùn) defines the unhindered eloquence of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) as the conventional truth, and the unhindered eloquence of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) as the ultimate truth. In the school of Nature, however, the single true nature is taken as the "phenomenon. [Emptiness and existence...]

The various distinctions such as these constitute the meaning (*artha*). Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the chapter on the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmika*), states: "Dharma refers to knowing self-nature (*svabhāva*); meaning refers to knowing the cessation of nature. Dharma refers to knowing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); meaning refers to knowing the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)," and so forth.

In all ten instances, Dharma is taken to mean the ultimate truth, while Meaning is taken to mean the conventional truth. Second, regarding the two names for the mind-nature (*citta-svabhāva*): they differ. The Śūnyavāda school consistently designates the source of all phenomena as "nature" (*svabhāva*).

The Svabhāvavāda school (Xingzong) mostly designates the source of all phenomena as "mind" (*citta*). As for designating it as "nature," the scriptures and treatises are largely consistent, so there is no need to elaborate further. Regarding its designation as "mind," the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* speaks of the "intrinsically pure mind" (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*), and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states that "all phenomena have from the very beginning been beyond words."

The names "mind" (*citta*), "object-condition" (*ālambana*), and so forth are explained as being, in the final analysis, nothing but this single mind. (3) Regarding the characters *xìng* (nature) and *tǐ* (essence/body): in the School of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-vāda*), the nature of all phenomena is their lack of intrinsic nature;

in the School of Nature (*prakṛti-vāda*), the nature is the essence that is numinous, luminous, eternally abiding, and non-empty. Thus, although the character *xìng* is the same, the essence (*tǐ*) differs. (4) Regarding true wisdom (*jñāna*) and true knowledge (*vidyā*):

in the School of Emptiness, conceptualization is taken as knowledge and non-conceptualization as wisdom; thus, wisdom is profound while knowledge is shallow. In the School of Nature, the subtle discernment capable of realizing the sacred principle is taken as wisdom, while the numinous nature that encompasses both principle and wisdom and pervades both ordinary beings and sages is taken as knowledge; thus, knowledge is universal while wisdom is circumscribed.

Fifth, the difference between the existence of a self and the non-existence of a self. (Regarding the Emptiness School [Kongzong]: it regards the existence of a self as delusion and the non-existence of a self as truth. Regarding the Nature School [Xingzong]: it regards the non-existence of a self as delusion and the existence of a self as truth. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:)

The absence of self is called birth and death; the presence of self is called the Tathāgata. Sixth, the distinction between negation (*paryudāsa*) and affirmation (*vidhi*): negation refers to the removal of that which is incorrect, while affirmation refers to the manifestation of that which is correct.

Furthermore, "negation" (paryudāsa) excludes all other things, while "affirmation" (vidhi) directly indicates the essential nature itself. As stated in various sutras regarding the wondrous principle of reality (dharmatā), such expressions as "neither arising nor ceasing," "neither defiled nor pure," and so forth, are all negational definitions (apavāda-prajñapti).

If one speaks of "knowing and seeing," "awakening and illuminating," or "spiritual discernment," these are all affirmative definitions (vidhi-prajñapti). If there were no essence of wisdom, vision, and so forth, what dharma could be manifested as the nature [of reality] when it is taught that dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing? It is like saying of water: "not dry" is a negation, and "moist" is an affirmation.

The various teachings often state that "severing the hundred negations" (jue bafei) refers entirely to words of negation (*paryudāsa*). Directly manifesting the one true reality alone constitutes affirmative expression (*vidhi*). The terminology of the Śūnyatā school (*Kongzong*) consists solely of negational definition (*apavāda*), whereas the terminology of the Nature school (*Xingzong*) possesses both negation and affirmation.

Those who merely negate have not yet attained full understanding; those who employ both negation and affirmation are precise and definitive. (7) Distinguishing between Recognizing Names and Recognizing Essence: This means that every phenomenon possesses both a name and an essence. Suppose someone were to ask:

"I have heard in various sutras that when deluded it is defilement and when awakened it is purity; when let loose it is ordinary and when cultivated it is sagehood; it can give rise to all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds—what is this thing? This question asks about its functional meaning (*artha*). The answer is: "It is the mind. This answers by citing the name.

Thus it is. The fool recognizes the name and immediately claims he has understood the essence. The wise person should further inquire: "What is this mind? so as to penetrate its substance. When answered, "It is the mind," this points directly to its substance. By inferring from this, we see that the names and substances of "mind" and "essence" each constitute a single character; all others are merely functional meanings.

The single character "knowing" (zhī) permeates the myriad functions and meanings of greed, anger, compassion, patience, good, evil, suffering, and joy. Nowadays, many students of Chan harbor doubts, asking: "Dharma only spoke of 'mind' (xīn); why does Heze speak of 'knowing' (zhī)? The answer is:

one must simply realize that "mind" is a name and not the substance, while "knowing" is the substance and not the name. Thus, whether true or false, defiled or pure, good or evil, there is no meaning that is not penetrated. Those of the Emptiness school (Śūnyatā-vāda) and others fear those of shallow faculties...

Because people give rise to attachments based on words, [the text] merely provides the names and negates what is incorrect, while extensively using the functional applications of meaning to lead to the underlying intent. In the Nature School (Xingzong), because those of superior faculties are made to transcend words to recognize the essence, the essence is directly pointed out by means of the single phrase "knowing" (zhī).

8. The Distinction Between Two Truths and Three Truths: [In the] Emptiness School (Kongzong), it is taught that all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds do not exceed the two truths; this is known by all scholars, so there is no need for further citation or explanation. In the Nature School, however, all natures, characteristics, and intrinsic bodies are subsumed within three truths:

taking all phenomena such as form arising through conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); taking the emptiness of all phenomena—which lack inherent nature—due to their conditional nature as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) (which is the same as the previous school); and [adding] the one true mind.

Its essence is neither emptiness nor form; it can be both empty and form. This constitutes the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (differing from the previous school). Ninth, there is a distinction between the three natures and emptiness (referring to the *parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Regarding the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), the Śūnyatāvāda school states: whenever the various sūtras speak of "existence," they refer to the *parikalpita* (imagined) and *paratantra* natures; whenever they speak of "emptiness," they refer to the *pariniṣpanna* nature. Thus, all three natures are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). The Svabhāvavāda school, however, maintains that all three natures possess the meaning of both emptiness and existence.

That is to say: the *parikalpita* is existent in terms of mental affliction (*kleśa*) but non-existent in terms of reality (*tattva*); the *paratantra* has existence in terms of appearance (*nimitta*) but no existence in terms of intrinsic nature; the *pariniṣpanna* is non-existent in terms of mental affliction but existent in terms of reality, non-existent in terms of appearance, yet existent in terms of intrinsic nature.

Regarding the difference between emptiness and existence concerning the ten virtues of the Buddha: the Śūnyatāvāda school asserts that the Buddha takes emptiness as his virtue; there is not even the slightest dharma, which is what is called Bodhi. To see him in form or seek him in sound is to walk upon a false path. The Svabhāvavāda school, however, [asserts that] all dharmas...

The Buddha’s own body possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity; its ten bodies and ten wisdoms, its true merits, its marks and signs, and its penetrating light are each inexhaustible. These exist inherently by nature from the beginning and do not depend on roots or conditions.

What has been clarified above shows that the ten differences are distinct and the two gates are radiant; how could these two schools be merged into a single teaching? Now, regarding the claim that they "converge" or "do not converge":
since the traditions of the masters differ, why is it necessary to provide a harmonizing interpretation? Or, to address them collectively: [End of excerpt]

The teachings on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the minor teachings (*hīnayāna*) are combined into a single school. By distinguishing and analyzing these to reveal the nature (*dharmatā*), they are opened up to form two teachings;

thus, they do not contradict one another. This is like the general discussion of the Great and Small [Vehicles]: the two vehicles constitute the Śrāvaka Vehicle, while the provisional and the real together constitute the Bodhisattva [Vehicle].
When the Great and Small are each opened up, they may be understood by their names. Using that as an analogy for this, it is naturally easy to see.
The Commentary states: "It would be better to give rise to a view of existence as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness even the size of a mustard seed.

This is because, although both the views of emptiness and existence are illnesses, there is a vast difference in the gravity of their consequences regarding the preservation or destruction of cause and effect;

thus it is said. Regarding the statement that "emptiness and existence are mutually identical," the question is raised: since you have already granted that the two dharmas of emptiness and existence are mutually [identical]...

If both the "that which identifies" (*neng-ji*) and the "that which is identified" (*suo-ji*) can equally be either with substance or without substance, does this not contradict the principle that the "that which identifies" is without substance while the "that which is identified" possesses substance?
Answer: This so-called "emptiness" (*kong*) is not a dharma that lacks substance; rather, it is because it is true emptiness (*zhenkong*).

Alternatively, it is based on the mutual identification of two things that possess substance: while the "that which identifies" (which possesses substance) is set aside, the "that which is identified" (which is empty) remains. Thus, it is called "empty."
Since the two natures are identical in essence, why is it necessary to specifically retain the dependent nature while specifically negating the imagined nature?

It is like the analogy of a rope and a snake, which share the same substance of hemp; for what reason is the snake alone dispelled while the rope remains? By means of this metaphor to illustrate the Dharma, the student may understand.

Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Commentary), "When benefiting sentient beings according to conditions, why is it necessary to reconcile [the teachings]?"—it is like praising *fuzi* (aconite) and censuring *gancao* (licorice) when treating a cold-natured illness, yet praising *gancao* and censuring *fuzi* when encountering a heat-natured illness; why would one need to reconcile them?

As for the statement, "If one refers to the latter gate, then the Dharma-nature school is considered 'complete' (*liaoliao*) and so forth," the intention of Jñānaprabha is that these are integrated within the Dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).
Regarding the two schools of the Nature (xing) doctrine: because they together constitute a single school, [the text] states, "Now, observing the intention of Xianshou...

and so forth. The former section, based on the text, describes how the principles of the two ancient schools are equal; the latter section, concerning their intent, shows how the meanings of the two new teachings differ.

Regarding the statement, "The 'encompassing of beings' is broad and taken as the ultimate, whereas the 'reaching' is limited; regarding things, it is only the Great that is taken as the ultimate," this refers to the faculty of the nature-root (xinggen).
Although it may be much, it does not equal the excellence of words that benefit sentient beings; although it may be extensive, it does not equal the clarity of the underlying principles.
Regarding the phrase "intermingled with unexamined [words]," the *Shangshu* states: "Do not listen to unexamined words; do not employ plans that have not been consulted.
The commentary notes: "Unexamined means lacking verification or proof; plans that are not consulted involve acting alone and will ultimately fail to achieve success."

Therefore, it is cautioned that one should not listen to or employ [such views]. Regarding the statement, "As for the four types of incomplete meanings, they all belong to the preceding school," the four incomplete meanings are:

first, the broad scope of encompassing sentient beings (because it transforms various classes of beings); second, the completeness of verbal teaching (because there is no lack of recorded teachings); and third, the inferiority of benefiting others.

(Because it penetrates the three vehicles) 4. It reveals the subtlety of principle. (Because reality is not yet fully realized) There are four kinds of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*): 1. Its inclusion of sentient beings is narrow (because it is for bodhisattvas alone); 2. its verbal teaching is deficient (because it is only for once-returners); 3.
its benefit to others is superior (as it approaches the attainment of Buddhahood); 4. its revelation of principle is more extensive (as it exhausts all marks of conditions).
As for the statement that "if one follows the intent of the sūtra, both assemblies together attain the beauty of the 'joined' [rain/sword]": this refers to the two aforementioned teachings based on—

Although this does not contradict the Buddha’s original intent, those who later studied and transmitted his teachings mostly clung to the literal text and became confused about the underlying meaning.
Some adhered to a single view and mutually refuted one another; others believed in both systems indiscriminately, remaining muddled and ignorant.

Therefore, Bodhisattvas such as Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva, relying on the teachings that deconstruct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), extensively expounded the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to shatter their attachment to existence, so that [the truth] might become perfectly clear.
One must understand true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). True emptiness is an emptiness that does not contradict existence.
Bodhisattvas such as Asanga and Vasubandhu, relying on the teachings of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), extensively explained names and characteristics and analyzed their nature and attributes;

yet, they did not penetrate the distinction between the defiled and the pure, and each separately refuted those who clung to emptiness, causing them to clearly understand wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*). Wondrous existence is an existence that does not contradict emptiness.
Although each [text] expounds a single meaning, they are complete in their entirety; therefore, there is no contradiction. Question:
If this is so, why is it that later masters such as Bhāviveka and Dharmapāla refuted one another? Answer:
This is actually mutual complementation, not mutual refutation. Why? Because the faculties of those who have not yet studied become gradually duller.

Because they mutually cling to emptiness and existence, Bhāviveka and others refute the characteristics of fixed existence until they are exhausted, reaching the ultimate empty truth (*atyanta-śūnyatā*);

only then does that wondrous existence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) become established. Dharmapāla and others refute nihilistic and partial emptiness, intending to preserve wondrous existence;

because this wondrous [existence] is preserved, it is only then that the text establishes the empty truth of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This is the intended meaning of their mutual refutation of characteristics.

Thus they mutually establish one another, because the wondrous existence and the true emptiness possess two meanings. First is the meaning of extreme opposition, which means that they mutually harm, completely seize, and exhaustively eliminate one another.
Second is the meaning of extreme conformity, which means that they are darkly unified into a single aspect, with the entire substance being fully encompassed.

If there were no mutual seizing and exhaustive elimination, there would be no way for the entire substance to be fully gathered; it is precisely through extreme opposition that [they mutually establish one another].
This is the ultimate accord. Nāgārjuna, Asaṅga, and others, by means of the gate of ultimate accord, thus establish one another.

Bhāviveka, Dharmapāla, and others, relying on the gate of ultimate contradiction, thus refute one another. Being sovereign in both contradiction and accord, their establishment and refutation are unimpeded;
there is nothing among all phenomena that they do not harmonize with. Alas! The later students of the sūtras and śāstras of these two schools in this land mutually disparage one another.

Mutual repulsion is no different from enmity. When shall we attain the realization of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*? Strive to achieve universal insight; do not remain partial or narrow-minded. Question:
If, according to the sages of the Western Regions, mutual refutation is itself mutual accomplishment, how can it be that in this land, mutual negation results in mutual hostility?
Answer: It is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known by oneself. Each must observe their own mind. Each...

Each should examine their own thoughts: one keeps medicine on hand to prevent illness, not merely for the sake of being healthy; one establishes laws to guard against villainy, not merely for the sake of being honest.

May those who lecture on the "Hundred Parables" take the instruction on washing the feet to heart, and may students of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* inscribe the parable of the blind men feeling the elephant upon their girdles.
Regarding the statement in the Śrāvaka-vehicle commentaries that only the Buddha alone possesses great awakening (*mahābodhi*), etc.:

Question: Since the Āgamas also bestow predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) upon Maitreya, how should this be reconciled? Answer: Because the tenets of the various schools (*nikāyabheda*) differ; or because although a prediction was given, it was not explicit;
or because it was stated for the most part that only the Buddha alone possesses the nature of great awakening (*mahābodhi-dhātu*). As in the Śrāvaka-vehicle...
This is an example of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* not teaching the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the citations from the sūtras in the five sections of the *Chao*, one may understand them by following the topical outline (*ke*).

As for the statement that "the three treatises are appended," the two treatises [of the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* and the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa*] are appended to the fourth [section], and another treatise is appended, namely the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi*. Regarding the statement in the fourth [section] that "although... [the text continues].

"Those who have not yet entered the state of rightness and departure from birth" (*samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti*). "Entry" (*avakrānti*) means to realize and enter. "Departure" (*niyāma*) means to be far removed.

That which is capable of departing is the true wisdom (*jñāna*) that realizes the principle immediately following liberation (*vimukti-anantara*) and abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*). "Rightness" (*samyaktva*) is the true principle (*tattva*) into which one enters.

"Birth" (*niyāma*) refers to the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) which are to be abandoned. Regarding the word "already" (*ya*), it refers to having reached the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); regarding "not yet," it refers to [the stage prior to] that.

This refers to that which precedes the abandonment [of afflictions] through the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Regarding the statement, "If one enters the Path of Seeing, one is then called the 'Assembly of Those Fixed in Rightness' (*samyaktvaniyatarāśi*)," this is not the threefold assembly (*triniyatarāśi*) discussed by Nāgārjuna.

This point merely concerns the distinction between those whose minds can be turned [toward the Mahāyāna] and those whose minds cannot be turned, as viewed from the perspective of the Hīnayāna in relation to the Mahāyāna; it discusses what is fixed and what is unfixed. Nāgārjuna, however, discusses only the three [assemblies] of the Mahāyāna.

There are three categories of those who have gathered [in the spiritual lineage]. Even those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are still considered part of the category of those fixed in the wrong way (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*).
How much less could one who has entered the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) be called one fixed in the right way (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*)? This can be understood through careful reflection.

Regarding the statement that "once one enters the Śrāvaka path of seeing, there is never a turning of the mind to become a Bodhisattva," one might ask: what about the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which speaks of those at the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) turning their minds after eighty thousand kalpas, and so forth? This...

What is the reconciliation? The answer is: because the faculties (*indriya*) and the teachings (*deśanā*) differ, there is no contradiction. This is because *prajñā* (wisdom) corresponds to the provisional (*upāya*), while *nirvāṇa* refers to the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Regarding the statement in the *Vivṛti* that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also speaks in this same way: it is because the meaning of "lack of lineage" (*agotra*) is likewise explained in the *Yogācāra*.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* combines these into one; the preceding treatise mentions only three. As for the "excellence of the six bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana-viśeṣa*) in the *Vyākhyā*, this is because while the words are general, the intended meaning is specific.

Among the internal and external six bases, it refers specifically to the internal six bases; among the internal six bases, it refers specifically to the sixth base. Within the sixth base, there are the eight consciousnesses;
within the eight consciousnesses, there is the eighth consciousness, which contains the seeds of the four wisdoms of the Buddha—conditioned and untainted (*anāsrava*). Therefore, it is so named.
Regarding the statement that "it is not without [this] because it is great and does not deviate from the intent of the *Shuyou chao*":

Xianshou said, "Although there are differences between the provisional and the real, they are both what the Bodhisattvas ride upon. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Only this one thing is the reality; the other two are not."

True. Furthermore, it is said that because they are the places where [the mind] rests, two types of bodhi are taught. As for the statement "to proceed" (*yāna*) and the mention of "two or three," *yāna* means intention, or it carries the sense of "heading toward."

The reflection is not produced from itself (not arising from causes), nor from another (not arising from conditions), nor from both (not arising from the two together), nor independently (not arising spontaneously).

These are the four meanings of non-arising, which manifest the emptiness of the noble ones. It is like the conditions for a mirror: the reflection is not produced from the mirror itself (because without a substance there is no appearance);

it is not produced from another substance (because without an object there is no appearance); it is not produced from the union of the two (because without both there is no appearance of a reflection); and it is not produced independently of the two (because without them, there is no reflection).

Therefore, it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* that "dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), dharma-abiding (*dharmasthiti*), and dharma-position (*dharmavyavasthā*) are all synonyms for *tathatā* (suchness). Thus, the subsequent excerpt states:

"That is to say, dharma-nature is the non-falsehood nature, the unchanging nature, the equality nature, the nature free from birth, the fixed nature of dharma, the abiding nature of dharma, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of empty space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm. (The above is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*).

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of the nature of emptiness and non-emptiness of true suchness (*tathatā*). (From the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*) The signless, unconditioned, and correct nature.

(From the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*) The dharma-position, true nature, selflessness, reality, mind-nature, and the single mind. (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*) The nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*), the absence of intrinsic nature, and the seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*).
(As stated in the first dedication: "Seal all roots of goodness with the seal of the dharma-realm. Quiescence (*śānti*). (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) Three.
Among the natures (*svabhāva*), it is called the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). Among the three bodies (*trikāya*), it is called the *dharmakāya*.

Among the three pure lands (*śuddhakṣetra*), it is called the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (Dharma-nature land). Among the three Buddha-natures (*buddhatā*), it is called the *prakṛtistha-gotra* (naturally abiding lineage). Among the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*), it is called *tathatā* (suchness).
Among the five treasuries (*pañcanidhi*), it is called all of them—namely, the *dharmadhātu-nidhi*, the *dharmakāya-nidhi*, the *lokottara-agratama-nidhi*, and the *svabhāva-nidhi*.

The *tathāgatagarbha* as the *viśuddhigarbha*; among the four types of excellence and two types of truth, it is called the "excellent ultimate" (*paramārtha-paramārtha*), which also encompasses realization and the ultimate truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) (Yogācārabhūmi 14.6);

among the six types of clear observation (*abhisamaya*), it is called the "true reality" (*bhūtārtha*); among the seven types of penetration into the truths, it is called the "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) (Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra);
among the two types of buddha-nature, it is called the "buddha-nature of principle" (*li-fóxìng*); and among the fourteen types of truths, it is called... [the truth of principle].

In terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is called the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa-prajñā*) among the three types of *prajñā*. Among the Three Jewels, it is called the Jewel of the Single Essence (*eka-rasa-triratna*).

Among the three liberations, it is called the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*). (As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 74) Among the two fruits, it is called the fruit of wisdom (*jñāna-phala*).

In *nirvāṇa*, it is called "purity of nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and "expedient means" (*upāya*). Within the two truths, it is called the "truth of reality" (*satya*) and the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).

Within the three truths, it is called the "truth of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-satya*). (In the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-avadāna-sūtra* [仁王經],) within the four truths, it is called the "truth of cessation" (*nirodha-satya*), or the "truth of reality" (*bhūta-satya*)—the "one truth" as named in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (*Xianyang lun*).

Alternatively, it is called the "middle way" (*madhyamā-pratipad*) or "liberation" (*vimukti*). Within *nirvāṇa*, it is manifested through one hundred doors to distinguish its various aspects of liberation.

It is called by various names: sometimes it is named the "Gate of Non-dual Dharma" (advaya-dvāra), sometimes "Non-duality" (advayatā), sometimes "True Nature" (bhūtatā), sometimes "True Aspect" (bhūtalakṣaṇa), sometimes "Immeasurable Meaning" (ananta-artha), and it is also named "Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha-satya) and "Ultimate Emptiness" (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
The commentary states: the above are all alternative names for *tathatā* (suchness).

Regarding the statement that the cause contradicts conventional logic in establishing the impermanence of the three realms: since what has already existed returns to non-existence, it cannot be considered truly existent.
Nirvāṇa takes non-arising and non-ceasing as its ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the three realms take arising and ceasing as their ultimate truth.

That these two principles do not lean toward either extreme is called the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). He asks: "The two principles of permanence and impermanence are mutually contradictory."
What is the principle of the Middle Way that avoids partiality? The answer is: although these two principles differ, they naturally support one another. Why is this?

Because by departing from the notion of permanence, there arises the impermanence of the triple world; and because one understands the true nature of impermanence, the wisdom of permanence is realized.
Therefore, the meaning of the two birds cited in the sutra applies precisely here: the two principles do not illuminate in isolation.
It is like hanging a mirror in a lofty hall: the myriad forms are all reflected therein. Master Qingliang’s commentary states:
"Hanging a mirror in a lofty hall" means that it is a mindless, empty reflection; "the myriad forms are all reflected" means that it does not discriminate between the wicked and the beautiful.

Thus, by employing a pure mind that transcends both the permanent and the impermanent, one contemplates the perfect principle that is both permanent and impermanent—this is precisely the meaning [of the text]. The previous passage spoke of the divergence of causes.

Regarding the principle that the three realms are established as impermanent: due to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), one departs from the principle of the permanence of True Reality (*tattva*).
Through the conjunction of the true and the false, the three subtleties and six coarsenesses—the impermanent phenomena of the three realms—are formed. Question:

Is fundamental ignorance a provisional cause and condition? If it were without cause and condition, one would not be a son of the Śākya, but would instead be identical to the naturalistic non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
[Question: If there are conditions, what are they? [Answer: One view states that original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) is the cause and condition for its arising.
If that were so, would original enlightenment arise from its own nature, or would it arise following conditions? If it arises from its own nature, then within the state of Buddhahood—

Ignorance arises again because there is original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). If original enlightenment were itself a defiled illusion by nature, then if it were to arise in accordance with conditions, in accordance with what further condition would ignorance arise?
Even if there were another dharma that served as its condition, ignorance could no longer be called the "root.
Now, it is said in response: it simply functions through the perfuming of the preceding moment’s fundamental ignorance.
To stir the original enlightenment is to be deluded regarding the Truth; it is to be ignorant. To give rise to subsequent thoughts is for fundamental ignorance and delusive mentation to arise.
It is the non-awakening to the arising of thoughts. Beyond ignorance, there is no further dharma; therefore, it is called "fundamental."
If it is objected: "What serves as the condition for the primordial fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*)?"—this objection contradicts the scriptures.
All teachings unanimously state that ignorance is beginningless; how, then, can one object by asking about the "primordial fundamental ignorance"?

Just as in the Dharma-character (lakṣaṇa) school there are seeds, which give rise to subsequent moments of consciousness by taking preceding moments as their causes and conditions, and since this can be traced back to a beginningless past, no logical difficulties arise.
Furthermore, fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) is explained as possessing two meanings:
first, the meaning of having substance and power; second, the meaning of lacking substance and power. It constantly possesses both meanings simultaneously, neither preceding nor following the other.

In relation to the sense of having substance and power, it constantly acts as the perfuming agent; because it perfumes the original enlightenment (*prakṛti-vijñāna*), it is delusion regarding the truth.
It is not [the same as] the other. In relation to the sense of lacking substance and power, it is always that which is produced; because it depends upon original enlightenment, false thoughts arise.

One does not perceive the arising of thoughts. Just as the notion that "one perceives many" possesses both substance and power, while the notion that "many perceive one" lacks both substance and power, so too is it always the case that this is a phenomenon of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This principle is fixed as such.

It is also like the Dharma-characteristics school (*lakṣaṇavāda*), which, from the perspective of the causal relationship between mind and object, acts as the "transformer" (*pariṇāmaka*) because it transforms those objects.

From the perspective of the meaning of the fruit, it is that which is drawn along; because it is drawn by its object, one should say that the objects transformed by the mind can, within the same moment of mindfulness, in turn draw the mind.
This is comparable to how the mind is like ignorance (*avidyā*) and the object is like that awakening (*bodhi*); this can be understood through analogy.

Furthermore, it is explained that ignorance acts as the cause and functions as the perfuming agent (*vāsana*), perfuming the original awakening (*mūlabodhi*), thereby deluding the truth. It is not otherwise.

The essence of ignorance acts as that which is produced because it relies upon fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi); thus, it is viewed in relation to the arising of thought. It is the non-awakening that gives rise to thought.

This is like the Dharma-characteristics school (lakṣaṇa-vāda), wherein the seeds are the functioning of the eighth consciousness and act as the producer of the manifest activity (pravṛtti) of the eighth consciousness;
the self-verifying division (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) is the essence, yet it is itself what is produced. It is also like being the basis for the teaching.
This is because the "agent" is that which can give rise [to something], while the "entity" is that which is given rise to.

Furthermore, the interpretation that Nāgārjuna’s statement regarding the fundamental dharma of a single thought-moment being sovereign over the conditioned refers to delusion regarding reality is incorrect. It is not so; rather, it refers to the arising of false thoughts that produce those five kinds of conditioned phenomena.
It is not that the thought arises through conscious awareness; it is like the tail of that dragon-king which has not yet emerged from the storm-cloud.

Furthermore, the four marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are explained as conditions that perfume and stir the *mūlapratyavekṣā-jñāna* (fundamental awakening), causing delusion regarding the Truth. This is not [the case for] the arising of ignorance (*avidyā*), where false thoughts are produced.

It is not that the thought arises through conscious awareness. For it is because ignorance and the four marks are, from beginningless time, the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and they are established simultaneously.

This is because they serve as mutual conditions for one another. This is precisely the meaning of the two types of causal conditions—namely, "the superior acting upon the inferior" and "the inferior acting upon the superior"—expounded in Nāgārjuna’s treatise.
If this is so, and since they are mutual conditions, how can one distinguish between the primary and the secondary? The answer is: because of the distinction between the coarse and the subtle.

Furthermore, it is like the wick producing a flame and the flame [sustaining] the wick; although they are mutual conditions, they nonetheless exist simultaneously without contradiction. The wick serves as its...
The root is the flame, and the latter is its branch; thus, this meaning is profound and obscure, and many people are confused by it.
I shall now briefly set forth a distinction based on my humble views, and I further pray that the eminent scholars will each lend their clear discernment.

As for the so-called "characteristics of liberation" and so forth, they correspond respectively to the four virtues of self, bliss, purity, and permanence. As for the phrase "freed from all bonds of suffering":
"Suffering" refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). "Bondage" refers to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Regarding the statement that "the mark of eternal quiescence is the nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity," this is a re-explanation of the preceding sutra, interpreting it as nirvāṇa.

The phrase "mark of liberation" refers to *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), because one is liberated from afflictions (*kleśa*). The phrase "mark of detachment" refers to *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvāṇa).

This refers to being far removed from the two delusions. Regarding the term "characteristic of cessation" (nirodha-lakṣaṇa), it refers to *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), because both body and wisdom have ceased.
The *Chao* [Commentary] points to one type while implying the inclusion of the preceding three; students should reflect upon this.

The statement that "there are two kinds of ultimate" refers to the distinction between the causal seeds (*hetu-bīja*). To speak of "ultimate in the sense of finality" (*niṣṭhā-paryanta*) refers to the true cause (*tathatā-hetu*).
To speak of "worldly ultimate" refers to the contaminated seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*). To speak of "supramundane ultimate" refers to the uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).
Furthermore, according to another interpretation based on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*, it is explained as follows: in relation to the Small and Great [Vehicles]...
Because it is ultimate, it is called "final" (*atyanta*). Because cause and effect differ, they are divided into two types. Since the cause adorns the fruit, it is termed "ornamentation" (*vyūha*).
When the virtues of the fruit are fully perfected, it is called "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*). Regarding the mundane and supramundane, they are distinguished by their stages:
from the first stage (*bhūmi*) downward, they are collectively termed "mundane," as they are all subsumed within the world of transformation (*pariṇāmika-loka*); the Buddha is termed "supramundane."
It is so. Regarding the term "six pāramitās," this is translated as "reaching the other shore" (pāra-gata).
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, they can only be established as pāramitās when they are embraced by seven types of supremacy (*paramatva*). First is the supremacy of abiding:
