from the time the followers of the Two Vehicles enter the path of seeing until they reach the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they transform only the sixth consciousness, because it is only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) that arises.

In the Mahāyāna, the entry into the stages (*bhūmi*) also involves transformation. At the seventh stage, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) transform into the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), whereby the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is eliminated. At the sixth stage, they transform into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

At the seventh stage, they become untainted (*anāsrava*). As for the two consciousnesses—the fifth and the eighth—they only transform at the stage of Buddhahood, because they share the same objective sphere as the sense faculties (*indriya*) and because they serve as the basis for perfuming (*vāsya*).

It is accepted that the five preceding [consciousnesses] and the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) have a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana*), just as the latter three [transformations] do; however, these also directly transform their respective bases (*mūla*).

The eighth mind-king transforms its own self-enjoyment and the seeds that sustain its qualities. As for the remaining seven consciousnesses, they can only remotely condition [the storehouse consciousness]; it is not permitted for them to directly transform it.
When other bodies, lands, and relatives undergo transformation, it likewise does not contradict reason. The eighth consciousness is the "pure mind," like a great round mirror.
The seventh consciousness is "equality"; its name is established in contrast to the notion of a self. The two dharmas of "investigation" and "discernment" constitute the sixth consciousness.

The five sensory consciousnesses are called "accomplishing affairs" when they benefit sentient beings. In reality, they possess both universal and specific mental factors associated with the wholesome, totaling twenty-two; their power of discernment is preeminent.

It merely manifests the title of "Wisdom" (*jñāna*). While the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) may have intervals, the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] are continuous, being largely identical to their state as causes (*hetu-avasthā*). Their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*) are inconceivable;

they are permitted to transform the four types of objects. Among these, the three internal [objects] are all capable of mutual cognition, and in reality, they also cognize themselves, thereby achieving universal knowledge (*sarvajña*).

However, while the conditions for the new and the old differ in terms of being subject to transformation or non-transformation, there is no fault regarding the lack of perfuming. The eighth [consciousness] is not indeterminate; the seventh has neither increase nor decrease;

it is neither the perfumer nor the perfumed, and thus is not newly perfumed. Therefore, the merits of those who attain Buddhahood earlier or later are equal. Second, regarding the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*):
the term "mental factors" refers to those that always arise in dependence upon the mind, are associated with the mind, and are admitted to belong to the mind; therefore, they are so named.

Regarding mental factors (*caitta*): just as one designates "mine" (*ātmīya*) based on things belonging to the self, the mind (*citta*) grasps only the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of its objects, whereas mental factors also grasp their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Because they assist in accomplishing the activities of the mind, they receive the name "mental factors. It is like a master painter and his apprentice:

the master makes the outline, and the apprentice fills it with colors. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) can discern the general characteristics of an object; attention (*manasikāra*) discerns what has not yet been [discerned by consciousness]."

"Discerning characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-vijñapti*) refers to the distinct characteristics apprehended by the various mental factors (*caitta*). Contact (*sparśa*) is able to discern such characteristics as those that are agreeable;

feeling (*vedanā*) is able to discern such characteristics as grasping; perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to discern such characteristics as the cause for verbal expression; and volition (*cetanā*) is able to discern such characteristics as the primary cause.
In another passage, it is further stated that desire (*chanda*) is also able to discern the characteristic of desirable objects, and resolve (*adhimokṣa*) likewise discerns determined objects.

Regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): mindfulness (*smṛti*) is also able to discern the characteristics of habitual objects, and concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) likewise discern characteristics such as gain and loss;

therefore, the universal [mental factors] and the others are called mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*). All mental concomitants, with respect to their objects of focus (*ālambana*), simultaneously apprehend both the general and specific characteristics.

Although there is no difference in the names or meanings of the various mental concomitants, there are distinctions among six categories: first, the universal [factors], which pervade all four [categories].

Therefore, it is said that throughout the three natures and the nine stages, whenever any mind arises, there is never a lack of sequence; the eight consciousnesses are always present together. In what state do they abide? First is contact (*sparśa*).
Its nature is to cause the mind and mental factors to touch their objects, and its function is to serve as the basis for sensation, perception, and volition.

Second is attention (*manasikāra*). Its nature is to alert the mind, and its function is to direct the mind. Third is sensation (*vedanā*). Its nature is to experience objects that are favorable, unfavorable, or neutral.

Its nature is craving; its function is attachment. Fourth is perception (*saṃjñā*); its nature is the grasping of images; its function is the establishment of names and conventional expressions. Fifth is volition (*cetanā*); its nature is the formation of action;

its function is the directing of the mind. Next are the five object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣālambana*). They are called "object-specific" because they take as their objects specific domains that have been determined, previously experienced, or investigated.
Among the four categories of universality, these belong exclusively to the category of those whose nature is universal, yet their arising is not necessarily fixed. Fifth.

Feeling (*vedanā*) has the nature of experiencing [objects] and the function of being the basis for craving. Desire (*chanda*) has the nature of longing and the function of being the basis for exertion.

Resolve (*adhimokṣa*) has the nature of determining an object and the function of non-reversal. Mindfulness (*smṛti*) has the nature of clear recollection and the function of being the basis for meditative concentration. Concentration (*samādhi*) has the nature of one-pointed focus.
Its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom (*jñāna*). The five types of discernment (*prajñā*) have the nature of investigation and discrimination; their function is to sever doubt.

There are eleven wholesome factors that are exclusively associated with a wholesome mind and are designated as "wholesome" (*kuśala*). "Wholesome" carries the meaning of being conducive and beneficial; they are so called because they are beneficial both in this world and in future worlds.

Because they exist in the three stages [of the form realm] where vitarka and vicāra are present, all are included except for *praśrabdhi* (pliancy), which does not exist in the desire realm. The remaining factors are common to all three realms and the five [classes of consciousness].

Among the three [types of sensation], only *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) is excluded; it does not coexist with *daurmanasya* (mental grief) or *duḥkha* (physical pain). The others possess all five sensations.

These are all capable of being associated with the object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*), as they are not mutually contradictory. 1. *Śraddhā* (faith): Its nature is a profound acceptance of, and a longing for, reality, virtue, and capability, characterized by mental clarity.

Its function is to delight in what is wholesome. 2. *Hrī* (moral shame): Its nature is the veneration of the noble and the good. Its function is to restrain from unwholesome conduct. 3. [The third factor...]

1. *Hrī* (Moral Shame): It has the nature of lightly rejecting violence and evil, and its function is to cease unwholesome conduct. 2. Non-attachment (*alobha*): It has the nature of being without clinging toward existence and the requisites for existence.

3. Non-hatred (*adveṣa*): It has the nature of being without malice toward suffering and the requisites for suffering. 4. Non-delusion (*amoha*): It has the nature of clear understanding regarding the principles of the Truths (*satya*).
These three share the common function of performing wholesome deeds. 5. Diligence (*vīrya*): It consists of the cultivation of the wholesome and the abandonment of the unwholesome.
Vigor has courage as its nature; its function is to fulfill wholesome qualities. Eighth, pliancy has the harmonious flexibility of body and mind as its nature;

its function is the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Ninth, heedfulness has the prevention of non-virtue and the cultivation of virtue as its nature; its function is the perfection of wholesome matters. Tenth, equanimity has the equalizing of the mind as its nature;
its function is to remedy restlessness and abide in tranquility. Eleventh, non-harming has the non-injury of sentient beings as its nature.

Its function is to remedy harm and to have compassion as its essential nature. Among these eleven factors, three are nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*): namely, heedfulness (*apramāda*), diligence (*vīrya*), and the three roots.
Regarding these four factors, that which is able to both prevent [the unwholesome] and cultivate [the wholesome] within the context of abandonment and cultivation is called heedfulness;

it does not possess a separate substantial entity, as it lacks any distinct characteristic. Equanimity (*upekṣā*) likewise consists of these same four factors, wherein it causes the mind to remain free from agitation (*auddhatya*).

The obstacles to equanimity are countered by "abandonment" (*upekṣā*), which is defined as dwelling in tranquility; it is not a separate entity. "Non-harming" (*avihiṃsā*) is simply a portion of non-aversion (*adveṣa*);

it is metaphorically termed "non-harming" when one refrains from inflicting injury or affliction upon sentient beings. Non-aversion uproots suffering, whereas non-harming bestows happiness; this is the distinction between their coarse characteristics.

As for the remaining eight [wholesome mental factors], they are substantially real because their characteristics and functions are distinct. Among the four afflictions, there are six; these six, beginning with greed (*rāga*), constitute their essential nature.
These are the roots that receive the name "afflictions" (*kleśa*). 1. Greed (*lobha*): Its nature is attachment to existence (*bhava*) and the requisites of existence (*bhavopakaraṇa*).

Its function is to obstruct non-greed and to give rise to suffering. 2. Hatred (*dveṣa*): Its nature is the intensification of resentment toward suffering and the requisites of suffering. Its function is to serve as the basis for unease and unwholesome conduct (*akuśala-caryā*).
3. Delusion (*moha*): Its nature is confusion and darkness regarding all principles and phenomena (*dharmas*). It serves as the basis for all forms of defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
4. Pride (*māna*). Its intrinsic nature is loftiness; its function is to give rise to suffering. 5. Doubt (*vicikitsā*). Its intrinsic nature is hesitation regarding the [Four] Truths;

its function is to obstruct the factors conducive to the wholesome. 6. Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). There are five distinctions in the characteristics of its modes of activity: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

1. The view of self and what belongs to self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because of clinging to "I" and "mine. 2. The two types of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), because of clinging to the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. 3. False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), because of repudiating cause and effect. 4. Adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). 5.
Adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), because of clinging to one's own views and precepts as being supreme, pure, and capable of attaining *nirvāṇa*.
Their characteristics consist of striving in vain and undergoing hardships without benefit, and so forth. Among these ten afflictions, both in their general and specific aspects, six are pervasive.

[The first five afflictions] arise both innately (*sahaja*) and through discrimination (*vikalpita*). Among the latter three views, they arise only through discrimination. Greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*), as well as doubt (*vicikitsā*), certainly do not arise simultaneously.

Greed can be associated with pride (*māna*) and the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-moha*). Hatred can arise together with pride, doubt, and delusion; however, it is necessarily dissociated from the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*).
This [hatred] can be associated with the three types of view-delusions. As for pride, regarding its object it is certain; as for doubt, it is—

Not so; there is no sense of association [between them]. Pride may arise simultaneously with all five views, yet it certainly does not arise together with the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), nor does it do so with one portion of the view of false selfhood (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
Doubt, being characterized by lack of certainty, is contradictory to views and definitely does not arise together with them.

The five views are necessarily not associated with one another, because there cannot be multiple instances of wisdom (*prajñā*) within a single moment of mind. Ignorance (*moha*) [is associated] with nine...

All [afflictions] are associated with the mental factors of feeling (*vedanā*). Since the arising of all afflictions necessarily depends on delusion (*moha*), the three—greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion—are both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*);
all of these may be associated with the five feelings. Conceptual pride (*vikalpita-māna*) is associated only with four feelings, because it does not exist in the three miserable realms (*apāya*).

Innate pride (*sahaja-māna*) is also associated with the feeling of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*). Regarding doubt (*vicikitsā*) and the latter two views (*dṛṣṭi*), they may be associated with four feelings, excluding only the feeling of suffering.

Regarding the [two types of] views: the two innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*) can coexist with all five feelings (*vedanā*). The two conceptually acquired views (*vikalpita-dṛṣṭi*) exclude only the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).

Among the three natures (*tri-śīla*), hatred (*dveṣa*) is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), because it harms both oneself and others; the remaining nine [mental factors] pertain to both [the wholesome and the unwholesome].

Those belonging to the two upper realms are comprised solely of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because they are suppressed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) arise through conceptualization, they are comprised solely of the unwholesome, as they incite evil conduct.

Therefore, if they are innate (*sahaja*) and give rise to unwholesome karma, they are subsumed under the unwholesome; otherwise, they are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Regarding their distinction by the three realms (*dhātu*):

hatred (*dveṣa*) exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the others pervade all three realms. Among the six root afflictions (*kleśa*), views (*dṛṣṭi*) are conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*) because they are a division of wisdom (*prajñā*);

the others are substantially existent (*dravyasat*) because they have distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). There are twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), which are exclusively divisions of the root afflictions.
Because they are of the nature of outflows (*niṣyanda*) that differentiate states, they are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). These twenty types are divided into three categories:

first, the ten beginning with anger (*krodha*), which arise individually, are called minor secondary afflictions (*parīttakleśabhūmika*); second, shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), which is pervasive among the unwholesome, is called a medium secondary affliction;

and third, the eight beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*), which are pervasive in all defiled minds, are called major secondary afflictions (*mahākleśabhūmika*). However, there are only ten minor [secondary] afflictions.

1. Anger (*krodha*): Its nature is the outburst of indignation; its function is the grasping of a staff. 2. Resentment (*upanāha*): Its nature is the binding of enmity; its function is the torment of burning distress.

3. Concealment (*mrakṣa*): Its nature is the hiding [of one's faults]; its function is the remorse and distress [that follows]. 4. Vexation (*pradāsa*): Its nature is perversity and stubbornness; its function is the stinging of malice.

5. Envy (*īrṣyā*). Its nature is jealousy; its function is sorrowful distress. 6. Avarice (*mātsarya*). Its nature is secret hoarding; its function is stinginess. 7. Deceit (*śāṭhya*). Its nature is guile;

its function is wrong livelihood. 8. Sycophancy (*māyā*). Its nature is crookedness; its function is refusing instruction and admonition. 9. Harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*). Its nature is injury and affliction;
its function is pervasive torment. 10. Arrogance (*mada*). Its nature is intoxication and haughtiness; its function is defiled dependence.

Their function is to promote unwholesome conduct. The two intermediate [universal] factors are: first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), which has the nature of disregarding and rejecting the noble and the good;

second, lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), which has the nature of honoring and valuing violent thoughts. Their common function is to promote unwholesome conduct. The eight great universal [defilements] are:

first, restlessness (*auddhatya*), which has the nature of making the mind unsettled; its function is to obstruct the category of tranquility (*śamatha*). Second, lethargy (*styāna*), which has the nature of making the mind incapable [of functioning]; its function is to obstruct...
1. Its function is to contemplate [objects]. 2. Lack of faith (āśraddhya): its nature is defilement of the mind; its function is to serve as a basis for indolence. 3. Indolence (kausīdya):
its nature is laziness regarding the tasks of cultivation and abandonment; its function is to obstruct diligence and increase affliction. 4. Heedlessness (pramāda):

its nature is the failure to guard and cultivate while being dissolute; its function is to serve as a basis for increasing evil and diminishing good. 5. Loss of mindfulness (muṣitasmṛtitā): its nature is the inability to clearly remember.
Its nature is distraction; its function is to serve as the basis for mental scattering. Seventh, mental scattering: its nature is to cause the mind to wander;

its function is to serve as the basis for unwholesome wisdom (*duṣprajñā*). Eighth, lack of correct awareness (*asaṃprajanya*): its nature is erroneous understanding; its function is the violation of precepts. These twenty [mental factors] all include both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*) types.
Among these twenty, the ten minor ones do not arise simultaneously with one another, because they are mutually contradictory. Regarding the middle [ten]: [text continues].
Second, all [secondary afflictions] associated with unwholesome minds may arise together with the minor and major [afflictions] as appropriate.

The major secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) pervade all defiled minds; they may all arise together among the minor and intermediate [afflictions]. The intermediate and major [afflictions] are entirely associated with the five feelings (*vedanā*).

The three—deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), and pride (*mada*)—may coexist with all five feelings. The seven factors beginning with anger (*krodha*) exclude only the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), because they belong exclusively to the desire realm. Second.

The ten universal mental factors may arise together with the object-specific factors (*viṣayaviniyata*). Among these, the essence of false mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*)—which are respectively mindfulness and wisdom—may correspond with the other four [object-specific factors] as appropriate.
Those that are branches of delusion (*moha*) are associated with all five [object-specific factors].

Wrath (*krodha*) is associated with mindfulness, because it departs in a single moment from the categories previously cultivated. There is no fault in non-concentration (*vikṣepa*) being associated with concentration (*samādhi*), for even within defiled concentration, it remains remote.

Because they are agitated, the two middle [categories] of the great [afflictions] are associated with the eighteen [great] afflictions. The ten small [afflictions] certainly do not arise together with views (*dṛṣṭi*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*), because their natures differ in terms of coarseness and subtlety.

The five factors beginning with anger (*krodha*) may be associated with pride (*māna*) and delusion (*moha*), but not with greed (*rāga*) or hatred (*pratigha*), because they are all subdivisions of hatred.

Stinginess (*mātsarya*) is associated with delusion and pride, but not with greed or hatred, because it is a subdivision of greed. Arrogance (*mada*) is associated only with delusion; its mode of understanding differs from that of pride, and it is a subdivision of greed.

Because they are divisions [of other afflictions]: concealment (*mrakṣa*), deception (*māyā*), and guile (*śāṭhya*) do not contradict the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), and envy (*īrṣyā*), as they are divisions of greed and delusion.

Among the seven minor [afflictions], only those categorized as unwholesome (*akuśala*) are included; the three major [minor afflictions] and eight [of the minor ones] also extend to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Among the seven minor [afflictions], two are restricted to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);

deception and guile belong to both the desire and form realms (*rūpadhātu*); the remainder extend across all three realms. Among these twenty [secondary afflictions], the ten minor and three major [afflictions] are definitely nominal (*prajñapti*).

There are [twenty secondary afflictions]. Resentment (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāsa*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) are established based on hatred (*dveṣa*). The three—concealment (*mrakṣa*), flattery (*śāṭhya*), and deception (*māyā*)—are established based on greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*).

The two factors of avarice (*mātsarya*) and arrogance (*mada*) are established based on craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Heedlessness (*pramāda*) refers to the inability to guard and cultivate [the mind] due to laziness (*kausīdya*), as well as greed, hatred, and delusion.

These are collectively termed *pramāda* (heedlessness); they do not possess a separate substantial entity. All others [among the mental factors] are substantially real. Among the six indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), there are four;

because they are indeterminate with respect to both the wholesome and the defiled, unlike *sparśa* (contact) and others which are necessarily universal to the mind, and unlike *chanda* (desire) and others which are necessarily universal to the ground [of consciousness], they are designated as "indeterminate.
1. *Kaukṛtya* (remorse): Its intrinsic nature is regret; its function is to obstruct *śamatha* (calm abiding). 2. *Middha* (sleep): Its intrinsic nature is dullness and brevity...

[The nature of] vitarka (applied thought) is to obstruct insight; its function is to cause the mind to engage with an object in a coarse manner. [The nature of] vicāra (sustained thought) is to cause the mind to engage with an object in a subtle manner.
Both of these have as their function the basis for the states of the body and mind being either settled or unsettled.

Among these four [mental factors], vitarka and vicāra are never associated with one another, because they differ in their coarseness and subtlety. Based upon vitarka and vicāra, there is defilement; [and] apart from...

The distinction between the three stages is established based on their defilement (*kleśa*), not on whether they arise in dependence upon those destinies (*gati*) or views (*dṛṣṭi*); therefore, there is no confusion.

All [of these] may be associated with the former two [mental factors], and the former two also have the sense of being mutually associated. Among the five feelings (*vedanā*), remorse (*kaukṛtya*) excludes joy (*saumanasya*) and pleasure (*sukha*), because it functions exclusively as a state of dejection (*daurmanasya*).
Sleep (*middha*) excludes the feeling of pleasure, because it exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) pervade all five feelings.

Because they belong to the first dhyāna, all four [mental factors] may arise together with the particular objects (viśeṣa-viṣaya). This is because their modes of activity (ākāra) and objects of focus (ālambana) do not conflict.
Regret (kaukṛtya) and torpor (middha) may both coexist with the ten wholesome [factors]; these exist only in the desire realm, as there is no pliancy (praśrabdhi) there.
Vitarka and vicāra may coexist with the eleven wholesome [factors], because they coexist with pliancy within the first dhyāna. Regret, however, can only coexist with ignorance (avidyā). This...

The modes of activity (*ākāra*) of these are coarse because greed and the other [root afflictions] are subtle. Sleep (*middha*), vitarka, and vicāra coexist with all ten root afflictions, as they do not mutually contradict one another.

Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) may coexist with the intermediate and major derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*), but not with the ten [specific types] such as anger (*krodha*), because each of those functions as a primary [affliction].

Sleep, vitarka, and vicāra may coexist with all twenty [derivative afflictions], since they arise during all states including sleep and so forth. These four are all common to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.

Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): because regret (*kaukṛtya*) also occurs in relation to neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma, it is common to both innate (*upapattilābhika*) and applied (*prāyogika*) wholesome states.

It is also common to all three [wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral] of the defiled and pure neutral categories. Since regret is not defiled and its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is coarse and intense, it does not arise from the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Among the four types of neutral states, regret is limited to the middle two; because its mode of activity is coarse and intense, it is not the result of concentration. Sleep (*middha*) excludes the fourth [the neutral state of the fruit of concentration], as it is not induced by concentration. As for discursive thought (*vitarka*)...

Investigation (*vicāra*) excludes the first [dhyāna]. Its understanding is weak and subtle, as it is unable to investigate the meaning of names and so forth. Vitarka and vicāra are conventional (*prajñapti*), being a synthesis of volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are substantial (*dravya*). Vitarka and vicāra take the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as their cause; remorse and sleep are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*). Remorse and sleep exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Vitarka and vicāra exist in the desire realm and the first dhyāna. In the remaining realms and stages, all factors are tranquil and sublime.
These mental factors, in relation to that mental sovereign (citta-rāja), are identical in terms of simultaneity, common object, and basis;
since their substance is one, they and the sovereign are termed "associated" (saṃprayukta). Third, matter (rūpa-dharma) consists briefly of eleven types:

namely, the five faculties, the five objects, and that which is subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana). That which possesses resistance and is subject to transformation is called matter. Regarding the five faculties: first, the eye.
The faculties: second, the ear faculty; third, the nose faculty; fourth, the tongue faculty; fifth, the body faculty.

These have as their essence the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements, which are not shared [with other consciousnesses]. Because they serve as the specific, non-shared bases for the five consciousnesses, they are called "faculties.

Regarding the five objects: first, visible form; second, sound; third, odor; fourth, taste; fifth, tangible objects. When the faculties and objects are correlated, the five consciousnesses are directly [engaged with them].

Regarding the characteristics: by taking the general from the particular, and the obscure from the luminous, the various internal and external forms that are the objects of the eighth [consciousness] are likewise included herein.

These are subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and consist of five categories: first, the extremely condensed (*paramāṇu-saṃkṣipta*), which is the reduction of obstructive matter down to the measure of an atom (*paramāṇu*);

second, the extremely remote (*paramāṇu-dūra*), which is the reduction of obstructed matter to a point where it can no longer be reduced; third, the form produced by what is induced by feeling (*vedanā-niṣyanda-rūpa*), which is—

1. Unmanifest precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*). 2. Matter produced by the mastery of the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), namely, matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*). 3.

Matter arising from false conceptualization (*parikalpita-rūpa*), which is apprehended by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and is distinct from the preceding four types; all such cases are included herein. 4. The twenty-four factors dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*).
Briefly stated, there are twenty-four. These are termed "dissociated formations" because they are not associated with mind, mental factors, or matter. This excludes non-existence (*abhāva*).
To establish these names: first, *prāpti* (acquisition), because it accomplishes the functional utility regarding all phenomena;

second, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because it maintains the continuity of matter and mind throughout a single lifetime—determined by its specific distinction—by means of the power of karma following the seeds of the eighth consciousness that manifest in this birth;

third, the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*), because it functions as the similarity among members of the same class of persons or phenomena; fourth, the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). Seeing...

Because the seeds to be abandoned prevent that noble nature from functioning, [the following are included]: (5) the concentration of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*) and (6) the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Both take as their essence the seeds of the extremely subtle mind and the obstruction of the mind’s functional capacity, characterized by twenty-two factors—both wholesome and universal, both general and specific.

These two attainments are distinguished by whether they are contaminated or uncontaminated, and whether they are attained by ordinary beings or noble ones. (7) The maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) is that very attainment...
That which is matured results in rebirth among the Longevity Devas (*dīrghāyus-deva*). Among these, the sixth is a distinct retributive result (*vipāka-viśeṣa*).

It consists of eleven dharmas that pervade the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and obstruct its functional capacity; it takes the state of non-conception (*acittaka*) as its essence. The eighth [category] is the "name" (*nāman*), so called because it denotes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The ninth is the "phrase" (*pada*), so called because it denotes specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*).

The tenth is the "syllable" (*vyañjana*), which serves as the basis for both of the preceding two, thereby manifesting those two states. This [treatment] is based solely on this land [of Jambudvīpa], relying upon sound.

These are established by convention (*prajñapti*). If one includes other realms, there are likewise eleven [characteristics] of arising (*jāti*), because they indicate what was previously non-existent;

twelve of abiding (*sthiti*), because they indicate temporary existence; thirteen of change (*anyathātva*), because they indicate transformation; fourteen of cessation (*nirodha*), because they indicate subsequent non-existence;
fifteen of flux (*pravṛtti*), because cause and effect continue without interruption; sixteen of fixed differentiation (*pratiniyama*), because causes and effects are each unmixed; and seventeen...
21. Correspondence (*samyoga*): because cause and effect accord with one another. 22. Velocity (*java*): because their movement and transformation are extremely rapid. 23. Succession (*anukrama*):

because cause and effect do not exist simultaneously. 24. Direction (*diś*): because it is distinguished by the demarcations of manifest color (*varṇa*). 25. Time (*kāla*): because the three periods of time are distinct.
26. Number (*saṃkhyā*): because of the distinctions between one, many, and so forth. 27. Conjunction (*sāmagrī*). 28. [Twenty-fourth...]

They are not in conjunction, because the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) arise and disperse due to the distinctness of their conditions. As for the five unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), there are briefly six kinds.

Their fundamental nature is quiescent and still; from the beginningless past, their essence is true reality, free from existence and non-existence. How could they possess arising and ceasing? Both activity and motion are utterly extinguished.
Therefore, they are designated as "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*): 1. Space (*ākāśa*), because its essence is devoid of the nature of form and it unobstructedly accommodates all things; 2.

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which refers to the manifestation of cessation by means of the power of wisdom that eliminates hindrances; 3. Cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is the nature of non-arising due to the absence of conditions, obtained through the suppression of afflictions within an inherently pure nature;
4. The Unshakable (*āniñjya*), because it is not moved by the formations of suffering or pleasure; 5. The Extinction of Perception and Feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).

Because it is manifested by the non-functioning of perception and sensation (*saṃjñā-vedita*). There are six types of *tathatā* (suchness). Because it is free from delusion and distinct from inversion, its nature is eternally pervasive.
The former five are provisional, as they are established based on conventional meanings; the latter one is real, as it accords with the fundamental reality of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

The former five may also involve the transformation of consciousness, whereas the latter one refers exclusively to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). One must not fail to understand these essential points regarding the characteristics of phenomena. May all... [beings attain] them.
Let later students not grow weary of the prolixity of the text.
Regarding the term "seed-consciousness" (*bīja-vijñāna*) and so forth: one interpretation states that because the seeds are not separate from consciousness, they are called "seed-consciousness";

this refers exclusively to the essence of the seeds themselves. Another interpretation states that because consciousness maintains the seeds, it is called "seed-consciousness"; this refers exclusively to its present substantial entity.

Third, regarding the "seed-nature" (*bīja-svabhāva*) as the essence of consciousness, the name is established based on its function (a *karmadhāraya* compound). "Seed" refers to that which manifests and grasps [objects]. Now, according to the first interpretation, there are two types: 1. **Innate nature** (*prakṛtistha*):

This refers solely to the seeds of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). 2. **Produced by practice** (*samudānīta*): This encompasses both original and newly acquired seeds; it includes those that are originally present (and further strengthened) as well as those produced through new perfuming (*navavāsanā*).

Since the commentary establishes that consciousness arises solely from karma and afflictions: this is because the eighth consciousness in its entirety and the first six consciousnesses in part are the direct results produced by karma and afflictions as their maturation (*vipāka*);
whereas the seventh consciousness in its entirety and the first six consciousnesses in part are the indirect results produced by karma and afflictions, as they depend upon the matured consciousness.

Regarding the commentary’s analysis of "that which is produced by conditions": first, it is said to have the meaning of "falsehood"; second, it is said to have the meaning of "conceptualizing objects.

As for the statement that "the pure portion of the dependent nature is also the perfected nature," there are two gates regarding untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*): first, the gate of the permanent and the impermanent;
this [pure portion] is subsumed under the impermanent dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Second, the gate of the tainted and the untainted; this [pure portion] corresponds to the untainted.

It is subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the statement, "The term 'nature' (*svabhāva*) reveals that the two emptinesses are not the perfected reality," this explains the character "nature.

The two emptinesses are merely the two selves that are to be eliminated; they serve as the gateway. It is the true nature (*tattva*) which is capable of being distanced from [the two selves] that is the perfected reality.
Now, when we speak of its "nature," it refers to that which is capable of distancing itself, thereby distinguishing it from that which is to be distanced. This is why it is stated thus. (Vasu)

It is said that *śūnya* is translated as "emptiness" (*kōng*). In Sanskrit, *dharmatā* is translated as "nature" (*xìng*). Therefore, it is known that the nature and the two kinds of emptiness differ greatly in essence.
When it is said that "True Suchness is a nature that is free from existence and free from non-existence," this explains the aforementioned "nature.
The meaning is that the true nature is such that it naturally transcends all attachments to both existence and non-existence.

Regarding the passage in the *Subcommentary* (*Śāstra*) based on the ninth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* which states, "There are four kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), etc.," the specific names are abbreviated as they appear in that text.

As for the explanation of their names and the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), I shall now present them briefly. First, the explanation of the names; second, the determination of the essential nature. The first section further has two parts: first, the explanation of the general name;
second, the explanation of the specific names. Regarding the explanation of the general name, Dharmapāla explains: "The world (*loka*) refers to that which is concealed."

The meaning of "destructible" refers to that which is conventionally called "manifestation," in the sense of following worldly conventions. This truth should logically be named the "truth of concealment and manifestation.

It conceals the principle of emptiness while manifesting with signs, just as when a handkerchief is tied into the shape of a rabbit or other object, the original handkerchief is concealed and the appearance of a rabbit manifests.
This case is likewise. Now, following ancient nomenclature, it is termed conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Furthermore,

Furthermore, that which arises and ceases through the transformation of nature is called the "world" (*loka*). Because its essential characteristics are coarse and manifest, it is termed the "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*). "World" is itself the conventional; thus, it is named "the conventional world" (*lokasaṃvṛti*).

Alternatively, "the convention of the world" (*lokasya saṃvṛti*) is also not contrary to the meaning. As for "truth" (*satya*), it carries the sense of reality: that which exists as it truly is, one knows as existing;
that which does not exist as it truly is, one knows as non-existent. Since existence and non-existence are not false, it is called "truth. The conventional is itself truth.

Regarding the truths of the mundane world, there are two explanations in successive order. "Ultimate" (*paramārtha*) refers to two kinds of meanings: first, the meaning as an object; second, the meaning as a principle.
The fourth [truth], the ultimate truth, is frequently explained in various treatises as that which is "ultimate" and is itself the "meaning.

Alternatively, all four types of ultimate truth are the meaning of being "ultimate. The treatises state that the two natures—the dependent and the perfected—correspond accordingly to their respective faculties.

Because it is the object of both the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), that untainted true wisdom (*anāsrava-tattva-jñāna*)—regardless of which truth it resides within—is also defined by "excellence" (*parama*), as its object is *tathatā* (suchness).
Thus, it is analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* compound. The fourth ultimate (*paramārtha*) is for the most part based on the meaning of "reasoning" (*yukti*);
since it is not an objective domain (*gocara*), the linguistic expression is set aside to discuss the intended meaning. The first three [types of] ultimate are termed "objects."

*Artha* means "meaning. *Satya* (truth) means the sense of reality. Regarding phenomena (*vastu*), it is the phenomenon as it truly is; regarding principles (*naya*), it is the principle as it truly is. Because phenomena and principles are not erroneous, they are termed *satya*.
Ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) is itself truth; thus, it is the "truth of ultimate meaning. These two explanations are as previously stated.

Just as with the Four Noble Truths, because noble ones are able to know them, and because their existence or non-existence—both in terms of phenomena and principles—is not falsely established, they are designated as *satya*. Next, the individual names are explained.
The worldly conventional (*loka-saṃvṛti*) conceals the ultimate truth; it consists of the dispositions of the present age and falls into the midst of falsehood, hence it is called "worldly.
All ordinary people claim that things exist; names are established based on these dispositions, and this provisional designation is called the "conventional.

The rational conventional (*yukti-saṃvṛti*) refers to the establishment of phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*) according to their respective meanings; this is called "rational," as the characteristics of things manifest therein.

The distinction is easy to understand; it is called the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). To realize the conventional means to establish the distinctions between the causes and effects of affliction and purification, thereby causing one to enter [the path];
this is called "realization. That which has characteristics and is cognizable is called the conventional.

Regarding the ultimate-conventional (*paramārtha-saṃvṛti*): that which excellently transcends all phenomena and is known by the noble ones (*ārya*) is called the ultimate (*paramārtha*). It is established through provisional characteristics.
It stands that the non-essence which is beyond words is called the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Herein, "the world" (*loka*) is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*);

even up to "the ultimate" (*paramārtha*), it is the conventional truth. These are all *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds. Regarding "the worldly ultimate" (*lokaparamārtha*), its phenomenal characteristics are coarse and manifest.

That which is still subject to destruction is called the "mundane" (*loka*). It is also what the noble ones (*ārya*) know. That which transcends the first [type of] conventionality is called the "ultimate" (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the ultimate as principle (*yukti-paramārtha*): the knowledge of, the abandonment of, the realization of, and the cultivation of the distinctions between cause and effect is called "principle.

The object of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), which transcends the two preceding types of conventionality, is called the "ultimate. As for the attainment of the ultimate (*paramārtha-prāpti*), it is based upon noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*).

Explanation: The gate of emptiness reveals the principle and is called "attainment by the noble ones" (*ārya-prāpti*). That which ordinary, ignorant beings do not transcend—the three conventionalities—is called the "ultimate" (*paramārtha*).
As for the "ultimate of the ultimate": its essence is subtle and beyond words; it transcends all phenomena and is thus called the ultimate.

It is internally realized by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) and, surpassing the four preceding conventionalities, is further named the ultimate. Within this context, the mundane world itself is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Up to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all are *karmadhāraya* compounds; alternatively, as a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the truth of the ultimate," there is no fault.

Next, regarding the definition of their essential nature: first, concerning the conventional nature, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that it refers to things such as jars, armies, forests, the self, and sentient beings as they are conventionally established.
Alternatively, they lack substantial reality; they truly do not exist, being merely nominal designations, and thus entirely devoid of essence.

In nature, however, there are two types of phenomena: those that are functional and those that are non-functional. Vases and the like are functional; the self (*ātman*) and so forth are non-functional. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, chapter thirteen, states:

"There are names but no reality, such as the self (*ātman*), sentient beings (*sattva*), and so on, up to the wheel of fire, as well as names, phrases, and so forth—these five kinds of worldly phenomena are called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Sentient beings and the like have no functional utility; the wheel of fire and so forth [are likewise non-functional]."

The first [conventional truth] has no substantial entity (*tattva*). Regarding the second conventional entity, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that it refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) as they are established.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also says that the aggregates, elements, and bases are called "conventional. This includes unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena as well;
these dharmas possess distinct entities and functions that differ from the first type of conventionality. Regarding the third conventional truth, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*...

The *Śāstra* explains that this refers to the established fruits such as the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), as well as their basis—namely, the principles of the Four Noble Truths and so forth regarding the various noble fruits.
Regarding Nirvāṇa, it is also said that there are eight characteristics of suffering, which are termed conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

As for the essence of the fourth conventional truth, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is the nature of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as it is established; the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* likewise speaks of it.

Whether it be burning, cutting, death, or dependence, these are termed "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*). Because they are subject to burning, cutting, and so forth, they lack the characteristics of a permanent, unitary self or phenomena;

thus, the two kinds of selflessness are called "worldly truth" (*loka-satya*). The first conventional reality is established as a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), while the latter three conventional realities are established with specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
As for the first ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*), it is established as the [nature of] Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that the entities such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also says that what possesses both name and reality is called the ultimate;

thus, the aggregates, bases, and elements are likewise the ultimate. Regarding the second type of ultimate—the substantial entity—the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that it refers to the causal and resultant entities such as the Four Noble Truths.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also says that suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path are called the ultimate.

The third essence of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* as the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness, revealed through the gateway of verbal expression.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states that the absence of the eight characteristics of suffering is called the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).

Because one observes all phenomena collectively as being devoid of the two forms of self, there is no suffering and so forth; this is termed the ultimate truth. The fourth essence of ultimate truth is explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
This refers to the non-conceptually established single true *dharmadhātu*. It is also called "Nirvāṇa" and "Ultimate Truth.

Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s space-like *buddhadhātu* is free from burning, cutting, and so forth; this is named the "First Meaning" (*paramārtha*) because it reveals the truth without relying on selflessness.
The first three types of ultimate meaning are conceptually established because they possess characteristics (*sanimitta*), whereas the fourth ultimate meaning is without characteristics (*animitta*).

Regarding the establishment [of the two truths]: the first conventional truth consists of external objects that do not exist; these are established based on mental perception and are thus called "conventional.

The second conventional truth consists of the phenomena transformed by the mind; the latter two [truths] consist of the principles transformed by the mind, which are distinguished through conceptual designation.

These are the aforementioned three natures (*trisvabhāva*). As for the fourth nature, it is realized solely through internal wisdom; it is not a principle manifested by the transformation of the mind.

According to their respective applications, these correspond to the three natures. The above has clarified the names and distinguished the essential bodies and objects. There are further gateways [of analysis] fully contained in the *Fayuan* (Garden of Dharma).
This is the standard for the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); do not grow weary of the prolixity of the text.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "the four characteristics perish simultaneously, manifesting subsequent non-existence": when established, the four characteristics exist simultaneously; when manifested, cessation alone is past.
This is merely a distinction based on the temporal sequence of the perishing of the characteristics within the continuum of sentient beings.

Regarding the commentary’s explanation that "the *yiqian* (single-pronged) contemplation definitely illuminates individually": First, it is called *yiqian* contemplation in the sense that the primary and subsequent [moments] follow one another; yet, when the primary and subsequent are discussed separately, they actually illuminate individually.

Second, it is said to be *yiqian* contemplation in the sense that the essence of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) is identical; however, because the functions of the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) differ, they definitely illuminate individually.

Third, it is said to be *yiqian* contemplation in the sense that the fundamental [wisdom] cuts off [afflictions] together; whereas the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) cuts off [them] singly and definitely illuminates individually.

4. Subsequent Attainment Universal Knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-sarvajñatā*) is explained as "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*): while the fundamental [knowledge] focuses exclusively on a single object with certainty, this [subsequent knowledge] illuminates distinctly.

5. Thoroughly Understanding the Conventional by Realizing the Ultimate is explained as "contemplation": these two knowledges are not fused and their two objects are not identical, yet they constantly illuminate them separately.

Regarding the "paths of abandonment of the mundane and supramundane": this refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which takes both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*) as its objects.
Alternatively, it is called "mundane" because the subsequently attained wisdom takes the mundane world as its object; it is called "supramundane" because its nature is untainted (*anāsrava*).

The statement, "Abandoning delusion regarding phenomena and principle means observing the objective realm of principle," etc., is an explanation of the meaning of the Dharma-character school (*lakṣaṇa-yāna*) based upon the Nature school (*prakṛti-yāna*). This is because the Nature school explains that...
That which is abandoned is precisely the objective referent (*ālambana*). Therefore, it is said that one illuminates the fundamental emptiness of delusions. Furthermore, Nāgārjuna stated:

"The coarsest among the coarse is the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)," and so forth. This is not the case in the Dharma-characteristics school (*lakṣaṇavāda*), which maintains that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) takes only ultimate truth as its object, thereby severing both the delusion regarding principle and the delusion regarding phenomena;
whereas subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) universally takes both principle and phenomena as its objects, severing only the single delusion regarding phenomena.
Because of delusion. Alternatively, fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) directly takes the realm of principle as its object and is able to sever the delusions that obscure principle;
subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) directly takes the realm of phenomena as its object and merely severs the delusions that obscure phenomena.

As for the statement that it "should be called 'explained in terms of meaning' regarding simultaneous severance," this refers to fundamental wisdom; whereas "actually severing them separately" refers to subsequently attained wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*) and so forth: "all aspects" refers to the objects of observation, or alternatively, it refers to the distinctions among the categories of the observing subject.
The term "mind" (*citta*) refers to the eight consciousnesses.

The term "mental factors" (*caitasika dharma*) refers to the five universal factors, the five object-specific factors, and the eleven wholesome factors. The phrase "and their various types" encompasses all five aggregates (*skandha*).
▲ Regarding the "four foundations of mindfulness," these are body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.

▲ Regarding the statement that "the great perfect sphere of object and wisdom is accomplished as self-enjoyment and so forth," this is because the eighth pure consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) cites its proximate, superior dharmas.

Otherwise, there would be twenty-two faculties within the body; furthermore, the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) would have to be a faculty, because it teaches the Dharma. Each of the four wisdoms...
This is another interpretation.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the characteristics of dharmas are few," it is like saying that there are many waves and little still water in the ocean;
for apart from the waves, there is still water, and all waves are of the nature of water.
The *Chao* (Commentary) states that only the True [Nature] is non-arising. A question is raised: Are not the merits of the Buddha-fruit also the True Nature?
The answer is: This refers to deluded consciousness; it does not mean that the first stage [of Bodhisattvahood] is like water at rest, which does not depend on the conditions of wind.
Furthermore, this is stated by citing the deluded to manifest the True; it is not that only the True Nature is meant.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “But it is because this is *tathatā* (suchness) and so forth,” the subsequent commentary explains *tathatā* as follows: “Unchanging is ‘true’ (*tathā*); conforming to conditions is ‘thus’ (*tā*).
Because it is unchanging, it has the sense of being non-identical with conditioned phenomena; because it conforms to conditions, it has the sense of being non-different from conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, the *Awakening of Faith* states: “Non-dispelling is ‘true’ (*tathā*); non-establishment is ‘thus’ (*tā*). This refers exclusively to...
Negation (paryudāsa) reveals its principle instantaneously, yet it is not the true nature itself.

Regarding the passage in the *Commentary* (Śāstra), "If the nature of moisture were lost, what would follow the wind? and so forth, the subsequent sub-commentary (*Vivaraṇa*) explains that water possesses ten meanings.
Because it is identical to the true nature (*tathatā*): 1. The essence of water is clear and limpid; this is a metaphor for the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*).
2. When it encounters mud, it becomes turbid; this is a metaphor for the pure mind being unstained yet appearing stained. 3. Although turbid, it does not lose its pure nature;

this is a metaphor for the pure mind being stained yet remaining unstained. 4. If the mud is settled and clarity appears, the direct mind has exhausted delusion and the nature is manifested. 5. It becomes cool.
6. Ice possesses the function of hardness; this is a metaphor for how the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) acquires its functional nature through conjunction with ignorance (*avidyā*).

Although it has acquired the function of hardness, it does not lose its soft nature—this is a metaphor for the fact that phenomena are eternally true. 7. Warmth causes the ice to melt and become soft; this is a metaphor for the storehouse consciousness returning to stillness. 8.
Although it moves and fluctuates with the wind, its still nature is not altered; this is a metaphor for the Tathāgatagarbha following along with ignorance.
9. Though the wind causes waves to rise and subside, it does not change its own nature of being neither born nor extinguished;
this illustrates how the True Mind flows and pours along with conditions while its nature remains eternally tranquil. 10.
Though it conforms to the squareness or roundness of the vessel, it does not lose its own nature; this illustrates how the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) pervades all realms of existence.
Regarding the Dharma, the Dharma loses its own-nature (*svabhāva*). To briefly distinguish ten meanings, because they partially resemble the truth, water is frequently used as a metaphor.

Although the *Śūchāo* (Commentary) has already clarified that the lack of nature in the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is itself the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and its principle is thus manifest, I still fear...

For beginners, this still dispels confusion and delusion. By forcefully employing the "conch-shell of the mind," one repeatedly draws from the ocean of meaning to explain these three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and open up those two gates.

First, the correct principle is directly elucidated; second, remaining doubts are resolved through discernment. Regarding the first, the elucidation of the correct principle: each of the three natures has two meanings. Within the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature, there are two meanings:
first, the meaning of immutability (*avikāra*), and second, the meaning of following conditions (*anuparivartana*). Within the *paratantra* (dependent) nature, there are two...

Regarding "meaning" (artha): first, the meaning of appearing as if existent; second, the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Regarding the two meanings of the grasped object (*parikalpita*): first, the meaning of existence from the perspective of conventional reality (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*); second, the meaning of non-existence from the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva*).

Because the true nature does not change and the dependent nature lacks intrinsic nature, that which is grasped is non-existent according to ultimate principle. It is by virtue of these three meanings [that this is established].
The three natures are of one limit, identical and without difference. This is precisely "not destroying the branches while remaining constant in the root.

As the Sūtra says: "Sentient beings are themselves nirvāṇa; they do not further undergo extinction. Furthermore, based on True Suchness (tathatā) following conditions, there is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), wherein there appears to be something grasped through the power of delusion (parikalpita-svabhāva).
By virtue of these three meanings, they are likewise without difference. This is precisely "not moving from the root while remaining constant in the branches. The Sūtra...
It is said that the Dharma-body flows through the five paths of rebirth and is called "sentient beings. Thus, by virtue of these three meanings, it is not the same as the previous three meanings.
Therefore, the Real (zhen) encompasses the delusive (wang), and the delusive penetrates the source of the Real; essence and appearance are mutually integrated.
"Unobstructed and unimpeded. Question: "Regarding the statement that 'the dependent nature appears as if existent' and so forth, how can this be the same as the existence of the imagined nature?

Answer: "It is due to two reasons; therefore, there is no difference. First, because those who cling to it take what appears as real, there is no separate phenomenon [of appearance]. Second, if one were separated from the imagined nature, the appearance would not arise.
One should know that the same applies to the true nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) when it follows conditions, because there is nothing to be clung to therein."
Because there is no following of conditions. Question: How is it that the three natures each have two meanings without contradiction? Answer: Because these two meanings do not differ in nature.
Why do they not differ? For instance, although the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) follows conditions to manifest as either defiled or pure, it never loses its own nature of purity.
Precisely because it does not lose its own nature of purity, it is able to follow [conditions].

Defilement and purity are established through conditions, just as a bright mirror manifests both defilement and purity. Although it manifests defilement and purity, it never loses the clarity and purity of the mirror itself.
Precisely because it does not lose its clarity and purity, it is able to manifest the appearances of defilement and purity.
By means of the manifestation of defilement and purity, one knows the mirror is bright and pure; by means of the mirror’s brightness and purity, one knows the manifestation of defilement and purity.

Therefore, these two meanings are of a single nature. Although pure phenomena manifest, they do not increase the mirror’s brightness; although defiled phenomena manifest, they do not soil the mirror’s purity.

It is not merely that it is unstained; rather, it is by means of this that the mirror’s clarity and purity are manifested in turn. One should know that the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is likewise:

it is not merely that its nature is unmoving and pure; it becomes defiled and purified. Furthermore, it is precisely through the process of becoming defiled and purified that its inherent purity is revealed.
It is not merely that it does not destroy defilement and purity while clarifying its inherent purity; rather, it is precisely because of its inherent purity that it is established as such.
Thus, defilement and purity are mutually inclusive in their entirety; since they are of one nature and non-dual, how could they be contradictory?

Although within the dependent nature there is an appearance of existence due to causes and conditions, that which exists therein must lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because all that is dependently originated is devoid of characteristics.
If it were not without intrinsic nature, it would not rely upon conditions, and thus it would not be a semblance of existence. It is a semblance of existence.
If something is established, it must arise from a multitude of conditions. Because it arises from a multitude of conditions, it necessarily lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Therefore, by virtue of lacking intrinsic nature, it is established as being like a conventional appearance; and because it is established as a conventional appearance, it is thus without intrinsic nature. Hence, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Contemplate all phenomena."
Arising from causes and conditions; arising from causes and conditions, it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is ultimately empty (*atyanta-śūnya*). That which is ultimately empty is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*.

This means that because things arise through conditions, they reveal the absence of intrinsic nature. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Because emptiness exists, all phenomena are possible. This is due to the absence [of intrinsic nature].
Because it is their nature, this clarifies dependent origination. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "They exist because of causes and conditions; they are empty because they lack intrinsic nature.

This means that the absence of intrinsic nature is itself dependent origination, and dependent origination is itself the absence of intrinsic nature. This is because it is the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Not only are these two meanings not mutually contradictory in their nature, but they also encompass one another in their entirety; ultimately, there is no duality. As for the grasped nature...
As for the "intermediate" [delusion]: although it accords with one's feelings and is grasped as existing in the present, it is ultimately non-existent according to the principles of reality.
This is because one falsely imagines existence where there is no basis for it, just as one might falsely perceive a ghost in a tree stump.
Yet, the ghost is ultimately non-existent in that wood; if the ghost were not non-existent in the wood, one could not say that one was falsely imagining the presence of a ghost. Because...

A ghost in a tree does not exist because of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Since one now engages in such arbitrary construction, it is clearly known that it lacks reality in principle. Because it lacks reality in principle, arbitrary construction is established;

and because arbitrary construction is established, one then knows its lack of reality in principle. Therefore, there are not two [realities], but only a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*). One should know that the principles of what is grasped are likewise so.
The foregoing concludes the direct exposition of the correct principle (*samyaktattva*). Hereafter, the remaining doubts shall be resolved. Question:

The thoroughly imagined nature is non-existent; the dependent nature exists as an illusion; the perfected nature exists as reality. Their principles are fundamentally distinct. How can they be identical? Answer:

It is precisely because, in this school, the fundamental truth is solely the single perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). However, by following conditions (*pratyaya*), it manifests as the other two natures. Why is this?
Due to the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the various consciousnesses, its entire substance becomes the dependent nature. This occurs through the conceptualization of the deluded mind.

Therefore, the entire substance functions as the nature of pervasive imagination (*parikalpita*). Just as the substance of hemp becomes entirely a rope through conditions such as subtle conjunction, so too, due to the deluded mind, the entire substance becomes a snake.
Although they differ according to their respective meanings and are thus divided into three natures, their substance is no different;

therefore, they are identical in essence. Furthermore, another interpretation provides a general explanation: through the perfuming of consciousness and the discrimination of the deluded mind, the two natures—the dependent (*paratantra*) and the imagined (*parikalpita*)—are established. However...

Because the past and the present are distinct. Why? It is because that which is the *paratantra* (dependent nature) is established through long-term perfuming and conceptualization (*vikalpa*) from beginningless time;
however, the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is established anew through fresh perfuming and conceptualization in the present.

This is like a newborn child who originally has no name, which is similar to the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature). Thus, it is called "the habitual tendency of the Yang family" (the family of transformation).

The Sūtra establishes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) based on self and other; yet, suppose there were a person who, upon suddenly calling out "Yang's family," would instead call them "Zhao's family.

Everyone would say this is incorrect (like the *parikalpita-svabhāva*), for while there are differences according to the gate [of perception], the three types [of natures] are opened up as being non-different in their fundamental totality—this is precisely the characteristic [of the dependent].

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that if one considers its original state to be false and delusive, it constitutes the dependent nature; that is, the very difference of delusion is what is termed [the dependent].

The parikalpita (imagined nature) is like suffering from a cold disease; (this is identical to the pariniṣpanna [perfected nature]). Dreaming of drowning in a river at night is like the paratantra (dependent nature). Fearing death and seeking rescue is like the parikalpita nature.

These three characteristics are simultaneous; their meaning is no different from what was stated previously. Furthermore, each of these three natures possesses four propositions. "True" refers to immutability.

From the perspective of the dependent nature (*paratantra*), it exists in terms of its characteristics; from the perspective of the imagined nature (*parikalpita*), it exists in terms of its conventional appearance. Thus, both are "existent. From the perspective of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) according to ultimate reality, it exists in terms of its following conditions;

from the perspective of the dependent nature, it exists in terms of its essence; and from the perspective of the imagined nature, it exists in terms of its principle. Thus, all are "empty. Their simultaneous presence and their mutual sublation are as can be understood from the usual [teachings].

If these four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are present regarding the possession of qualities, then the negation of their non-existence likewise transcends the four propositions. One should reflect upon this by reversing the above; there is no need for further elaborate explanation. Furthermore...

There are further meanings which should be understood in their entirety by reference to this. The doctrine of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the essentials of the two schools, and all phenomena of nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) take this as their source.
I hope that students will not reproach me for the prolixity of the text.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “the three meanings above are fully present in the causal conditions”: emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is that which is grasped as an object; the provisional (*prajñapti*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and the middle is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the commentary’s further point:
“If one says it is non-existent, cognition should not be twofold”—how then are the two categories of reasoning (*yukti*) and valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) distinguished? If one says it exists...
This wisdom should not be considered as one, for true wisdom is internally realized and should be seen as having characteristics. It is said:
"Now you have no listener"—this is inconceivable. "I now have no speaker"—this is beyond discussion. There is neither listening nor speaking.
This constitutes a single meaning. The two meanings arise from the inconceivable; the meanings of "one" and "two" are sovereign and unimpeded.
Alternatively, "you" and "I" are distinguished as two according to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), whereas "neither hearing nor speaking" is called "one" according to the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Thus, it is said that in the signless ultimate truth there is no self, no other, and no agent. The first phrase indicates the essence, while the second phrase negates [duality].
It is held that it is far removed from all signs (*nimitta*). Being signless and unsurpassed, it is called the supreme true knowledge (*paramārtha-jñāna*).

Its object of cognition (*ālambana*) is the meaning (*artha*), which does not depend on the activity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or the truths (*satya*), nor does it depend on the activity of homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), nor does it depend on the activity of single causes;
thus it is called "not self-made. It does not depend on Brahmā, nor does it depend on maturation causes (*vipāka-hetu*) and so forth. It does not depend on...

To depend on a single condition is called "not being created by another. That causes and conditions are fundamentally self-existent and that there is no creator other than themselves is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The dharma of causes and conditions has existed from beginningless time; it does not arise through its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or through the self-activity of such truths.
▲ Regarding the statement "the three provisional designations," this refers to the naming of phenomena (*dharma*). ▲ Regarding the statement "in understanding, it is always inherently one":

(The solitary compassionate mind is impartial, like a clear mirror that has no name). "In truth, it is always inherently two": (Sentient beings are the same whether enemy or friend, yet they differ like reflections of beauty and ugliness being distinct).

To penetrate this non-duality: (First interpretation: to penetrate the non-duality of the ultimate and conventional truths; second interpretation: to penetrate the non-duality of the mind-mirror). These statements all rely on phenomena to establish the eighth truth as unique.
One who dwells beyond worldly affairs asks: Within the three categories of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*), both the *dharmadhātu* and the *dharmāyatana* encompass ultimate truth (*tattva*).

Within the four truths (*catuḥsatya*), the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) also encompasses ultimate truth. Furthermore, the suchness of the two emptinesses (*dvividhaśūnyatātathatā*) is entirely ultimate truth.

How can this be reconciled? Answer: There is a principle that transcends existence; all [the aforementioned] are discussed in terms of their designations (*vyañjana*). All are said to be "matters" (*vastu*). Only the eighth truth [the truth of the path] sets aside [designation].

When explaining the ultimate meaning (旨), one dwells beyond phenomena; when speaking of "two," they are not two. (This concludes that in the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* [Renwang jing], objects are two while the mind is one.
They have never been separate. (Originally, there is only the Single Truth. The upper phrase concludes the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra*; the lower phrase concludes the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Regarding the statement, "The Single Truth is the Real, while the four phrases constitute the Expedient": one interpretation holds that by discarding the expedient expressions (詮), the ultimate meaning (旨) is the Single Truth—the True Emptiness.
There are four such [interpretations]. Second, it is said that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the "True," while the Four Noble Truths of suffering and so forth are the "Provisional.
Third, it is said that emptiness and existence are mutually identical as one. Fourth, it is said that the two truths are reiterated to constitute four.

Regarding the statement that the wondrous purport of the Middle Way does not merely concern phenomena (refuting the School of Characteristics), the *Commentary* states that because extinction is taken as the nature of extinction, it can be simultaneous; this refers to the extinction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-nirodha*).
At another time, both schools agreed that the nature [of phenomena] and their cessation are simultaneous; however, one school established its own independent position.

Furthermore, the *Xiàochāo* (Volume 11, Part 1, page 38, end) states: "If the characteristics are fused into four, then gathering conditions is called 'arising,' yet arising is itself without intrinsic nature.
Emptiness and existence are unimpeded, and these provisional appearances are established as 'abiding. Yet abiding is itself non-abiding; through this perfect fusion and mutual negation..."

To undergo transformation according to conditions is called "difference. Difference is itself non-difference; when both characteristics are exhausted, each lacks intrinsic nature—this is called "cessation.
Cessation is itself non-cessation; this is thus the nature within the characteristic, wherein nothing at all can be apprehended.
Regarding the statement, "I teach the meaning of momentariness (*kṣaṇika*) by saying that all phenomena (*dharma*) are unarisen":

"all phenomena" refers collectively to dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). As for "unarisen," it means that the myriad dharmas arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);
