The distinctions between good and evil, as well as all movements and activities—such as the initial recognition of the arising of mind and the stirring of thought according to the Hongzhou school—are all false and illusory.

Thus, a sutra says: "All phenomena whatsoever are false and illusory," and so forth. One should know that those schools mistake the false and illusory for true nature. When one correctly perceives blackness, it is black.

The light is not black; it is simply its luminosity. Blue is not blue; it is simply its luminosity. This applies even to red, white, yellow, and all other colors—they are all likewise so. They are simply its luminosity.
Since, within the various characteristics of form, one sees in each instance only a brilliant, pure, and perfectly luminous clarity, one will no longer be deluded regarding the pearl.

(All things are empty; only the mind is unchanging. When deluded, one knows this; one knows that the source is originally non-deluded. When thoughts arise, one knows them; one knows that the source is [without]—)

When one thoroughly knows each instance of love, joy, anger, grief, desire, and aversion, and realizes that their source is empty and quiescent, then through this knowledge of emptiness and quiescence, one clearly understands the nature of the mind and is free from delusion. This [realization] is entirely distinct from all other schools.

If one is not deluded regarding the pearl, then blackness is simply the absence of blackness; blackness is itself the pearl. All colors are likewise so. Thus, existence and non-existence are sovereign, and light and darkness are interfused.

What further obstruction could there be? (This is identical to those two schools. "Blackness is simply the absence of blackness" is the same as the Hongzhou school of the Niutou tradition; herein lies the entirety of this [teaching]).

"All are non-existent" refers to the statement "and black is itself the pearl," and so forth. Hongzhou said: "All things are Buddha-nature; ordinary and sage, good and evil, are entirely without obstruction. From this point onward, the intended meaning of the metaphor again uses the fundamental school of Heze to distinguish and select among the three schools, saying:
"If one does not recognize that clarity is the essence that manifests, it is forever without change or alteration" (Heze).

To say only that "black and so forth are the pearl" (Hongzhou). Or to intend to seek the pearl apart from the black (Beizong). Or to say that both clarity and blackness are utterly non-existent (Niutou). These are all [errors].

"The jewel has not yet been seen" (this is the *knot*). The commentary states: Regarding that [previous section], it was based on the gate of dhyāna; thus, according to individual insights, there were varying degrees of depth and breadth.

However, according to the principles of the Dharma, the sources of the North and South are the same. This [current section] is based on the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*); thus, while following phenomenal appearances, the practice ultimately unfolds in detail, yet according to the nature of the mind, the beginning and the end are perfectly interfused.
Although the purports of the Sudden and the Perfect differ, the underlying intent of the Dharma and its metaphors is no different. Therefore—
This is the ultimate perfection of sudden, wondrous realization. It is not that students do not understand when they maintain their minds [on this principle].
As for the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary), why does it say "etc. within the initial section on the "Gate of Distinct Entities"?

The *Chao* establishes "identical entity" (*tongti*) based on the meaning of non-mutual dependence, and establishes "distinct entity" (*yiti*) based on the meaning of mutual dependence. The *Shu* (the Commentary) explains this in reverse; therefore, the *Chao* poses the question and provides the answer.

The text states: It is said that one must rely on individual distinctness (the "distinct substance" [yītǐ] of the commentator) in order to depend upon conditions (the "distinct substance" [yītǐ] of the sub-commentator), and one must rely on universal correspondence.

(The *Sūtra Commentary* [Śū] on "identical substance" [tóngtǐ]) maintains that they possess their own inherent virtues (*guìdé*). (The *Sub-commentary* [Chāo] on "identical substance") bases its argument on the direct discussion of mutual dependence through distinct substances (*yìtǐ*), whereby various phenomena (*zhūfǎ*) support one another;

therefore, they do not depend on one another when identical in substance, as each possesses its own inherent virtue. The *Sūtra Commentary* bases its argument on the reason for mutual dependence being identical substance;
because they mutually depend, each possesses its own inherent virtue, which constitutes identical substance. It is not the case that they do not depend on one another.
This is why distinct entities must each maintain their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) before they can mutually depend upon conditions; this is what constitutes "distinct entity.
Regarding the phrase "one coin, when taken as its own essence, is inherently one, etc.," Xianshou says: "This is merely based on the present coin."
How much more so in the case of that *dhāraṇī* dharma of the "Inexhaustible Dependent Origination for Once-Returners," which does not mean that the dharma is merely like this.
One should set aside one's preconceptions and contemplate it according to principle. Yet, fearing you may still not understand, I shall now briefly explain further.

For instance, a single Buddha (who is fundamentally one) manifests in accordance with many faculties. Since the objects of perception differ, the Buddha necessarily appears in diverse forms (that is, the many within the one).

Although their manifestations must correspond to various conditions and thus are not uniform, their fundamental substance is non-dual (the multiplicity of manifestations does not obstruct the fundamental unity).

This is true not only for Buddha after Buddha, but also for every phenomenon (dharma) without exception. Therefore, the *Chao* states: "Using ten coins as a metaphor, within the inexhaustible phenomena of the differentiations of the Dharma-realm, each manifests universally;
thus, according to each individual [manifestation], it possesses the differentiations of the entire Dharma-realm."
This is the Dharma. Fearing that one might become attached to the metaphor, I urge you to set aside your conceptual thoughts.

Regarding the "Sevenfold Meaning of the Mutual Interpenetration of the Identical Substance" and so forth: Question: How can the principle of a single substance establish the profound gate of mutual interpenetration?
For if there is mutual interpenetration, the substances of self and other must still exist, yet they simply intermingle with one another. Answer: This is the Dharma of identical substance.

When ordinary beings perceive it, they may determine it to be of the same substance (*ekātman*). However, when observed by the wisdom of the noble ones (*āryajñāna*), there is no obstruction regarding sameness or difference.

Therefore, one can establish the profound gate of mutual interpenetration (*xiāng rù*). For example, how could the World-Honored One at the Bodhimaṇḍa and the World-Honored One in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven not be established as mutually interpenetrating?
If that were so, would they not still be of different substances? Why then call them "of the same substance"?

Yes. The answer is: because, with respect to the fundamental true essence (*dharmatā*), this and that are entirely identical; and because, from the perspective of the understanding of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are understood as a single essence.
If this were not admitted, how could phenomena of distinct essences be accepted as being of a single essence within the gate of mutual identity?

This is because no cause for their being distinct from one another can be found. Furthermore, how could it be established that phenomena lack a fixed nature? [This is] because they share the same essence and characteristics.
This can be understood by analogy with the present case.

Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Commentary) that "it is like one person looking toward his father and calling him 'son,'" this merely cites a metaphor to clarify the point; do not mistake it for an actual dharma.
Regarding the statement that "because of the mutual entry of different entities, there is mutual entry of identical entities":

since the root of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven has already entered the body of the Buddha at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), how could that Buddha of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven not also enter within the body of the Buddha at the site of enlightenment?
The same principle applies by analogy to their mutual identity (*samasvabhāva*).

The commentary states that the ocean of the same nature of the dark [reality] (*míng tóng xìng hǎi*) means that the first five phrases belong to the causal aspect (*yīn fēn*), as they possess traces that can be spoken of;
the sixth phrase belongs to the resultant aspect (*guǒ fēn*), as it is beyond dependence and transcends words.

Regarding the passage, "The commentary states that because they abide on one side, there is breadth and narrowness; this refers to the second section of the preceding Main Gate": If this were so, there would only be pervasiveness;
how could breadth and narrowness possibly be established? Answer: This is a case of building upon what precedes to initiate what follows, for they are not mutually exclusive.
Regarding the statement, "Because of this, that is precisely this; therefore, that is hidden and this is revealed": Question: How can that which is capable be non-existent?

Question: In what sense is the "entity" (tǐ) said to be hidden? Answer: When that which is identified as the capacity (néng jí) is precisely without an entity, it does not preclude that which is identified as the object (suǒ jí) from having an entity.

This dharma, which possesses an entity as the object of identification, is hidden from the perspective of the capacity of identification. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this raises a difficult case to illustrate an easy one:

if even the capacity of identification is non-existent, how could it not be called "hidden"? It is like saying that if even a defeated army is still dying, how could they not be considered "departing"?
Yes. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "mutual entry by way of distinct bodies entails mutual entry by way of identical bodies":
for example, the bodies of Vairocana Buddha in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and other realms all enter into the body of Vairocana Buddha at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
This body of Vairocana Buddha at the site of enlightenment further enters into the body of Akṣobhya Buddha. Since the body of Vairocana Buddha at the site of enlightenment which has entered...
Within the body of Akṣobhya Buddha, he is able to enter the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and so forth; the Vairocana Buddha remains present within the body of Akṣobhya Buddha as well.

Regarding the seven gates that follow in the commentary, which condense the three preceding births: these three births constitute the "mutual arising of conditions" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa-anyonya-utpatti*).
The latter seven [verses] are from the School of Mystery (Xuánmén) that manifest the cause by means of the fruit. Regarding the statement "Briefly stated, wisdom manifests principle," etc.:

the first two lines pertain to the stage of the cause, while the latter two lines pertain to the stage of the fruit. As for the phrase "the non-obstruction between speaking and not speaking is inconceivable," it means that cause and fruit are mutually fused, just as waves and water encompass one another. Furthermore, according to the commentary in the sub-commentary (*shù*) below: [The text continues: ...and so forth. The first two lines refer to the causal division; the latter two lines refer to the resultant division.

The statement that "speaking and not speaking are unimpeded and difficult to conceive" means that cause and fruit are mutually integrated, much like waves and water which contain one another. Moreover, according to the interpretation in the sub-commentary (*shù*) below: [The text continues: ...while...
There are many approaches. Since the meaning is profound and subtle, it must be analyzed in detail. I hope that the eminent scholars will not weary of the prolixity of the text.
Thus, that commentary states: first, [the greatness] from the perspective of meaning; second, regarding the greatness of the teaching; and third, the analysis of their mutual integration.

Within the section on meaning, there are three parts. First, regarding the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*), it can be generally indicated to lead people to understand that what is named "teachable" is, in fact, "unteachable."
To point out and designate a person by name is "unspeakable. Second, regarding the locus of realization:

since that which is realized is free from characteristics and names, it is further said that "this dharma is unspeakable. Because this very speech that negates words corresponds to that dharma, it is termed "speakable";

yet because these words themselves are negated, it is termed "unspeakable. (This is like using the tracks left by a bird's foot as a metaphor for what is realized, while stating that the place itself is not [the tracks].)

That which exists and is not non-existent can be described, yet because its traces cannot be pointed out and its name cannot be expressed, it is called "ineffable" (anabhilāpya). Third, regarding fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*):

it is called "describable" because it is understood through negation (*paryudāsa*), but it is "ineffable" because it cannot be reached by positive definition (*vidhi*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Non-conceptual wisdom..."

Because it is free from five characteristics, namely: sleep, intoxication, and so forth; because it cannot be reached by direct affirmation (*paryudāsa*); and because that dharma is demonstrated through negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

(That is to say, using the trace left in space as a metaphor for realized wisdom: to say "there is a trace in space" is expressible; to say "its length, shortness, largeness, or smallness cannot be shown" is inexpressible. As for the "five characteristics": first, freedom from non-attention (*amanasikāra*);

second, freedom from the stage of discursive thought and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*); third, freedom from the cessation and tranquility of perceived characteristics (*nimitta-saṃjñā-nirodha-śānti*); fourth, freedom from the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*); fifth, freedom from the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*).

Because they are distinct conceptual constructions. Furthermore, according to the later commentary (*Hou-chao*), there are two additional meanings. First, regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*): when true dharmas manifest in mutual correspondence, this is termed "discourseable" (*vaktavya*). Since one cannot apprehend these natures and characteristics as separate entities, it is termed "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*). Second, regarding the relative opposition between the emotional and the real:

when viewed from the perspective of emotion toward reality, there is a "true" [nature] external to emotion, which can be discussed; however, when based on reality and directed toward emotion, there is no emotion external to reality—by what means could discourse arise?

Second, within the context of the Great Vehicle of Discourse (*vyākhyāna-mahāyāna*), there are also three points. First, regarding subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*): the modes of activity (*ākāra*) that follow phenomena can be analyzed through speech; thus, it is "discourseable. It is then...

It is said: because this is supramundane (*lokottara*), it is inexpressible. (Since subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) necessarily arises from the realization of the truth, how can that which is supramundane be expressed?

Second, with respect to preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*): because it is a conceptual-linguistic contemplation (*manojalpa-vipaśyanā*), it is expressible; yet because the verbal aspects within that contemplation do not reach [the object], it is called "inexpressible.

(For when one cultivates the Middle Way, one must cultivate in accordance with the nature [of reality]; since that nature transcends names and speech, it is all the more inexpressible. Maitreya said: "I have already briefly explained the coarse characteristics of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*)."
[It is] said: "All other true meanings can only be known by me. Thirdly, with respect to the dharmas upon which [the meaning] is based:

because these [expressions] can be used as bases to represent and cause others to understand the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they are called "explicable" (*vaktavya*). However, because these [expressions] cannot themselves be taken as the ten stages, they are called "inexplicable" (*avaktavya*).

Third, regarding the mutual integration of the two: within each of the six points mentioned above, it is taught that "that which is speech is non-speech" and "that which is non-speech is speech," such that the two are non-dual and mutually integrated;
this may be understood by applying the same principle. Furthermore, because the ocean of fruition transcends conditions, it cannot be described;

yet, insofar as the realization is attained through conditions, it can be described. Second, because the realized object is not something produced by cultivation, it cannot be described; however, the realizing subject arises through cultivation.

Then it can be described. Third, because the direct realization is free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it cannot be described; yet, because the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) carries these characteristics, it can be described.

Fourth, because the subsequently attained wisdom is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), it cannot be described; yet, by means of metaphorical representation through phenomena (*dharma*), it can be described.
The five preparatory contemplations (*prayoga-vipaśyanā*) are inexpressible because they are non-conceptual; they can only be expressed by resorting to dharmas as provisional designations.
All that is inexpressible above this is likewise not different from one another. Regarding the inexpressible, it is because cultivation through conditions has no intrinsic nature.
(Truth is ineffable. Because it pervades all phenomena, it may be spoken of. Since cultivation based on conditions is itself ineffable due to its lack of intrinsic nature, it is identical to truth;
thus, it is ineffable. The commentary states: That treatise has three broad meanings, and here we rely on the latter. It says that speaking and not speaking are unimpeded and inconceivable.
As for the term "shujī" (庶幾), it refers to what is said in the *Xici* (Appended Statements) of the *Zhouyi*: "The son of the Yan family was perhaps one who approached [the ideal]."
"Indeed. There has never been a case where he was not aware of what was not good, and once he was aware of it, he never practiced it again.
The commentary states: "Dai (peril) means 'near'; shu (multitude) means 'to admire'; ji (the point of departure) refers to the subtle movement of an event. This means that the Sage perceives the ji."
The worthy ones nearly attained it. Now, we cause later students to rank themselves alongside the sages and worthies.

Regarding the statement that "the phenomena arising from [True Suchness] are also endowed with inexhaustible virtues," this means that the dharmas arising from True Suchness must accord with its nature;
therefore, their virtues are inexhaustible. As for the remark that "this statement is not yet appropriate," this refers solely to... [but only]... [the text here appears incomplete].
This is the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It lacks the qualities of the unimpededness of phenomena and principles (*dharmārtha-apratighāta*) and non-emptiness (*aśūnyatā*).
In this commentary, fourteen qualities are briefly enumerated; however, according to the *Chao*, sixteen are listed.

This is likely because the two qualities of "extensive and subtle" (*guǎngxià* / *weixì*) were combined into a single quality as they universally encompass all phenomena, and the two qualities of "mutual identity" (*xiāngjí*) and "relying on phenomena" (*tuōshì*) were likewise merged.
In the middle [section], it shares the same essential nature as all phenomena; when combined, they form a single virtue, thus totaling fourteen.
Furthermore, regarding "having no limits" and "being eternally associated with all phenomena," these are absent from the sutra.
They must therefore refer to the fact that within the sutra, [this quality] pervades all places without boundary, and is without characteristics in relation to all phenomena.

This contradicts [the scripture]. Regarding the two virtues, according to the sutra, the four virtues consist of day-and-night, year, kalpa, and [the fourth]. This *Chao* (Excerpts) combines these in its discussion and mentions only two virtues;
otherwise, it agrees with the sutra. If one follows the old *Chao*, although the headings are the same, it appears to contradict the sutra.
The sutras at the beginning and end each open into two parts, while the *Chao* (Commentary) combines them into one; let the student examine this in detail.

Regarding the lines "The commentary [rests] upon the pillow for a brief moment," these two lines are from the poem "Spring Dream" (*Chunmeng*) within the *Leishi* (Classified Poetry) of the Tang and Song dynasties.
They were composed by the ancient poet Cen Shen. The full text reads: "Last night, the east wind arose in the inner chambers..."
"Far I recall the beautiful woman by the waters of the Xiang River / Within a fleeting spring dream upon my pillow.
The first two lines of this verse do not elaborate upon the present context; therefore, they are not cited in the *Chao*.

The statement that "all things are like a dream" means that all phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), are like the objects of a dream; it is for this reason that one enters into mastery over them. Therefore...
Master Rui said: "Within the long night, all that is produced is a great dream. It is entirely due to the mind’s painting that it universally creates myriad forms;
the spirit transmigrates through the five paths, wandering in solitude until its cultivation is exhausted. If one can awaken to this, one immediately shatters ignorance."

Regarding the phrase "the six [sense objects] are like images," the character for "image" (影) is likely an error; it should be "mirror" (鏡). One may verify this for oneself by consulting the *Chao* (Excerpts). Thus, Master Rui said:

"The form does not enter the mirror, yet it appears through the illumination of light. The world is likewise: one receives the 'images' of karma. Those who do not understand this will long remain entangled in its faults;
if one can awaken to it, one returns to the source of spirit and breath. Alternatively, the character for "image" (影) may be used here as a metaphorical illustration.
The meaning of "voidness and sovereign freedom" is also established. Thus, Master Rui said: "Where light does not shine is called shadow;
where the illumination of wisdom does not shine, birth and death arise and endure for a long time. One abandons the distant, level path to travel through thorny thickets.

If one can awaken to this, madness and delusion will naturally subside. Regarding the statement that there are briefly two meanings, according to the commentary below, there are actually four meanings.

There are four reasons: first, due to false discrimination; second, due to the perfuming of the various consciousnesses; third, because they do not mutually cognize one another due to their lack of intrinsic nature;
and fourth, because True Suchness follows conditions. Since this passage mentions only two of them, it is said to be "abbreviated."

The sub-commentary (*shu*) on the following passage from the Sūtra states: "Although distant objects and near objects both manifest as reflections, these reflections do not possess distance or proximity according to the objects themselves.
The *Dàochào* (18, upper half, p. 33) says: "It is like holding a mirror over a pond; when the moon in the pond appears, this reflection is not 'near.
The moon in the sky is forty-two thousand *yojanas* above the earth, yet its reflection falls into the pool, and likewise [it is not 'far']."

It is not distant. This is illustrated by the fact that although the Bodhisattva dwells far away in another direction, he constantly abides here; and although he dwells in this place, he is always there.
How, then, could there be any distinction between the characteristics of distance and proximity? All instances of distance and proximity can be understood through this analogy.
The *Chao* states, "It is simply that it can accomplish the Buddha-dharma; being able to do so" explains that this is solely a mark of virtue (*guṇalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the statement, "That which preceded was the mark of virtue, while this is the functional activity (*karmaprayoga*)," one might ask: the previous commentary distinguished that the eighth [stage] pertains to the fruit and is exclusively a mark of virtue;

how then does the present citation from the *Chao*, which serves as proof, accord with functional activity? Answer: The *Chao* speaks in terms of benefiting sentient beings; therefore, it accords with functional activity.

Regarding the "function" (*yòng*): the *Sū* (Commentary) explains that, according to the Buddha’s realization, this refers exclusively to the aspect of merit (*guǒxiàng*). Therefore, the *Sū* states: "In terms of the Buddha’s function, it is also the function of merit, because it is the function of merit within the aspect of merit.

The *Chāo* (Sub-commentary) encompasses the preceding three [aspects] as well. That these all represent the boundaries of the Distinct Teaching (*biéjiào*) is because the Distinct Teaching subsumes the Common Teaching (*tóngjiào*).
Regarding the statement that there are five faults in grasping the meaning according to the literal sound, the sub-commentary below explains them as follows:

First, lack of correct faith, because interpreting according to the words does not accord with reality. Second, the loss of vigor, because one is unable to transcend appearances to reach the ultimate truth.

Third, deceiving others, because one explains one's own erroneous understanding to others. Fourth, slandering the Buddha, because one points to one's own erroneous understanding as being the Buddha’s teaching.

Therefore, the fifth is "slight regard for the Dharma," because one interprets the profound meaning with shallow and superficial understanding; that is, one does not treat the Dharma with earnestness according to its words.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Commentary) that it is called "inclusive" (*jiān*) because it concerns those who have not yet attained realization:

this refers to the sons of gods in hell who, upon hearing the Dharma from the celestial drums, immediately transcend the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). This is the primary intended audience (*zhèngwéi*). However, the present passage concerns the time when the seeds were first perfumed in a previous life; therefore, it is categorized as "inclusive."

Question: At that time, one who hears the sutra and disbelieves it or slanders it falls directly into hell; this should belong to "distant karma" (*yuanwei*). Why then is it called "combined karma" (*jianwei*)?
What is the basis for calling it combined karma? Answer: There are two classes of celestial beings in hell.
First, those who slander the sutra belong to the category of distant karma. Second, those whose precepts are lax are to be included under combined karma. Therefore, there is no error in this.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “borrowing the name of the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) of the Three Vehicles,” a question arises: Is this the sequential arrangement that is identical to the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*), or is it a sequential arrangement distinct from the perfect fusion?
If it were a sequential arrangement distinct from the perfect fusion, it would be a case of parallel practice and would not accord with the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
If, however, it is the sequential arrangement identical to the perfect fusion, then it is indeed the meaning of the Perfect Teaching, and one should not say that it is merely “borrowed.”

Answer: It is precisely because the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) possesses both the sequential (xingbu) and the integrated (yuanrong) aspects. Among the ten schools, it is the school that fully embodies all virtues.

Within the ten stages (bhūmi), its integrated nature is concealed while its sequential nature is manifested. At first glance, their names appear similar, yet they are exclusively designated as sequential;

furthermore, the names are merely borrowed [from the other]. Moreover, if one considers the path of true realization, it is solely integrated; however, if one follows the teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings...

The Way penetrates both the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) and the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*). Therefore, the memorial states: "Sequential arrangement is the provisional designation of the teachings;

perfect fusion is the functional virtue of the rational nature. Thus, the name is borrowed [from the *Huayan jing*]. Regarding the statement that "the provisional teachings and ultimate fruits have no real substance," this is an implicit application of the meaning of Tiantai.
Hence, the sub-commentary says: "Although Zhiyi spoke of the ocean of fruition of the four teachings and three teachings..."

There is no substantial reality; it is only within the context of the teaching that a "fruit" is provisionally established. Once one has entered the stages, the fruit is immediately empty. As the Separate Teaching (biejiao) says:
regarding the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages (*bhūmi*), what is there to be cultivated during the cultivation of the three stages of worthiness?

Even upon realizing the stages, there is nothing further distinct [to be realized]. (This refers to the path of realization. The realized realm of the ten stages of the Separate Teaching is merely the abiding of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). (This is based on...)

The teaching-path abandons the distinct [vehicles] to proceed toward the Perfect [Vehicle]. It is precisely by virtue of this meaning that the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching possesses mastery that transcends the [lower] stages.

Regarding the phrase "provisionally acting as equals," this refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who provisionally manifest as beings of the same class and employ skillful means for their sake; therefore, it is called "provisional" (*upāya*).
As for the statement, "Or, within the Dharma assembly, some appear deaf or blind to manifest their exclusion from the [path]," this is because they are intended to be transformed [by the teaching].

The term "śrāvaka" (voice-hearer) also reveals the profundity of the Dharma. Furthermore, the statement "or manifesting as being on the path so that those with minds capable of awakening may transcend" indicates that he transforms himself into a śrāvaka to simultaneously demonstrate the vastness of the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "falling into the pit of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*): because once one falls into the correct position of the unconditioned it is difficult to emerge, it is likened to a deep pit; furthermore, because [the lack of] the water of compassion takes up the ashes of severance, it is like that hell.

Regarding the statement "destroying the roots of goodness... to the water of craving": false views negate [reality], while craving soaks and rots [the seeds]; both are likened to water because they do not admit the roots of goodness, and because they lack the condition of earth, they are not places where [seeds] can grow.

Regarding the statement "never having weariness or abandonment": the previous section relied on manifest evil and the lack of conditions to induce weariness and fear; however, since all equally possess Buddha-nature and will surely achieve Buddhahood in the long run, one does not feel weary or abandon them. This is so.
This demonstrates that if evil were non-existent, it would not exist; since evil must necessarily exist, [the teaching] holds. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Although an icchantika has severed all roots of goodness, they still possess Buddha-nature. If they can resolve to generate the aspiration for enlightenment, they are no longer icchantikas. Question: What follows from this?

That which was previously excluded—namely, the five classes who are not vessels—is now contradicted by what is included here. This is like water and fire; how can these two be reconciled? Answer: [As follows in the text below...]
The Commentary states: "It is like the distinction between the commoner and the noble, which are separated by a vast gulf (this is 'discrimination').

Yet, when the King gathers people unto himself, then within the entire realm, there are none who are not the King’s subjects (this is 'gathering'). Therefore, if one summarizes this universal gathering, all sentient beings are without exception endowed with the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
how much more so regarding the untainted causes and effects of the two vehicles? If one were to compare their excellence..."
Inferior beings, even those Bodhisattvas who have long practiced the provisional teachings, do not yet believe or hear this; how much less so the followers of the Two Vehicles?
Even the leaders of the Two Vehicles are like the deaf and blind; how much more so ordinary people and non-Buddhists?

Regarding the commentary’s intent to assign [the remaining types] to the "unfit" category so that they are exhausted: Question: Why is it called "exhausted" when only the preceding four are assigned? Answer:
Because the few follow the many, and because the provisional does not contradict the ultimate reality.
Regarding the phrase "Although slander leads to rebirth in the evil realms, it still reaches the ears and ultimately leads to awakening," this is explained according to the commentary below;

its meaning is thus even more profound. The *Tathāgata-rahasya-garbha-sūtra* clarifies that reviling medicine when taken gains its efficacy, reviling incense when burned makes it fragrant, and reviling the Buddha is superior to making offerings to various non-Buddhist teachers.
If this is so, does one not incur the sin of reviling? Indeed, the sin of reviling is not non-existent.
Now, let us speak of the benefit for those far removed [from the Dharma]. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that Bhadrapāla and others reviled the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging;

for a thousand kalpas they fell into the Avīci Hell and underwent great suffering. Once these karmic retributions were exhausted, they returned and were further transformed by the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* uses the analogy of a drum smeared with poison: even if one wishes not to hear its sound, there is no one who does not die [from the poison]. Therefore, [the Buddha] said: "Bodhi..."
Those who hear the name of the Buddha yet proceed to slander it, saying, "Slander is still far from beneficial; how much more so for deep faith? How much more so for understanding and practice?
How much more so for realization?"—those who hold such views, O Buddha, should be urged to reflect upon this text.

Regarding the passage in the Commentary stating, "The great ocean flows secretly so that there is nowhere it does not reach; likewise, the Tathāgata’s wisdom [pervades all]," the subsequent commentary says:

"The reason we know that Buddha-wisdom is omnipresent is that there is not a single sentient being who lacks original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi), for their essence is no different from that of the Buddha.
While the preceding statement of "flowing secretly" implies that Buddha-wisdom pervades other sentient beings, the present passage reveals that it is inherently possessed by every living being.
Therefore, it is said that [the Tathāgata-garbha] is all-pervasive. This has two meanings. First, it clarifies that there is not a single sentient being who does not possess it;

thus, one knows that those without the nature (asattva) do not belong to the category of sentient beings—meaning that things such as grasses and trees have already transcended the view of the five natures.

Second, because sentient beings, while still enmeshed in afflictions (*saṃsāra*), already possess the Buddha who is the fruit of having emerged from those entanglements, it is said that they possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and not merely the potential for the nature.
It will only be accomplished later; it is also illogical for wisdom to precede [the practice]. Thus, one knows that nirvāṇa is said to possess a nature only in relation to former expedient means.
Even after subsequent study, people still speak of having a "storehouse" while being empty; how much more so when hearing of the fruit-wisdom of equality—who would believe it?

Third is the wisdom of the fruit within that cause; this is precisely the fruit-wisdom of other Buddhas. According to the school of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the causes and fruits of self and others are non-dual in essence;
therefore, it is not as [the others] claim. If one says that sentient beings possess the fruit, how can this be called "expounding the Buddha-wisdom"?
This is indeed profound upon the profound. There is no such principle outside the Huayan school. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "breaking through the dust to bring forth the sutra":
Regarding the phrase "scrolls and so forth," the sub-commentary further states: The *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* and other texts set forth nine similes to illustrate the *tathāgatagarbha*.
These are: like a blue lotus in muddy water that has not yet emerged from the mud; like a poor woman who carries a noble embryo within her;
like a precious gem wrapped in a soiled garment; and like a *maṇi* jewel that has fallen [into the mud].
Deeply concealed, it is like a statue of pure gold covered by tattered rags; like the flowers and fruit of the *āmra* tree before they have matured;
like rice grains within their husks and chaff; like gold in its ore; like an image within a mold—all these are instances where the meaning of the Buddha-body exists amidst the defilements.
Regarding the statement in the *Commentary* (鈔): "That which is said to be 'subjected to' non-sentient things (非情) means that the sentient thing subjected is itself non-sentient," one asks:

If the sentient is itself non-sentient, then the essence of sentience is already discarded. What could possibly be the object subjected? It is impossible for a non-sentient thing to be the object subjected.

Even if it were so subjected, since it utterly lacks consciousness and intelligence, what utility would there be? It is not possible for the essence of sentience to remain undiscarded while being identical to the non-sentient.

If the essence were not abandoned, it could not be called "identical. Answer: Because it is eternally identical yet eternally non-identical, it is therefore designated as being both non-sentient and that which is encompassed by the teaching.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "the first five are only the substance (*tǐ*)," a question arises: the subsequent commentary distinguishes the substance of the preceding three layers, stating, "Thus, although the various schools of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna generally employ the four dharmas, their principles differ.
Based on this, would it not follow that they do not fail to accord with principle? Why, then, is it said that they are "only the substance"? The answer is:

the substance of the first five layers is fundamentally only the phenomena of conditioned things (*dharmas*). It is by applying the profound meaning of the subsequent [layers] that one distinguishes [them from] the preceding four; thus...

Because its principle is thus understood, there is no error. Furthermore, it was asked: "If one takes the essence of what is signified as the general meaning, would that not also be understanding the principle?
The answer is: "This is because [the term] refers to the direct signification; or because the few follow the many; or because the nature follows the characteristics."
Regarding the commentary’s subsequent threefold analysis stating that "the preceding lacks the succeeding," etc.: Question:

Since the first four [stages] are common to the Small Vehicle, the first seven are common to the Three Vehicles, and the first eight are discussed in terms of the *tongjiao* (teaching of commonality), and since all are said to be "common" (*tong*), one should understand that this refers to the Great Common [Vehicle], the One Vehicle, and the *biejiao* (distinct teaching).
If it is granted that they are all common, why is it said that "the preceding lacks the succeeding"? Answer: [The text continues...]

The teaching-body (*śarīra*) is not selected based on what is inferred, because there is nothing preceding it; rather, it is selected according to the meaning of that which performs the inference, because there is nothing preceding it.

In the Hīnayāna, the latter six are absent; in the Three Vehicles, the latter three are absent; and in the Common Teaching (*sāmānya-dharma*), the latter two are absent. Therefore, this statement was made. From this discussion, further questions arise. Question:

Regarding the vivid manifestation of the Sea-Seal (*sāgaramudrā*), its essence accords with the *Huan-yuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source); please point to the original text of the treatise.

How could awakening be the same as the teaching? If it is taken as the essence of the *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*, it belongs exclusively to the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), because it praises the provisional being;
yet this can be extended to all assemblies. If it is taken as the "ten thousand vehicles," it refers only to a single person.

The *Śāstra* states: "From the speech of the Buddha up to what is called the 'Buddha's teaching'—if one asks whether this single category of 'path of speech' consists of mental consciousness or the lips and so forth, and since these are not sound, what constitutes the essence of the teaching?
The answer is: "In terms of its specific nature (*svabhāva*), it is not; however, by way of its conventional characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it may be so."
"Regarding 'the *Śāstra* correctly sets forth the essence of the present teaching' and so forth: this correctly sets forth the essence of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Regarding 'the *Śāstra* states that speech is a synonym for teaching' and so forth: this is in agreement with the *Nyāyānusāra*. That is to say, speech has sound as its essence;

therefore, it is called verbal teaching (*vāk-karma*), which is also simply sound. It is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Name (*nāman*), however, is a non-associated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) by essence."

That which is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of names (*nāman*) and verbal expressions (*abhilāpa*). Their essential natures are distinct. [The question asks: "What is the nature of verbal expression?
The intent of the question is that verbal expression is simply speech. The intent of the subsequent answer is as follows: because it is the verbal expression of speech, name constitutes its essence.
For example, when one says "Son of the Buddha," the Buddha himself does not constitute the essence; rather, it takes the disciple as its essence.
Regarding the statement that "the reflection in a mirror arises from the provisional": A questioner asks, "The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that both the coarse and the subtle are real;

how then can it be called provisional? The answer says: "It is called provisional merely because it relies upon many atoms (*paramāṇu*); it does not mean that it is unreal or illusory. Alternatively, it is said: "Originally, this was considered [to be real]."
In reality, although this is considered provisional, the meaning can also be understood accordingly.

The *Śāstra* states that the Mahāyāna has three great points which are the same as those previously mentioned. In the Hīnayāna, the first two [categories] may either take "sound" (*śabda*) alone or "name" (*nāman*) and so forth alone.
The Mahāyāna is not like this; when it takes "sound," it necessarily includes "name" and so forth, and when it takes "name" and so forth, it likewise includes [the others].
Regarding "because it is sound":
the "sound produced by the perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) refers to the sound produced by the perfected nature.

Regarding "if it is due to the appropriation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)": this means that it is due to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) appropriating the four great elements of sentient beings.

This refers to sound produced by the primary elements (*bhūta*). The other two [types of sound] are to be understood accordingly. Regarding the phrase "if it is commonly established in the world" and so forth:

these refer, respectively, to sounds produced from the three natures—the dependent (*paratantra*), the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*), and the imagined (*parikalpita*). The term "nature" (*svabhāva*) in the expression "sacred word of nature" (*svabhāva-ārya-vākya*) means "correct."
"Only the gods receive [it], not others" means that those foolish people have no one in the world to employ them;
they can only survive through the compassion and love of the gods. Furthermore, among those honored by the world, none surpass the gods; among those despised by the world, none exceed the foolish.
To address a base and lowly fool with the title of a "god"—a name established for the most exalted—is like calling a slave a "lord."
He teases him playfully, saying: "Fie upon you, O Deva! You are truly pitiable. Therefore, he is called *Devānāmpriya* (Beloved of the Gods). Only one who speaks thus would say this;

no other person of intelligence would speak in such a manner. Regarding the distinction between the objects of the two unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—those of phenomena (*dharma*) and those of expression (*nirukti*):

the object of the knowledge of phenomena consists of names and so forth, while the object of the knowledge of expression consists of sounds. This is what is meant by the term "aggregates" (*skandha*).

Regarding the fact that the inclusion within the *dhātus* and *āyatanas* also differs for each: sound (*śabda*) is included in the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the sound element (*śabda-dhātu*), and the sound base (*śabda-āyatana*);

while names (*nāman*) and so forth are included in the aggregate of formations, the mental-object element (*dharma-dhātu*), and the mental-object base (*dharma-āyatana*), respectively. As for the phrase "The *Nyāya* [school] attempts to rescue [the position] by saying 'etc.'": their fundamental tenet is that there is a curvature (*vakratva*) within sound itself, which constitutes the name, phrase, and syllable;

they do not yet maintain that it exists as something separate from the sound. As for the phrase "Based on all states, it is not...": [this refers to the objection that if the phonemes were the same across all positions, they would lack distinctness].
Regarding "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*): it refers to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), for they are not noble ones (*ārya*).
As for the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they manifest immeasurable names and phrases within a single syllable. As for the statement that "the essence is not manifest":

this refers to the meaning of the distinct syllables, which possess no sense of alteration or transition. In principle, such [essences] do not express meaning and cannot be translated; for example, when in Sanskrit one says *bodhi*, this is so.
This is translated as "awakening" (bodhi). For instance, if one were to say only "bo," it would be a mere syllable without any referential meaning;

because it cannot be translated [into a meaningful term], its designation remains unchanged. Regarding the statement that "many *kṣaṇas* of sound aggregate to form a single syllable," the question is:
when the first *kṣaṇa* of sound is in the present, has the subsequent *kṣaṇa* of sound already reached the present?
The preceding sound has already ceased; how, then, can its syllables be integrated? Now, the general explanation is as follows:

although the primary entities (the sounds) do not see one another across time, their reflected images are permitted to appear simultaneously in a continuous succession; therefore, they are integrated.

Furthermore, it is explained that although they are not simultaneous, they are provisionally established by the interpreting mind, which grasps the preceding and connects to the succeeding, just as in the case of a fire-wheel, which is real [only in appearance].
It is not a wheel; rather, it is a wheel created according to the mind. Furthermore, as the Buddha said: "The deer king of former days is my present self.

The names, phrases, and questions and answers should be understood according to the characters. Regarding the so-called "specific and general characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): that which is restricted to and attached to its own substance is called the specific characteristic;

that which penetrates and connects with other meanings is called the general characteristic. Because form is characterized by resistance and consciousness by being an object of cognition, each is restricted to its own substance; therefore, they are [termed] specific characteristics.

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is that which is unique to a thing. Because [characteristics] such as emptiness and selflessness pervade all things, they are called common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

This is the correspondence regarding their essential nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, there is a correspondence regarding breadth and narrowness: the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is called a common characteristic (it is broad), whereas the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) is called a specific characteristic (it is narrow).

Furthermore, there is a correspondence between that which transcends language and that which involves language: even down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), it is a common characteristic (involving language); that which transcends language is inexpressible.
This is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). (It is beyond verbal expression. Furthermore, there is the pair of superimposition (*samāropa*) and non-superimposition.

That which does not apprehend an object through direct perception, but proceeds by way of conceptual understanding and penetrates many phenomena, is called the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). (This is superimposition. Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) apprehends an object;

its activity is free from fluctuation and it is strictly restricted to the original reality. This is called the particular characteristic. (This is non-superimposition. Furthermore, there is the pair of having functional efficacy (*arthakriyā*) and lacking functional efficacy.

Correct. For example, when conditions transform an object such that it possesses functional efficacy, this is called the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*). When conceptualization transforms an object such that it lacks functional efficacy, this is called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "one door": it manifests as ordinary and mundane. Regarding the "two marks and signs": [it manifests as] the marks and signs of a Great Being.

Because it manifests the Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). Regarding the three types of roots and forms: because it manifests male and female. Regarding the four flavors: one should say "salt," because it manifests the flavor of food;
one should say "pattern" (vyañjana), because it manifests the flavor of meaning (artha).

The commentary clarifies the principle that there is no fixed direction (*dig*). "Direction" (*fang*) here means "comparison" (*bi*); it refers to the absence of a comparative principle. Alternatively, it reveals that the essence of the meaning has no fixed spatial location or boundary.
This is because even in this single region of Sahā, matter (*rūpa*) and other phenomena are permitted to function as the Buddha’s activity;
thus, it differs from the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) school, which maintains that in this specific region, sound alone must be used as the Buddha’s activity.

The commentary states that the seven sages and four fruits consist of: the three stages of provisioning (the five contemplations for settling the mind, the contemplation of specific characteristics, and the contemplation of general characteristics); and the four stages of application (Heat, Peak, [Patience, and Supreme Mundane Dharma]).

Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) constitute the seven noble persons (*saptakula-putra*). The Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and Arhat (*arhat*) are the four fruits (*catur-phala*).

Regarding the term "Stream-enterer": it is so called because one has for the first time entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya-srotas*). As for the afflictions of attachment (*rāga*) abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are not fixed;

[the latter] may range from one to five [categories]. For the first fifteen moments of mind, these six persons are termed "candidates" (*pratipannaka*); at the sixteenth moment of mind, the vision of the truths is perfected, and all six [attain the fruit].
This is called the fruit. Regarding the term "once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin): following the first fruit, one proceeds to abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation;

from the first to the sixth category [of afflictions], the six paths of uninterrupted activity (ānantarya-mārga) and the first five paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) are all termed "candidates" (pratipannaka). In the sixth path of liberation, the mind becomes relaxed and at ease.
This is designated as the fruit. Transcending the first fruit, one who has previously suppressed the sixth, seventh, and eighth grades [of defilements] ascends to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The preceding fifteen moments of mind are also called this "candidate" (*pratipannaka*). At the sixteenth moment of mind, one transcends to realize this fruit.

Regarding the realization of the first fruit by omitting certain grades, or the realization of the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) at the end, the meaning of the Sūtra should be considered. However, in terms of the sequential order, it is based on the state of being entirely free from desire (*vītarāga*).

Because the [cultivation of the path] for the lower three grades moistens a single rebirth in the desire realm, one is named "Once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*). By extension, those who have transcended [the lower stages] and realized this fruit are also given this name.
Regarding the "Non-returner" (*anāgāmin*): following the second fruit, one proceeds to abandon the afflictions of the desire realm;

the subsequent three grades, consisting of three paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and two paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), are all termed "candidates" (*pratipannaka*). Only upon the third path of liberation does one finally attain [the fruit].

This is called "Coming" (āgāmin). Surpassing the previous two fruits, one first suppresses the nine grades [of afflictions] and the sixty-three grades of the upper seven stages; thus one comes to ascend to the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).
The first fifteen moments of mind are called the "candidate for the fruit of Non-returner" (anāgāmipratipannaka), and the sixteenth moment of mind realizes the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmiphala).
After having realized the fruit, one will certainly not return to birth in the desire realm.
By the power of having practiced such matters as these, one realizes nirvana without relying on further application;
this is called "attainment without application" (*anabhisamskāra-prāpti*). Whether by leaping over stages or proceeding sequentially...
Whether partially or fully, they reach up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven and realize nirvāṇa;

this is called [the dhyāna of] dwelling in happiness in the present life through meditative concentration. Thirteenth, those of the nature of reflection: if they do not reflect, they immediately fall away.
14. If one has reflected thus, one does not fall away, because one guards the Dharma through mental attention (*manasikāra*).
15. One abides in the state of equanimity, neither refining nor regressing. 16. Because one is capable of realization and penetration. 17. The nature of immovability;

this refers to those of sharp faculties who, having attained the unsurpassed progress, do not regress from the lower stage. 18. Wisdom-liberation (*prajñā-vimukti*); [this refers to one] who has merely severed...
Because it is an obstacle to wisdom. Nineteenth, [he attains] mere liberation; furthermore, because he has severed the nature of fixed determination.
The *Chao* (Commentary) states that the one who was rebuked was rebuked for the inequality of his alms-gathering.

Regarding the phrase "placing the bowl and wishing to depart," Vimalakīrti questioned the principle of cessation and extinction; Subhūti, not knowing the reason for this, set aside his bowl and wished to leave.
He emerged from his dwelling. As for the statement that "Vimalakīrti says that all dharmas are such," it was intended to cause Subhūti to realize that words are identical to illusions;
to realize that illusory transformations are identical to reality; and to realize that one's own self is like a magical creation.

Therefore, it is said that "all dharmas have the characteristic of being like illusions and transformations. Thus, Master Rui said: "Sentient beings are like transformations; they are neither existent nor real. Not...

One who attains this turns [the wheel of Dharma] like a chariot wheel; they understand that the Dharma is cool and pure, devoid of self and person, with all defilements eliminated like a sun free from clouds.
Regarding the statement, "The nature of words and letters is detached; there are no words or letters":

one interpretation holds that the first phrase indicates the principle and the second phrase provides the explanation. This meaning is as follows: the true nature of words and letters is fundamentally detached from the characteristics of words and letters. Below...
The commentary on the verse states: "There are no words. Furthermore, this can be interpreted by reading it twice: first, that the nature of words is detached from words, meaning there are no words;
second, that the nature of words is detached from words, meaning there are words. Thus, both existence and non-existence are simultaneously negated.

Regarding the statement that "words are extinguished" while communicating the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden [teachings]: "words" refers to dependent origination, and "the extinction of words" refers to the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, "following" (sui-shun) refers to the transcendence of words through which one gains entry. To say that "one can see and hear" refers only to the path of teaching (*shōdō*):

it concerns the gate of conformity (*suijun-mon*) according to the Sudden Teaching of True Emptiness (*shinkū-donkyō*), and the gate of conventional truth (*zokutai-mon*) according to the Initial Teaching of the Destruction of Characteristics (*hassō-shikyō*).
As for the term "foundations of mindfulness" (*nenjō*), it signifies the illumination of quiescence (*shōjakku*).

Regarding the "five aspects" (*pañca-lakṣaṇa*): first, the "phrases" (*vyañjana*) refer to either the expressions corresponding to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, or the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others who can expound them;

since these all serve to manifest the meaning, they are termed "phrases. Second, the "single ground" (*eka-bhūmi*) refers to the provisions (*sambhāra*), the preparatory application (*prayoga*), and so forth.

Third, the "two aspects" (*dvi-lakṣaṇa*) refer to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Fourth, the "seven mental attentions" (*sapta-manasikāra*) are the seven types of attention. Fifth, the "bases" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) are the supports.
These are the three bases. Fifth, the objects of censure and aversion are phenomena that are despised. Sixth, the objects of praise are phenomena that are commended.
Seventh, the phenomena to be countered are greed, hatred, and so forth. Eighth, the counteragents are the contemplation of impurity and so forth.
Their brief and detailed designations may be understood from their names.

Regarding the statement "performing Buddha-works through the *shū* (commentary)": this refers solely to the essence of the teaching (*kyōtai*). To gather and transform sentient beings, causing them to sever evil and advance toward good, is what is called performing Buddha-works.
Regarding the phrase in the *Shō* (sub-commentary), "Is it not the case that speech has a nature, or that all things have a nature?"—on the character "non" (*hi*), add a single [dot/stroke].
The meaning of the word "mo" (not) is now clearly revealed. The intent of this question is as follows:

because there is the nature of the expressive words, one knows that all phenomena (dharma) which are expressed possess a nature. Alternatively, the word "mo" may not be added; it merely restates the words of the Blessed One.
The final character "ye" (ya) is a term of inquiry. "The Buddha said" introduces the answer. First, he answers that although phenomena lack an intrinsic nature, they nevertheless exist.
This refers to the teaching that dispels through verbal expression. Furthermore, it is said that the subsequent answer indicates there is no verbal expression to be dispelled by words.

The intention behind Mahāmati’s question is that phenomena must necessarily depend upon one another. The intention behind the World-Honored One’s answer is that phenomena do not depend upon one another.

First, he clarifies that there are words even in the absence of phenomena; subsequently, he clarifies that there are phenomena even in the absence of words. Therefore, the concluding statement below says that phenomena do not [depend] on one another.
"It must be so. (Sū ya. This is the section where Mahāmati cites examples to establish the point. The commentary states:
"Since speech, silence, gazing, and blinking are all 'teaching' (*deśanā*). Question: How is it that silence is called "teaching"?

What is its mode of operation (*ākāra*), and furthermore, what dharma serves as its teaching-substance (*deśana-śarīra*)? Answer: Because by abiding in silence one causes the faculties (*indriya*) to give rise to understanding, it is called "teaching. Alternatively, [it is so called because]...

Taking the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of that person as its substance refers to the perspective of phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, taking ineffable *tathatā* (suchness) as its substance refers to the perspective of rational principle (*dharmatā*).
As stated in the *Chao*: "Sound being form is the reflection manifested by both; it is the reflection manifested by the two consciousnesses of the ear and the mind."
Some say that this refers to the images manifested by two consciousnesses.
The commentary’s statement that "only the fundamental [consciousness] lacks images" is like the sun extending its light; it refers to the new illumination of the fundamental dharma.

Furthermore, when the commentary speaks of the "manifestation of the five minds gathering," this does not mean that the five mental factors and so forth manifest; rather, it simply means passing through the five stages.

The mental image appears as a collection. Regarding the five types of mind: first, the impulsive mind (*āvega-citta*), which is the initial encounter with an object when no understanding has yet arisen;

second, the investigative mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*), which seeks out the preceding object while still remaining in hesitation; third, the determinative mind (*niścaya-citta*), which understands the preceding object and gives rise to conviction;
fourth, the defiled or pure mind (*kliṣṭa-śubha-citta*), which, having already recognized the preceding object, performs either wholesome or unwholesome actions.
The five types of resultant minds (*niṣyanda-citta*) are as previously explained, because they continue in succession from the subsequent moments of wholesome or unwholesome states.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that there are "twelve minds in total," this refers to listening to the sūtras with a distracted mind; when listening with a focused mind, there are only eight minds.

Regarding the two characters "constant" (*nitya*) in the context of "activity" (*saṃskāra*), because the two minds of "sudden occurrence" (*ābhoga*) and "seeking" (*paryeṣaka*) are excluded, it is said that there are fourteen characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

One view holds that these are the images of fourteen persons; another view holds that they are the characteristics of the four types of sound, as the remaining characteristics are provisionally established based on sound.
The *Chao* states that among the five minds, the first and last are common to all six consciousnesses, while three are exclusively the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The *Fayuan* says: "The sixth [consciousness] possesses the five [minds] and functions according to its inclination; it is also a state of seeking (*paryeṣaka*), because there is aspiration.
Otherwise, this mind would not be included within the five. A sudden, initial moment of thought has not yet produced certainty; if it were not seeking, it would constitute a major error."

[This is] lost. Since the determinative mental consciousness (*niścaya-manovijñāna*) has already persisted for a long time, it lacks the inherent power to induce its own arising through defilement or purity;
rather, the fruit itself possesses the causal conditions that have such power. According to one interpretation, the five consciousnesses are autonomous from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.

The preceding and succeeding moments induce one another, thereby constituting both the defiled and the pure. Since you admit that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses can induce what follows them as defiled or pure minds, why should the fifth [consciousness] not do so?
Therefore, we know that the causes of the five sensory consciousnesses also possess all five types of mind. To summarize: the first six consciousnesses possess all five;

the seventh and eighth each possess four (the eighth lacks *vitarka* because it is the initial transformation of the basis at the start of the eighth realm, and the seventh may have *ābhoga* when encountering a new object; the remaining three types are to be understood accordingly).

Regarding this, there is one interpretation: the five consciousnesses possess only two types of mind—namely, the *sateri* (sudden) and the *t’engliu* (outflowing)—because it is accepted that when the five [consciousnesses] arise following the stages of investigation (*sōngkyu*) and so forth, they are themselves outflowing minds arising in a state of distraction. The present text follows the latter view; thus, the *Chao* states accordingly.
As for the statement, "Furthermore, the first three are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), while the latter two are common to both wholesome and unwholesome," the *Fayuan* says:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the first three moments of mind are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), while the fourth and fifth may belong to any of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).

This is based on the possibility of encountering non-confused objects during the stage of a causal being (*hetu-bhūmi*). Regarding the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), it is taught that one of them arises in immediate succession with the sixth consciousness.

However, if one is in the stage of a causal being and the objective spheres are powerful and dominant, the various consciousnesses arise in a mixed fashion, and all five moments of mind arise simultaneously, each of which may belong to any of the three natures.
[Included] within what is subsumed. If it is in the untainted state (*anāsrava*), one then attains mastery over all manifold virtues.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Only the reflection exists, but not the original," which means that according to the Mahāyāna definitive teaching (*siddhānta*), the sacred teachings are merely reflections within the minds of sentient beings:
Question: If this is so, why does the subsequent section, when discussing the "Complete Inclusion" (*quan shou*), state that the Final Teaching (*zhong jiao*) also [includes them]?
This possesses four propositions. Or, it may be said that [the Buddha] speaks only because he manifests from his own mind, and so forth. Now, I respond generally:

according to that school, since the beginning is identical to the source and all characteristics are exhausted upon becoming a Buddha, how could there be any fundamental substance? It is merely taught that the body manifests in accordance with the transformations of the deluded mind; is this not then merely a reflection?

Thus, the sentient beings who manifest the capacity to hear are the listeners, while the reflected Buddhas who manifest the capacity to speak are the teachers. This is the essence of the true mind of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*).

Because it encompasses both [aspects], it is said that "preaching and listening are fully subsumed. For example, as in a dream, there are two ways in which the meaning is established: first, one sees a Dharma master ascending the seat to preach the Dharma while listening to him preach;
second, even though there is only a reflection and no original object, the meaning is nonetheless established.

Furthermore, with respect to self-benefit and internal realization—namely, the three preceding mirrors of the nature of purity following the defiled wisdom—it is called "only a reflection with no original object. With respect to benefiting others and external manifestation:
"The Mirror of the Nature of the Inconceivable Karmic Activity that Follows Defilement and the Pure Conditions of Edifying Influence" encompasses both the speaker and the listener.

Regarding the statement in the *Śū* (Commentary) that "the preceding four [sections] explain the gathering of sentient beings," this refers respectively to the two meanings of perfect fusion (*yuánróng*) and sequential arrangement (*xíngpù*).
This refers either to the two meanings of "completely inclusive" and "completely exclusive," or to the two meanings of the "distinct teaching" (biejiao) and the "common teaching" (tongjiao).

Regarding the statement in the *Shu* that both [teachings] are preserved and the two teachings are established as equal: one might ask, since the distinct and the shadow-like (or fundamental) teachings have separate categories, how can they now be said to be equal?

Although their manifestations differ, the essence of these teachings is no different; they fully encompass both this and that, and thus both gates are taken together. Therefore, it is said they are "established as equal."

The Commentary states that the beginning and the fundamental are non-dual and the three greatnesses are identical, yet each person within their own mind must cultivate and realize this for themselves.

This is, for example, like a single pearl whose inherent nature is luminous and pure (like *mūla-awakening*, *benjue*). Having long been buried in mud (within ignorance), it is polished until it is fresh, luminous, and pure (like *ādi-awakening*, *shijue*).
The new and the original are no different (the non-duality of beginning and fundamental). Such is the substance of lightness and heaviness, and the characteristic of perfect luminosity.
The function of producing jewels is of a single flavor without distinction (the three greatnesses are identical). They universally face many mirrors (corresponding equally to many minds).

When one mirror is polished, it becomes supremely bright and pure; its solitary illumination is no different [from the others]. Regarding the three aspects of essence, attribute, and function (within the mind of one person, the light of cultivation is uniquely realized as the Great Three), the other mirrors have not yet been polished and thus do not reflect;
their differences remain unmanifest. (The other minds have not yet cultivated or realized the two greatnesses. The *Avataṃsaka* is not like this: polishing and not polishing [are simultaneous].

The two mirrors reflect each other; therefore, this differs from what preceded. Question: Regarding the inclusion of objects within mind alone (*cittamātra*), the claim that "only the fundamental [consciousness] exists and there are no images" is a tenet of the Hīnayāna.
Why, then, were the first four [points] of the preceding text compatible with the Hīnayāna, while the latter six are exclusively Mahāyāna?

Answer: The statement that "only the fundamental [consciousness] exists and there are no images" is not the meaning of *cittamātra*. It was mentioned incidentally in order to clarify the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). Thus, the Commentary states: "Only the fundamental... and so forth.
"Shadow" (yǐng) refers precisely to this meaning: that the Hīnayāna does not understand that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Furthermore, it is asked:

since the "Complete Inclusion of Speaker and Listener" section already contains the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*), why are the first eight [sections] called the Common Teaching (*sāmānyavyavasthāna*)? The answer is: since the word "only" (*mātra*) is absent, what logical obstacle is there?

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “according to any one sacred teaching, neither of the two minds exists”: Question: Since both minds have been extinguished, how can that teaching still exist?

Furthermore, if the mind is extinguished while the teaching remains, why do you say that the apprehended object is subsumed within mind-only? Answer: This term “extinguished” does not mean falling into emptiness;
rather, it refers to their mutual negation as they return to the single mind. Thus, there are no difficulties regarding the two aforementioned points.

Regarding the commentary’s statement on “converging conditions to enter the true substance”: in the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), which establishes characteristics, "converging conditions" refers to the subsuming of characteristics, while "entering reality" refers to proceeding from nature.

In the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), the fact that dependently originated phenomena lack intrinsic nature is called "converging conditions to enter reality. In the Sudden Teaching (*tadaṅga-yāna*), the exhaustion of characteristics and the manifestation of nature is called "converging conditions to enter reality.

In the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), the returning of the mutually dependent characteristics of dependent origination to the rational nature in a state of seamless integration is called "converging conditions to enter reality."
Although the meaning applies generally in this way, it specifically refers only to the initial sudden [teaching].
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth taught here in this land are likewise in the ten directions;

this is the teaching of the primary and its associates (*mukhya-pakṣa*)," the intention is that the teachings spoken are divided into the primary and its associates based on the person who speaks them. How could one possibly take the teaching as consisting of both the speaker and the listener?
This distinguishes between the principal and its retinue. By this analogy, one should understand that in the preceding text, the principal and its retinue are layered upon one another;

they resound throughout the ten directions simultaneously, yet this does not depend on a listener. Regarding the statement that "the retinue teachings, although they cannot be the principal, are nonetheless of the same class as the retinue":
for example, when cause is contrasted with fruit, the cause cannot be the principal but can only be the retinue. Why is this so? It is because the inferior is contrasted with the superior. Question:

Question: Since all phenomena accord with their own nature (*dharmatā*), how can one distinguish between superior and inferior? Answer: This statement is made in reference to the ritual procedures for the manifestation of non-disintegrating forms.

The commentary states, "For example, written characters universally apply to all things," meaning that just as writing any character allows one to designate whatever phenomenon comes before the eyes, so too, when it is said that [the practitioner] acts within those phenomena while having no fixed designation, it means they perform the rite without a determinate focus.

Regarding the phrase "the essence of the Sea-Seal clearly manifests": the preceding nine are specific instances, while this one is the general whole. Subsuming the specific into the general, this samādhi constitutes the essence.
It is like the myriad reflections in a fragrant sea, all of which take the fragrant sea itself as their essence.
The commentary states that the masters of the various schools collectively maintain that this [school] is not "receptive. "Receptive" (*shou*) means to believe or to accept.
Regarding the classification of the "Eightfold School of Emptiness and the Severance of Phenomena": first, it includes the Initial Teaching of the Refutation of Characteristics;

second, it subsumes the Sudden Teaching. Question: Why is the Sudden Teaching listed before the Final Teaching? Answer: This is based on the speed with which Buddhahood is attained according to the teachings. The Final Teaching is slow.

The sudden [teaching] is placed first because it is swift; the ultimate [teaching] is placed last because its doctrinal synthesis is broad. The sudden is narrow and thus precedes [the ultimate] (referring solely to the *dharmadhātu* of principle);

the ultimate is broad and thus follows (encompassing all three *dharmadhātus*). Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "signlessness" (*animitta*), the correct [teaching] and the initial [teaching] include the sudden, and thus they precede the ultimate.
