Regarding the meaning of "transcending relativity," since it refers exclusively to the sudden, it follows after the ultimate.

Regarding the statement in the *Shu* (Commentary) that "these ten schools (*zong*) and five teachings (*jiao*) have mutual variations in breadth and narrowness," the textual meaning is somewhat obscure; I shall now briefly point it out.
First, when comparing the teachings (*jiao*) and the schools (*zong*) through the lens of scriptural materials: the teachings are broad and the schools are narrow.

This is because a single scripture may contain multiple teachings (broad), whereas a single scripture belongs to only one school (narrow). Second, when comparing the schools and the teachings through the lens of doctrinal systems: a single school fully encompasses many [teachings].

*Sūtra*. (Zongkuan) When a single teaching (*śāsana*) encompasses only a small portion of a single *sūtra*, the teaching is narrow (*śāsana-saṃkoca*). Furthermore, when considering the number of [teachings] possessed, one may discuss the breadth or narrowness of the teaching:

the teaching is broad while the doctrine (*artha*) is narrow; that is, a single *sūtra* can contain many teachings (the teaching is broad), yet a single *sūtra* possesses only a single doctrine (the doctrine is [broad]).

When considering the breadth or narrowness of encompassing the entirety of a *sūtra*, the doctrine is broad while the teaching is narrow; that is, a single doctrine fully encompasses many *sūtras* (the doctrine is broad). A single teaching...
The [teachings] are subsumed within the scriptural texts (the teaching is narrow). One should provide an analogy: the scripture is like a single kingdom, and the doctrine is like the sovereign king.
The teaching is like the common people; a single kingdom may contain many subjects (it is broad), yet there is only one king (it is narrow).
The various classes of subjects do not encompass the entire nation (they are narrow), whereas the single king universally governs the entire nation (he is broad). Reflect upon this.

As for the commentary stating that Nāgārjuna refers to this as the *Mahā-acintya-sūtra*, it follows the same principle as within this Qingliang tradition, where the character "great" (*mahā*) is occasionally omitted.
If the character "great" were absent, the distinction from similar terms would not be exhaustive;

thus, it remains the same as Xianshou’s response regarding terms such as "Dharmadhātu-origination," where the meaning is equivalent to the character "great" in order to distinguish it from other forms of inconceivability, such as supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and liberation (*vimokṣa*).
The second fascicle of the Commentary (*śāstra*) reconciles the differences between the versions. Its textual presentation is concise and simple, yet its encompassed meaning is profound and vast;
it weaves together the grand framework and investigates the subtle essence. Moreover, the eighty-fascicle *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is so immense that its entirety is contained within this gateway;

how much more so for the hundred-thousand-verse original, whose profound subtleties are all included herein. Therefore, the text of this sub-commentary (*piṇḍārtha*) grasps both the beginning and the end, tracing the source of the oceanic stream.
The flow follows the assembly’s intent as it first presents its purpose; based on each chapter, the main text is now explained in sequence.

Stepping upon what precedes to initiate what follows, the principles are distributed clearly like stars across the heavens. Discerning the paths and opening the school, it is as bright as the moon descending upon the ocean of nature.

Following the teachings of weeping at the crossroads and grieving over the silken thread, how could I dare add embellishments? Relying on the rites of the divided robe and the broken staff, I humbly bask in this radiant grace.

In form, it rivals the five sacred peaks with its crags and precipices; how could it begrudge a speck of dust? In its vastness, it shares the four seas with its surging waves; it does not decline even a drop of water.

(Xian Yan) Formerly, when I was merely expounding and proclaiming [the text], I still wished to record these details; now that I am about to take up the brush, I find it difficult to restrain my words.
Without reckoning my own rashness or my own mediocrity and emptiness, I shall briefly extend this re-explanation. This is truly because of the remaining arguments and...
The Sūtra reveals what is appropriate to the occasion; yet, by relying on a single momentum, these words and meanings manifest the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Its transformations are manifold, and thus, following the ten categories of the Great Commentary (*Mahāṭīkā*), they are distributed like the stars.
Gathering the true exegesis of this entire Sūtra, it takes shape like the full moon. Now, regarding the initial division of this primary section into three parts, it was first established by Tiantai.
The judgment accords with the texts of the Buddha-ground; from ancient times to the present, it has been a common guide, and both Chinese and Indian traditions have received it together.

From the time of Guṇabhadra down to the era of Qingliang (Faxiang), it was generally the practice to divide this single scripture into three sections: the "Chapter on Wondrous Adornment" as the introductory section (*nidāna-bhāga*); the chapters from "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" downward as the main body (*saddharma-bhāga*);
and within the "Chapter on the Dharma-realm," the passage beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī emerged from the Good-Abiding Pavilion" downward as the concluding section (*paryavasāna-bhāga*).
This is the general principle. As for the three [divisions]: when the compassionate dragon sends down rain upon the eight directions, it first spreads dense clouds;

when the Great Sage discourses on the Truth throughout the three periods of time, he first manifests the formal preparations (*parikarman*). Therefore, this is followed by the Introductory Division (*nidāna-vibhaṅga*). When the King of Physicians treats the world, he invariably bestows the divine elixir upon those afflicted by illness;
when the Sugata disciplines the faculties, he proclaims the wondrous Dharma according to the capacity of the vessel. Therefore, this is followed by the Main Division (*samyaktva-nirdeśa*).

The source is as vast and boundless as a celestial lake, its tributaries flowing across the four directions; the ocean of the Teaching is expansive and deep, its transmission extending through the three periods of time.
Although the fundamental assembly has completed its cycle, it is the later generations that are honored for their successive propagation of the Dharma.

Thus, when the sun of the Buddha’s light fades, the lamp of the Dharma must continue to pass its flame from one to the next; therefore, this is received as the stage of circulation, encompassing the beginning, middle, and end.
The three excellences [of beginning, middle, and end] can thus be observed from start to finish. The three seasons—spring, summer, and winter—are arranged in their proper order of cold and warmth.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on Initial Sublime Adornment" serves as the introductory section (*nidāna*), which generally sets forth the six accomplishments and reveals the perfect doctrine of the seven locations;

it universally adorns the three worlds and serves as the general introduction for the nine assemblies. Taking the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" and those following as the main body (*samyak-artha*), it is divided into five...

The precious verses of fifteen fascicles shine as brightly as the sun amidst the surrounding stars; they comprise thirty-eight chapters of jade-like stanzas, strung together like pearls and linked like polished gems.
Having briefly distinguished the grand outlines beginning from the "Coarse Robes" chapter, and since the underlying principles have been made manifest and the True Dharma is about to be expounded:
the forty recollections arise from the ocean-like assembly, raising the opening questions; the fivefold marks appear before the Tathāgata, providing the responses.
The light from the face summons the myriad lands, signifying birth from the Buddha; the light from between the eyebrows shines upon Samantabhadra, indicating the Master of the Dharma.
As divine power descends with majestic authority, the network of lands trembles; as auspicious omens are bestowed through manifestation, the various faculties are awakened and exhorted.
Wondrously colored flowers spring forth from the earth, revealing the discourse on the fruits of reliance; a multitude of sublime voices issues from a single pore, manifesting the teaching.
The Buddha’s flow [of teaching] serves as the initial point for the exposition of the Dharma; therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Tathāgata Manifesting Signs.

These two auspicious signs become increasingly manifest as the Lord of Dharma is about to proclaim the teaching. Beholding the light from the *ūrṇā*, they intuitively comprehend the mind of Vairocana;

illuminating the principles of the Dharma, they personally enter the Samādhi of the Hidden Body (*kāyaguhya*). Internally contemplating phenomena and principles, and externally discerning the capacities and suitability of beings, they receive the empowerment of the Buddhas above and act for the sake of others below.

This concludes the "Section on the Tracks of Phenomena. Therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Samādhi of Samantabhadra. Having entered the ultimate meditative concentration, he invokes all Buddhas and offers praise;
uniquely bathed in superior conditions, he strengthens the faculties of sentient beings so they may believe and accept [the teaching].

He describes the dependent retribution of the ten directions—the adornments of the ocean of lands—and gathers the ten kinds of causes and conditions for the formation of worlds. Therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Formation of Worlds."

Chapter Four: The Universal Basis of the Great Awakened One. Its essence is identical while its manifestations differ; yet we have not yet examined the distinct lands of our Original Teacher, wherein the cause is pure and the fruit is adorned, with adornments that are inexhaustible.
Each and every one is equal in measure to space, wondrous and supreme beyond thought, and within every atom, the entire Dharma-realm is universally contained.
Therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World. Fifth, as the environment of support has now been revealed...
The past causes should now be made manifest; they are like deep roots from which fruit flourishes, or a distant source from which a stream flows long.
Having cultivated the cause known as Vīraprabha (威光), he served inconceivable numbers of Buddhas. Upon attaining the fruit, he is named Samantaprabha (遍照), his adornments being inexhaustible.

Thus, by citing the person who has realized the fruit to reveal the Dharma of the cause, it is followed by the "Vairocana Chapter. The above clarifies the cause and fruit of that which is to be believed.
The first assembly is titled "Exalting the Fruit and Encouraging Joyful Faith.

Having already understood that the secondary environment (*upabhoga*) is adorned with immeasurable and sublime splendors, one wonders how the primary body (*mūlakāya*), which is inconceivable, is perfected and manifests in accordance with sentient beings.
Its body pervades ten billion worlds beneath the four heavens; it establishes names according to what is appropriate for each, thus establishing hundreds of billions of various titles. Therefore...
It is followed by the Chapter on Names and Titles. Seventh, universally according to the inclinations of beings, the Wheel of Dharma is extensively explained:
the specific names for the Single Truth number ten thousand, while the general designation for the Four Truths numbers four hundred billion; therefore, it is received as the Four Truths.

Eighth, the body and wisdom are manifested, with two lights reflecting upon two objects. Since these objects consist of both essence and characteristics without obstruction, the lights must be the perfect fusion of form and mind.

Therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on Radiant Awakening. The nine upper chapters constitute that which is to be believed; the three karmas of body, speech, and mind [are therein addressed]. The three lower chapters constitute the capacity for belief;
the three minds of practice through understanding, virtue, and [awakening] are [therein addressed]. The ten Bodhisattvas manifest their understanding to mutually stimulate and uplift one another;
the ten kinds of profundity reveal the mysterious to engage in successive inquiry and interrogation. Therefore, it is followed by the "Bodhi... [chapter].
In the "Chapter on the Inquiry into Wisdom," since right understanding has already been established, one must further cultivate superior practice.

This is like the way oil and light assist each other, or as the feet and eyes mutually support one another. One traverses various realms to engage in cultivation and encounters conditions to apply contemplation, refining compassion and wisdom while simultaneously benefiting both self and others;
therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on Pure Conduct. Eleventh, once wondrous understanding has been awakened and pure conduct has been cultivated, one attains completion.
Through these extraordinary causes, one must obtain supreme merit to adorn oneself with perfected virtues;

by establishing them through perfected power and function, one gathers the sages and saints of the forty-two stages and transforms the sentient beings of the twenty-five realms of existence. Thus spoke the Venerable Xianshou.
Therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (Śrīmālā). The above concludes the explanation of the second assembly, the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
The ten stages of faith being complete, the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) are about to be expounded. Without moving from the Bodhi tree, he ascends to the Śakra heaven. It is like this:
when the moon is reflected in a clear river, three boats may drift south or north, yet they do not leave the middle of the stream; remaining in that middle stream—
Constantly following [beings] to the south or north, the Tathāgata responds to their faculties; therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru.
Thirteen: according to the conditions of their faculties, the moon of the Tathāgata appears; praising the Buddha’s virtues, the clouds of Bodhisattvas arrive.

The substance of the clouds is revealed as profound and dark, and the true emptiness is manifested as vast and boundless; therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on Verses of Praise at the Summit of Mount Sumeru."

14. Since the resonance between the faculties and the teachings has been established, and the roots and the instruction have struck one another, one clearly attains entry into right concentration through the fulfillment of faith, and dwells securely in true emptiness through the profound discourse on wisdom;

therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes. 15. While the general stages and specific practices have already been manifested, it is now appropriate to clarify the universal cultivation of pure conduct.
One traverses the profound contemplations of the ten realms and mobilizes the wondrous mind of the four immeasurables to respond to [sentient beings].
The true wisdom of the Ten Powers gives rise to the supreme resolve of non-duality; at the very moment of the first aspiration, one attains perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, this is followed by the Chapter on Pure Conduct (*Brahmacarya-varga*). Once the practices of the sixteen stages are complete, their sublime virtues must be discussed.

To clarify the extraordinary merit of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), the superior virtues of the subsequent stages are illustrated by way of analogy; though these worldly metaphors are employed, they are merely equal in measure to empty space.

If we proceed according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), its merit is truly equal to that of the All-Knowledge (Sarvajñā); therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Merit of the First Arising of the Bodhicitta.

In the seventeenth [chapter], "The Lower Stage of Worthies," once the stage of the Middle-Worthy within the *Xingqi* (Nature-Arising) has been fulfilled, the "Gate of Sublime Wisdom" is expounded to demonstrate the superior progress of stimulating the mind;
therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma. The above clarifies the conclusion of the third assembly, the Ten Abodes. Eighteen.
The Ten Abodes having been perfected, one is about to discuss the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). These too must respond to the needs of sentient beings by descending to accord with their faculties;

therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on Ascending to the Palace of the Yama Heaven. (19) Once the Lord has responded to the needs of others, his retinue must surely offer praise, so as to reveal that the essence of the practices is profound and mysterious, and that they are vast and expansive based upon the Buddha’s wisdom; therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Palace of Yama. (2)

The ten stages (*bhūmi*) having been clearly elucidated, the main body of the teaching (*saddharma*) should now be revealed. Because one cultivates correct practice and attains the rank of a "Middle Sage" (*madhyama-ārya*), the "Chapter on the Ten Practices" (*Daśaprakaraṇa-paṭala*) follows.
Having completed the Middle Sage at the twenty-first stage and being about to enter the subsequent rank, one accumulates various practices with the intent to achieve perfect transformation;
therefore, the "Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries" (*Daśākṣaya-garbha-paṭala*) follows. The above clarifies the tenth stage within the fourth assembly.

[The preceding section] concludes. Having completed the twenty-two [sections on] the Perfected Sages (*bhadra*), and intending to reveal the aforementioned "Manifestation According to Capabilities," the Teacher responds to the call of those to be converted;
therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.

(23) Since both the principal and the retinue have now assembled, there is extended praise through both general and specific [verses], manifesting the gateway of vows for dedication. Relying upon the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, it is therefore followed by...
Having completed the twenty-four chapters on the gradual progression through the "Verses of Praise" (Gāthā-stava-parivarta) in the Tuṣita Palace, the fundamental doctrine should now be revealed.

It is divided into ten stages of dedication (daśa-pratipatti), which are unobstructed and unhindered; it revolves through three spheres in a manner that is inconceivable. Therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications" (Daśa-pratipatti-parivarta).

The fifth assembly has already been explained above. Now that the twenty-five [chapters] fully elucidating the three levels of worthiness (tri-śaikṣa) are complete, it is appropriate to discuss the ten levels of the noble ones (daśārya).
Tending toward the Buddha-wisdom, the four rivers flow together into the celestial lake; manifesting the exquisite flowers of virtue, the myriad things are born simultaneously upon the ground.
It resembles the great ocean of the ten virtues, wherein each virtue is all-pervasive; it is like the jewel of the ten virtues, wherein each virtue increases in excellence.
It serves as the stairway for the Bodhisattva’s mind and constitutes the wisdom-activity of the Tathāgata; therefore, one receives the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi) next.

Chapter. The sixth assembly concludes. Regarding the twenty-sixth [chapter]: With the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*) nearing completion and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) about to be realized, he establishes the extraordinary perfuming of supreme advancement and institutes the exalted station of Equal Enlightenment (*samatā-jñāna*).
He extensively opens many gates, their measure equal to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Briefly extending the teachings and meanings, he analytically reveals the profound and mysterious.
Through the wondrous samādhi of radiance, he thoroughly investigates the true source; skillfully manifesting supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he is able to give rise to wisdom.
Because of wisdom (*prajñā*), it is followed by the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" (27). This concerns the function of the twenty-seven profound samādhis;
the power of the wondrous wisdom of the Most Holy and Most Spiritually Intelligent is unobstructed and unimpeded. Therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers" (28).

This is the discourse on the gate of supernatural powers whose power of concentration is inconceivable. It takes the ultimate wisdom as its foundation and relies upon the profound sagacity as its source. Therefore, it is followed by...

By means of the ten stages of patience (*kṣānti*), the twenty-nine meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and the three functions of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), their immeasurability is distinguished; through the three gateways of numerical equivalence and analogy, the wisdom of the mind is unfathomable.

Repeatedly compared and weighed, they clarify that even Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is difficult to know; when each is individually measured against them, [the profundity of the Buddha's wisdom is revealed].
How much more so for the subtle and wondrous enlightenment! Since *asaṃkhyeya* is the foremost of great numbers, this is followed by the "Chapter on the *Asaṃkhyeya*.

Within a single instant, thirty moments and eons are perfectly interfused; their boundaries cannot be fathomed. Dust-motes and lands encompass one another, such that even the most minute atoms are inexhaustible.
Herein, Samantabhadra briefly provides an indication, roughly manifesting the Tathāgata’s power, wherein each subsequent land is ten times greater than the preceding.

the Dharma is profoundly mysterious, and it separately reveals the three thousand great [assemblies].
A thousand subtle dust motes; all people are virtuous friends. Regarding the tenfold principal and attendant elements that are inexhaustible:

Regarding the exhortation for the assembly to practice with diligent vigor, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) states:

"You bhikṣus, by day you should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas with a focused mind, ensuring that no time is wasted. During the first watch and the last watch of the night, do not let them go to waste either.
In the middle watch, recite the sūtras to refresh yourselves; do not allow this life to pass in vain due to the causes and conditions of sleep, resulting in nothing attained."
It is so. You should reflect that the fire of impermanence burns all worlds; seek early deliverance for yourself and do not sleep.
The thieves of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) constantly lie in wait to kill you, more so than any enemy; how can you afford to sleep without being startled into awakening?
The poisonous snake of affliction sleeps within your heart, like a black serpent slumbering in a room; you must [drive it out] with—
Use the hook of ethical discipline to remove them early. Once the sleeping snake has been drawn out, one may sleep in peace;
to sleep while it remains is the mark of a person devoid of shame. The garment of shame is the foremost among all ornaments.

Shame is like an iron hook, capable of restraining a person from what is unrighteous. Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should always maintain a sense of shame and remorse, never for even a moment neglecting them.
If one is devoid of shame and modesty, then all virtues are lost. A person who possesses a sense of shame possesses wholesome dharmas;
if one lacks shame, there is no distinction between them and the various beasts.

In the *Chao* (Commentary), it is said that before the gate of the Hell of Chao-di, one sees a monk who is identified as Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva; he then instructs [the practitioner] to recite a verse, beginning with "Equal... and so forth. Question:

Since the Bodhisattva possesses the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), why does he not teach universally? Answer: Because there are those with whom he has a karmic affinity and those with whom he does not;

because karma is either determinate or indeterminate; and because undergoing suffering may be beneficial for some while being of no benefit to others. Therefore, the sub-commentary below asks: "The Bodhisattva... and so on.
...of suffering. It is summoned by one’s own karma and transformed by one’s own mind; how then could a bodhisattva possibly take it upon themselves? Answer:

There are seven meanings through which the taking on of others' suffering is universally applicable. First, because compassion arises from the false augmentation of suffering by oneself. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (49) states:
"When a bodhisattva falls from the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and enters the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*)," and so forth.
"How does one transcend the various evil destinies and so forth? This question asks how a bodhisattva personally avoids the evil destinies and so forth;
this question asks how a bodhisattva personally avoids the evil destinies. The subsequent answer is extensive. Its meaning is as follows:
it refers to a bodhisattva who, having purified their mind regarding the world and having well accumulated the provisions, cultivates compassion for sentient beings who undergo manifold sufferings.
One contemplates them with compassion, free from other thoughts. Through this cultivation, one attains a disposition of affection and a disposition of pity.

One vows to dwell in the evil realms for the sake of benefiting sentient beings there, regarding those realms as if they were one’s own home. Even if one must remain in the evil realms, one is able to realize enlightenment and endure it;
for the sake of removing the suffering of others, one vows to take it upon oneself in their stead, so that their evil karma may be forever extinguished.
They do not manifest. All wholesome karma is constantly able to manifest due to the power of this compassionate vow (*karuṇā-praṇidhāna*).

By means of this power, all the heavy obstructions (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the category of afflictions within all the evil realms are eliminated from one's own basis (*āśraya*), and one attains entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The commentary explains: with respect to this, there is only the intention (*āśaya*) of compassion; the body cannot act on its behalf, because of that compassion.

First, one certainly attains supreme benefit for oneself. Second, regarding the bodhisattva’s original practice of seeking the Dharma through asceticism for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, this is already termed "substitution";
subsequently, being able to act as a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for others is also termed "substituting for [their suffering].

Third, regarding the bodhisattva’s practice of sharing the same activities while retaining afflictions (*kleśa*), they accept a body subject to suffering to preach the Dharma to sentient beings, causing them not to create the causes of suffering; thus, the causes perish.

It is also called "receiving in substitution. Fourth, if there are sentient beings who wish to commit an *ānantarya* (immediate) karma or the like, and the Bodhisattva transforms them so that they do not follow through, yet subsequently takes their life, the Bodhisattva personally undergoes the retribution of suffering in the evil realms to enable those beings to escape the great suffering of the *ānantarya* hells;
this is called "receiving in substitution," as stated in the eleventh fascicle of the *Liang Translation of the Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. [Nirvāṇa...]
King Bhasmanpreya was also like this; it was not merely a matter of intention alone.

Fifth, because Bodhisattvas first cultivate the correct aspirational vow to undergo suffering for the sake of birth, they attain mastery over their vows upon reaching the ultimate stage, remaining constantly in the evil realms to rescue and take the place of sentient beings, such as Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva and King Vyūharāja, even unto [the time of] famine.

The great fish of the world—the body, speech, and mind—are all of this same category. Whether by illuminating them with light or by secretly bestowing spiritual power through their supernatural faculties, such instances are not limited to one.
Sixth, because the Bodhisattva’s vow is in accord with True Suchness (*tathatā*), the suffering of those sentient beings is identical to the nature of Suchness.
By means of a vow that accords with Suchness, [the Bodhisattva] returns to and permeates that very suffering which is itself True Suchness. Based on this...

Integration is also called "receiving on behalf. Seventh, because Samantabhadra takes the *dharmadhātu* as his body, and all sentient beings are the *dharmadhātu*, whenever sentient beings undergo suffering, it is always the Bodhisattva who does so; therefore, it is called "receiving on behalf.

Of the seven meanings mentioned above, the first consists merely of the aspirational intention (*āśaya*), while the next two concern only acting as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). The fourth and fifth meanings, however, are actual...
Regarding the two meanings of "the body as a substitute" (the sixth and seventh [meanings]): in principle, contemplation and integration are harmonized. Question:

If one relies on the two meanings of the fourth and fifth [categories], one should be able to universally substitute for others. Why, then, do sentient beings still undergo suffering? Answer: There are three reasons for this.

First, it depends on whether there is a karmic connection or no connection; if one has a karmic connection with a bodhisattva, substitution is possible. Second, karma is either determinate or indeterminate.

Those whose [karma] is indeterminate may be substituted. Third, if undergoing suffering brings benefit, the Bodhisattva causes them to undergo it, for only through this can they ultimately achieve liberation from suffering.
It is like parents instructing their child to be treated by a strict teacher; such subtle benefit is beyond the comprehension of ordinary or inferior beings.
This Great Commentary, based on the abbreviated version of the Perfect Sūtra, encompasses the true essence of the one hundred thousand verses.
The entire text exhausts the profound depths of a single scroll; it accords with the magnificent capacity of Yueliang and fully manifests the expositions of the nine assemblies.
It connects those of the "warm" faculty according to the *Yuelü* and elucidates solely the趣 (qiù) of the eight gates. What is now being explained is precisely this text.
Truly, it may be said that its phrasing is like patterned Shu brocade, with every line vying to emit fragrance, and its meaning is like a black dragon’s pearl.

yet, if one exhausts their own ignorant sincerity, even the tip of a reed pen may suffice. First, I shall explain the title, seizing the essential points to lift up the main framework.

Thus, it is all-encompassing. As for its arrangement, it follows the tradition rather than creating anew; its name is the *Vairocana* Treasury of Teachings, and its intent is the heart-mind of Samantabhadra.

This sutra is both profound and vast; it reveals the inconceivable nature of the Teacher, who manifests as one or many without obstruction.

Moment by moment, he forgot all fatigue. As for those who sighed in admiration of its vastness and distance: it rivals Mount Sumeru as it spans the surface of the sea, towering high above all other peaks;

having long been submerged in the great ocean of the eight sufferings, they suddenly encounter a dragon boat; having forever fallen from the high mountain of the three types of awakening, they suddenly mount a celestial chariot.
I, He, am moved with gratitude and joy beyond measure, my delight exceeding all bounds. I am so overcome with exultation that I cannot find words to express it.

Were it not for the sages and worthies, who else could have known this? I shall briefly explain the titles of the chapters to reveal the subtle principles of the five pairs of meanings, and I shall provide a rough outline of the sections to manifest the adornments of the three worlds.

Within these eight gates, the meanings unfold in ten thousand ways; on this day, we shall collectively summarize one assembly. First, regarding the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching:
that it stirs the flanks of Mount Sumeru is truly no small cause; that it agitates and sways the vast ocean is indeed a momentous matter.

when the golden crow of dawn first arrives at the mountain peak, it manifests the fruition and virtue, wherein the primary and secondary realms merge in harmony, entering directly into non-obstruction.
Revealing the stages and positions, the perfect practice is sovereign, transcending thought and the unthinkable—this is the exposition of the supreme conduct, distinguished by its sudden perfection.
Universally perfected, it opens up heaven and earth to reveal the True Dharma. It merges the realm of principle with the realm of phenomena, analogous to the interpenetration of Yin and Yang.
For those who open the causal nature, there may be benefit both now and in the future; such supreme benefit is inconceivable.
Some may see it and some may hear it; its extraordinary efficacy is unfathomable. In a single *kṣaṇa*, one achieves the firm seed, its form like that of *vajra*.
In a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), one is born into the Buddha-family, one’s appearance identical to that of a prince. As for those with future conditions, they depend on time:

vertically, they exhaust all thought-moments and eons, such that the beginning and end, the extended and the brief, are mutually fused. As for their locus: horizontally, they pervade the atoms of all lands, encompassing both the defiled and the pure, the universal and the particular.

Yet they interpenetrate one another. Relying on the primary and responding accordingly, they transcend ordinary sentiment through meditative concentration; how could stillness and turbulence be fathomed? Manifest signs appear in various auspicious responses;

They are all identical. Generally, they are divided into twelve categories; yet, while the ancient and modern may differ, one must distinguish between the singular and the manifold. Regarding the general principle of separation and integration:
when separated, the shallow and the deep are vastly distinct, differing by a thousand variations according to the plants and trees;

when integrated, the great and the small are fundamentally the same, like the rain from heaven which is of a single flavor. Second, regarding the divergence or accord between the ancient and the modern: the sages of the Eastern Land and the Western Land...
The masters each spread their nets of teaching; the eminent scholars of the Dharma-nature school and the Dharma-character school alternately opened the profound gates.

The schools are enumerated as ten, distinguished by their varying degrees of depth. As for the "five teachings": those who realize simple emptiness practice self-benefit;

From the perspective of illusory existence and its conformity with conditions, there is a distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas; yet, based on the emptiness of their essence and its unchanging nature, there is no difference between quiescence and illumination.
Thus, regarding hindrances, when one is severed, all are severed; regarding causes, when one is cultivated, all are cultivated; regarding fruits, when one is realized, all are realized;
and regarding principle, when one is verified, all are verified. As for the statement of the "Ten Schools," their meanings will be explained in the subsequent sections.

There is no need for an elaborate preface. Regarding the fourth point, the general integration of the teachings: first, they penetrate all doctrines, with their depth or shallowness responding to conditions to benefit sentient beings;
subsequently, they harmonize the methods of transformation, following the capacities of beings to dispel delusions. Third, regarding the demarcation of principles and meanings:
It is both profound and vast; it clarifies the One Vehicle while encompassing immeasurable vehicles, fully excluding yet fully including.
It explains the Shared Teaching while carrying the Distinct Teaching, embracing the fourfold Dharma-realm with its four stages unconfounded, and subsuming the threefold gates of contemplation.
The three luminaries do not fall into disorder; they converge upon the four propositions of form and emptiness, which are never lost and fully embody their source.

The ten gates of principle and phenomena are divided yet identical within dependent origination. Discussing the ten profound portals, there are distinctions between the general and the specific, revealing the reasons for the ten stages.
Their virtuous functions differ; having exhausted principle and perfected nature, one further penetrates the fruit and encompasses the cause. Thus, regarding words and thought—

The objects of this ineffable teaching cannot be fully recorded even by brush and paper. Regarding those whose faculties are suited to the four teachings, this refers to the selection of those who are not yet vessels;

it serves to humble them so that they may resolve to seek awakening. To praise and encourage them to listen and receive the teaching, one matches the faculties against the teachings to measure whether their own strength is sufficient;
yet when matching the teachings against the faculties, from the perspective of the Buddha’s mind, there is nothing that is not [suitable].
This is why the bright orb of the moon casts no reflection upon a turbid pool, and the radiant hare-marked moon sheds its light from afar to shine upon murky waters.
How could the crest-jewel of a Wheel-Turning King be bestowed upon an unmeritorious subject?

Or how could the pearl in the garment of a kinsman be secretly given to a guest who lies drunk and asleep? Whether it is a matter of selection or bestowal, there is indeed a profound reason for this. The essence of the five teachings is shallow.

Regarding "profound": the *Abhidharmakośa* and *Vibhāṣā* differ in that they treat the subject and object either singly or in pairs; the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* differ in that they distinguish between essence and function, or emergence and disappearance.
Alternatively, [the latter] may comprehensively encompass the signified meaning, further incorporating ten meanings;

or it may fully include the manifesting capacity, possessing the six sense objects. Whether viewed as original or reflected, there are both the real and the provisional regarding the counterpart; whether speaking or listening...
Yet, while fully encompassing all, it also separately accords with conditions to enter the essence of reality; it either subsumes the derivative phenomena or reveals the suchness.

These three gates of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena may exist as distinct or as identical. The perfect sound of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena is fully endowed with the ten mysteries.
The teaching-essence of the *samādhi* of the Ocean Seal is ultimately subsumed within *samādhi*. Whether shallow or deep, sequential or simultaneous—

The latter two [sections] are precisely the core tenets of this sutra; they are perfectly integrated from beginning to end. The preceding eight [sections] are none other than the substance of the teaching.

Regarding the six categories of "tenets" (*zong*) and "purports" (*qu*)—their commonality and their specific distinctions: "tenet" (*zong*) means that which is revered and held supreme, like a retainer attending upon a lord.

"Purport" (*qu*) means the underlying intent, like a child seeking to nourish its parents. "Commonality" (*tong*) refers to being generally consistent with other teachings; the masters of both *dharmatā* (nature) and *lakṣaṇa* (phenomena) largely agree on these points. "Specificity" (*ju*)...
Regarding this specific sutra, the explanations of ancient and modern masters differ entirely. When one examines how these various teachers diverge, their positions are as scattered as the stars;
yet when one looks up to the Master of the Commentary, his solitary perfection is like the full moon.
Using four phrases for a single title, it is most wondrous and profound; arranging ten gates according to each phrase, it is inconceivable and beyond debate. These seven categories...
"Volumes" refers to the fascicles of a collection; they may be abbreviated versions or complete ones. "Categories" refers to their types; they may be similar or distinct lineages.
"Chapters" (pǐn) refers to differing titles; "assemblies" (huì) refers to different Dharma assemblies.
The ultimate discourse in eighty fascicles was translated by Nandā; the wondrous exposition in one hundred thousand verses was transmitted by Nāgārjuna.
The middle and superior versions were not received by the people of Jambudvīpa; they remained hidden within the dragon palaces.

As for the *Puyan* (Universal Eye) Sūtra alone, only the Bodhisattva Samantadṛṣṭi can know it. Even if one were to exhaust the ink of the oceans, its recitation would equal the number of atoms in all similar lands, making it impossible to compile as a single collection.
If expressed differently, it encompasses worlds of diverse categories, such that the number of its divisions is immeasurable. Its Master—
The companions chant together in successive layers; the retinues converse separately in every place.

As for "perfection," sometimes a single instance encompasses the whole, free from obstruction or hindrance; or sometimes many elements mutually include one another, transcending both words and thought.
The commentaries on the sutras by Vasubandhu and Nāgārjuna are fully preserved in the Western Regions (India); the treatises composed by Lingbian and Sengqian flourish in the East.

Regarding the eight translations of the *Gantong* (Miraculous Responses) during the Xia dynasty: first, the transmission of the translations was continuous, ensuring that those who studied them would have no doubts;

subsequently, the manifestations of spiritual resonance accumulated over time, causing all who saw or heard of them to look up with reverent faith. Although spanning successive dynasties, there were only two such translators.
Together with these supplementary works, there are now only four scriptures. Each has been honored by imperial edicts and incorporated into the Precious Canon.
Whether translated or transcribed, auspicious signs have become increasingly frequent; whether read and recited or expounded and transmitted, portents are too numerous to record.

(Xian Yan) first studied the Three Transformations of Consciousness in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, yet could not fathom its source; next he perused the Ten Causes in the *Avataṃsaka*, but found no [end].
I have exhausted my efforts to fathom its profundity; yet as I wave the fly-whisk and pass on the lamp, I am deeply ashamed of my superficial reception and reckless understanding.

As I take up the brush and pen to record these words, I fear that my scattered and vulgar compositions are unfit for such sacred texts. Nevertheless, at the request of my disciples—who, during the previous summer, continued to open the Dharma assembly and, by the early autumn, submitted a formal petition stating:

"We, the five hundred students including Man-gui and others, have long admired the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong). However, we are currently unable to distinguish between the differences in the interpretations of principle and phenomena, nor can we discern whether the Buddha and sentient beings are identical or distinct."* *(Note: The original text contains lacunae indicated by square brackets. The reconstructed meaning reflects the standard concerns of Huayan scholasticism regarding the relationship between *li* and *shi*, and the identity of the Buddha and sentient beings.)*

Blinded by the law of cause and effect, one fails to perceive retribution; deluded regarding defilement and purity, one errs in severance and realization. Within the scope of this profound discourse, and amidst the opening and closing of its thematic gates, I have briefly compiled these notes as a perpetual commentary on the meaning.

Though I am weary and lack leisure due to my humble diligence, I rely upon the hidden assistance of the multitude of sages to present this modest work. Should even a single phrase herein accord with reason, it would serve its purpose.
I only pray that you will probe the profound depths. Should there be any great principles that conflict with the sages, I truly hope only for your correction.
The verse of dedication says:
Having obtained the power of secret empowerment, I have compiled this text of definitive discernment; May it universally permeate all classes of sentient beings.
The Sixth (Final) Volume of the *Tanxuan jueze* (Discernment of the Profound Mysteries) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Great Vaipulya Scripture on the Universal Entry into the Gates of Liberation.
